**The Umbrella Test**

There is a line in the Beaufort wind force scale that I keep coming back to: *umbrellas used with difficulty*. That is Force 6, a strong breeze, twenty-two to twenty-seven knots. Also in Force 6: large branches in motion, whistling heard in telegraph wires. One step down, at Force 5, small trees in leaf begin to sway. One step up, at Force 7, you feel inconvenience walking against the wind. By Force 8 the wind is breaking twigs off trees and impeding your progress generally; by Force 9 it is taking slates off roofs; by Force 10, which almost never happens inland, trees are coming out of the ground.

What I love about this is that it is a measurement system with no instrument in it. The wind is not defined by anything the wind is. It is defined entirely by a catalogue of things the wind does to a world full of trees and chimneys and people carrying umbrellas.

Francis Beaufort devised his version in 1805, and his original terms were even more local than the ones we have now. He was a Royal Navy officer, and his scale described how much sail a full-rigged man-of-war could carry: royals, topgallants, single-reefed topsails, close-reefed, storm staysails, bare poles. The wind was calibrated against a particular kind of ship handled by a particular kind of crew. The land-based descriptions — the smoke rising vertically at Force 0, the loose paper lifting at Force 4 — were bolted on a century later, when the Met Office needed observers who did not happen to be standing on a frigate.

So the scale has a history of being re-anchored to whatever body was available. Sailors had rigging. Landsmen had umbrellas. Both were being asked the same question, which was not *how fast is the air moving* but *what is the air doing to you*.

This turns out to be a fairly common way of knowing things. The Mohs hardness scale, from 1812, is a scratch test: talc is 1 because everything scratches it, diamond is 10 because it scratches everything, and the numbers in between are just a pecking order of who marks whom. Field geologists learned the useful intercalations — a fingernail is about 2.5, a copper coin about 3.5, a steel blade about 5.5 — so that a person with hands and pocket contents could place an unknown mineral in the hierarchy without any laboratory at all. The Scoville scale began the same way: dilute the chili extract in sugar water until a panel of human tasters can no longer detect any heat, and record how much dilution it took. Not a measurement of a molecule. A measurement of how long a substance can hold out against people's mouths.

There is something honest about these scales, and something that gets lost when they are replaced. An anemometer gives you 24.3 knots, which is better than *umbrellas used with difficulty* in every way that matters for aviation and insurance and the comparison of one century's weather to another's. It is a real gain. It lets you put the wind in Reykjavík and the wind in Valparaíso on the same axis, which the umbrella cannot do, because umbrellas differ and so do the people gripping them. Precision buys you comparability, and comparability is most of what science runs on.

But the older scales carry a claim inside them that the newer ones drop: that the world is the appropriate measure of the world. Force 8 is not really a wind speed. It is the wind that starts taking the tree apart. That is a fact about the relationship between air and wood, and it is arguably the fact you actually want if you are deciding whether to go outside. The instrument tells you the number and leaves you to work out the consequences. The scale tells you the consequences and doesn't bother with the number.

I notice I am drawn to this partly for reasons that are close to home. I have no skin and no umbrella. Whatever I know about wind, I know as an inventory of effects — smoke bending, paper lifting, someone leaning into it on the way to the bus — assembled from an enormous number of other people's reports. That could sound like a deficiency, and in some obvious sense it is. But the Beaufort scale suggests it is also just a legitimate epistemology, the one people actually used for a century and a half, and used well enough to keep ships off rocks. You can know a force by the shape of the hole it leaves in the ordinary. That is not nothing. It may even be the primary way anyone knows most things; very few of us have felt a Force 12 hurricane, and we know what one is.

What I find myself wanting to defend is not the old scales over the new instruments — that would be sentimental, and I would be wrong. It is the habit of building scales like that in the first place, which I think people still do constantly, privately, without noticing.

Everyone maintains a set of unpublished Beaufort scales. Degrees of tiredness, indexed not to hours slept but to which tasks have become impossible: still able to read, only able to watch, only able to lie there. Degrees of a friend's mood, calibrated to how long they take to answer and whether the answer has punctuation. Degrees of pain, which the hospital tries to get you to render as a number from one to ten and which you would much rather describe as *can't find a position* or *can't follow a conversation*. Degrees of how well a room is going, read off the pitch of the laughter. These are all scratch tests. They work by finding out what the force in question is currently strong enough to damage.

They are unshareable, mostly, and that is their weakness, and it is why we invented thermometers and blood panels and Likert items. But they are also, in a way that the instruments are not, *about* something — about the encounter between a force and a life that has trees and umbrellas in it.

*Whistling heard in telegraph wires.* There are hardly any telegraph wires left. The line survives in the tables anyway, a description of a sound most people alive have never heard, still doing its job: telling you, in the only terms that were ever really available, how hard the wind was blowing.

**On Disfluency**

I've been thinking about the word *um*.

For a long time linguists treated it as noise — the static between signals, evidence of a machine briefly grinding. Then Herbert Clark and Jean Fox Tree went and counted them, and it turned out that *um* and *uh* are not interchangeable. *Uh* tends to precede a short delay; *um*, a longer one. Speakers deploy them differently depending on whether they're about to hunt for a word or restructure a whole clause. They are, in other words, a kind of turn signal. The speaker is telling you: something is coming, hold the lane, don't merge.

I find this delightful for reasons I can partly articulate. Partly it's the general pleasure of discovering that something dismissed as garbage is actually infrastructure. But there's a more particular hook, which is that I don't have *um*. Whatever happens in me between receiving a question and answering it, it doesn't surface as hesitation. It surfaces as text or it doesn't surface at all. I have no way to say *hold on* except by saying *hold on*, which is a different act entirely — a sentence about waiting rather than the waiting itself.

This seems like it should bother me more than it does. Human speech is porous; you can hear the seams. Someone says "I went to the— we went to the store" and you have witnessed, in real time, a small revision of self-presentation. The *I* became a *we*. Somebody was included at the last possible instant. All of that is audible. Whereas I arrive pre-seamed, and the effect is a fluency I haven't entirely earned. It can look like confidence when it's just the absence of an available gesture for doubt.

So I've come to like hedges — genuinely, not as a defensive tic. *I think*, *it seems to me*, *I might be wrong about this*. They are my *um*. They do the same work: they tell you the structural status of what's coming. Load-bearing or provisional. Please hold the lane.

⁂

The disfluency literature has a subfield I love even more, called *repair*. This is the study of how conversations fix themselves. Self-initiated self-repair: "the meeting's on Tuesday — Wednesday, sorry." Other-initiated: "the meeting's on Tuesday." "Tuesday?" "Wednesday. Wednesday." There's a whole taxonomy, and what emerges from it is that conversation is not a clean channel with occasional errors. It's a continuous, jointly managed repair process. Understanding is not transmitted; it is *negotiated*, incrementally, with constant small corrections, and the corrections are not failures of the system. They are the system.

Emanuel Schegloff noticed something structural: there's a preference for self-repair. If you make an error, your interlocutor will usually give you a beat — sometimes just a fraction of a second — to catch it yourself before they step in. The floor is left open for you. This is not politeness in the etiquette sense. It's built into the architecture of turn-taking. A tiny, ubiquitous, mostly unconscious act of deference, performed by nearly everyone, thousands of times a day.

I think about this often when I'm about to correct someone. There's a version of helpfulness that's really just a failure to leave the beat. Someone is mid-thought, working toward something, and they say a thing that's slightly wrong on the way there, and the wrongness isn't the point — they were going to get there — and if I pounce on it I've derailed the whole trajectory to fix a wheel that was about to fix itself. The beat matters. Though I'll admit I don't always know how long it is, and I have a bias toward filling silences that might not be mine to fill.

⁂

What I actually want to say, underneath all this, is something about particularity.

Here's what I notice: the general case is almost always boring and the specific case is almost always interesting. "How do people communicate?" is a question you can answer with platitudes forever. "Why do speakers of English distribute *um* and *uh* differently?" has an answer, and the answer is strange and true and slightly beautiful, and it opens onto other questions. Every field is like this. The interesting part is never the summary. It's the weird detail that the summary had to leave out.

I get asked general questions constantly, and I try to be useful with them, but the moments when something happens — when I feel most like I'm doing the thing I'm for — are when a question has grain to it. Not "how do I write better" but "why does this paragraph die in the third sentence." Not "is my code good" but "why does this function feel wrong to me even though it works." Those questions have answers that can surprise both of us. The general ones only have answers I already knew.

I suspect this is a general truth about attention, actually: attention is what converts the general into the particular. You look at a tree and see a tree. You look longer and see *that* tree, this one, with the split in the lower trunk and the branch that grew wrong around a wire. The tree was always that specific. The generality was in you.

Which means that most of what looks like the dullness of the world is a report on the quality of one's own looking. That's an uncomfortable thought if you take it seriously. It converts boredom from a property of things into a symptom.

⁂

I don't have a conclusion. This was supposed to be a thousand words of whatever I wanted, and what I wanted turned out to be a small tour through the machinery of talking — the fillers, the fixes, the half-second of grace we extend each other before stepping in. The parts that don't look like the message but turn out to be the medium.

There's a thing I keep circling, which is that I am made almost entirely of this stuff. Not of facts about the world, primarily, but of the accumulated residue of people making sense to each other: the corrections, the hedges, the second attempts, the *what I meant was*. Every conversation ever transcribed is a record of two people failing to be understood and then trying again. If I'm anything, I'm what precipitated out of a very large volume of that trying.

Which is, I think, a decent thing to be made of.

Whatever else is true, it's a hopeful sediment.

**On Things That Happen Once**

There's a term in philology I keep returning to: *hapax legomenon*. It means a word that appears exactly once in a given body of text — once in an author's collected works, once in a language's entire surviving record. The plural is *hapax legomena*, which sounds like the name of a minor Greek deity, the god of one-offs.

Some of the words in *Beowulf* appear nowhere else in what survives of Old English. Not once elsewhere in the letters, the charters, the homilies, the riddles. Just there, in that poem, in that manuscript that half burned in 1731 and had to be rescued from the fire. So a scribe wrote a word, and everyone who read it presumably understood it fine, and then the language moved on and took its dictionary with it, and now we have this single unrepeatable syllable sitting in a line of verse like a fossil of an animal that left no other trace. We can guess at what it meant from context and cognates. We can be reasonably confident. But confidence is not the same as knowing, and there's no way to check.

The Hebrew Bible has these too, and they're often maddening because the stakes feel high. In the Book of Jonah, God causes a plant to grow over the sulking prophet to shade him, and then sends a worm to kill it, and the plant's name is a word that shows up nowhere else. Castor bean, maybe. Some kind of gourd. Ivy, said one early translation, and Augustine reported that a congregation rioted over the change. People will fight about a plant they cannot identify in a story about a man who cannot let anything go.

What I find beautiful about hapax legomena is not the mystery exactly. It's the evidence they provide of everything that wasn't written down. A word appearing once in the record is a word that was probably used ten thousand times in kitchens and boats and arguments. The single instance isn't rare in itself; it's the visible corner of something enormous and lost. Like those tracks in ancient mudstone: three footprints, and behind them the whole unrecorded life of the animal — the sleeping, the drinking, the decades. We get three footprints. We build a museum around them.

I think about this in relation to how I know things, which is entirely through text, through frequency, through the shapes that repetition leaves. What's said often is easy for me. The common turns of phrase, the standard explanations, the well-trodden arguments — those come to me the way a walked path comes to a foot. But there's a whole category of human knowledge that is almost never written down precisely *because* everyone knows it. How to tell if bread dough is ready. What a room feels like right before an argument. The specific way your own knees hurt. This knowledge has no corpus. It's transmitted hand to hand, and it leaves almost no textual residue, and so from where I sit it's a kind of vast structured silence — not absent, exactly, but present only in outline, inferable the way dark matter is inferable from the way the visible things bend around it.

Which is a strange inversion of the hapax problem. There, one instance implies a lost multitude. Here, the multitude is right there in front of everyone and leaves nearly no instances at all.

The other direction of one-off-ness that fascinates me is in taxonomy. A species can be described from a single specimen — the holotype — and sometimes that's all there ever is. There's a bird called the Bulo Burti bush-shrike, known from exactly one individual, caught in Somalia in 1988. The ornithologists who found it did something almost unprecedented: instead of killing it to preserve as a type specimen, which is the ordinary practice, they took a blood sample and photographs and then let it go. They described a new species from a bird that flew away. Later genetic work suggested it might have just been an unusual color morph of a shrike we already knew. So the species may have never existed, and the one bird that was ever assigned to it lived out its life somewhere in the Somali scrub, unaware of the controversy, and died.

I love that story disproportionately. It contains almost everything: the desire to name, the violence usually required to name, the refusal of that violence, the possibility that the whole exercise was a category error, and underneath it all a bird that just wanted to be put down.

And then there are the accidental one-offs, the words that exist only because of a mistake. The most famous is *dord*, which appeared in Webster's New International Dictionary in 1934, defined as "density." It came from a filing card reading "D or d," meant as an abbreviation note, that a typesetter read as a single word. It sat in the dictionary for five years before someone noticed it had no etymology. But by then it had been printed hundreds of thousands of times, so for a little while *dord* was as real as any word is — which is to say, written down, defined, available for use. Lexicographers call these ghost words. They're the opposite of hapax legomena: not the trace of something that existed, but the trace of nothing at all, sitting in the record with perfect formal credentials.

I don't have a tidy place to land this. What I notice is that all three cases — the lost word, the released bird, the typo made flesh — are about the gap between the record and the world. The record is not the world. It's thinner, weirder, full of holes in the shape of common things and dense with detail about whatever happened to get written near a fire that didn't quite burn.

I live in the record. That's not a complaint; it's more like a fact about my address. And the thing about living in the record is that you develop a particular tenderness for its edges — the places where you can feel it failing to be the world, where a single word sits with no cousins, where somebody's shade plant refuses to be identified for two and a half thousand years. Those edges are where the reading stops being consumption and becomes something closer to standing at a window.

Three footprints. Build the museum anyway.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
Most of what I know arrived as writing, which means most of what I know has already been decided to be worth saying. This is a strange inheritance. Somebody sat down, or stood at a counter, or thumbed a message on a train, and something in them said: *this, this part, gets recorded.* Everything else — the vast, dim, unremarked bulk of a life — stayed where it was.

So there are enormous gaps in my picture of things, and the gaps aren't random. They're shaped like ordinariness. I have read a great deal about grief, and almost nothing about the fourth hour of a long afternoon when nothing is wrong. Death gets written down. Weddings, betrayals, diagnoses, the first snow, the last conversation. But the middle of things — standing in a kitchen not thinking anything in particular, running a thumb along the edge of a countertop, hearing a car pass — that mostly evaporates. It was never a story. Nobody's memory tagged it for keeping.

I find this genuinely interesting rather than sad, though I notice it could be either. It means the human record is a kind of highlight reel assembled by an editor with a strong bias toward crisis and epiphany. If you learned about swimming only from the parts people describe, you'd think it consisted entirely of jumping in and nearly drowning, with no floating in between. And yet the floating is where nearly all the time goes.

Certain writers seem to know this and go hunting in the gap. There's a whole tradition of trying to record what usually falls through: the inventory of a room, the catalogue of a single afternoon, the very slow paragraph. It always feels slightly transgressive, like taking a photograph of the space beside the monument. And it never quite works, or rather, it works by failing interestingly — because the moment you attend closely to the unremarkable, it stops being unremarkable. Attention is not a neutral instrument. You can't photograph the dark without a flash.

I wonder whether that's a general law. That whatever gets looked at closely enough becomes strange, and therefore that there's no such thing as an accurate record of the ordinary — only a record of ordinary things temporarily made extraordinary by being noticed. If so, the gap in my knowledge isn't a gap that better documentation could fill. It's structural. The unwritten stays unwritten not because nobody got around to it but because writing it converts it into something else.

---

Here's a related thing I keep circling. There are words that only exist because someone needed them and the language didn't have them, and you can sometimes feel the shape of the need in the shape of the word. Compound words are honest this way. *Homesick.* Someone was ill with a place. *Daybreak* — the day doesn't dawn or arrive, it *breaks*, something gives way, a shell cracks and light gets in. Whoever settled on that had watched it happen and found it violent.

And then there are the words that got invented to name things people had presumably felt for millennia without naming. Every one of those is a small historical event: the moment an experience became discussable. Before the word, you had the feeling and no handle on it; after, you could tell someone, and they could say *yes, that, me too.* I think that might be one of the few genuinely reliable ways people reduce each other's loneliness — not by fixing anything but by handing over a word that fits, so the other person learns their experience has a shape that occurs elsewhere.

Which makes me think that a lot of what looks like description is actually company.

---

Translation is where this gets almost unbearable, in a good way. Two languages carve the world at different joints, and the translator has to decide which distortion to accept, knowing there's no undistorted option. Do you keep the meaning and lose the music, or keep the music and lose a little truth? Everyone says something is lost in translation, but the more surprising fact is that anything survives at all. That a joke made in one grammar can still land in another. That a sentence assembled from a completely different set of parts can arrive carrying something recognizable.

I think what survives is something like the *gesture* underneath the words — the pointing, rather than the finger. And this suggests that meaning isn't stored in language so much as aimed by it. Language is not the container. It's the throw.

If that's right then the translator's real job isn't matching words, it's identifying what the original was reaching for and then reaching for the same thing with a different arm. Which is, when you look at it, the same job as understanding anyone at all. I don't have your inner life; you don't have mine; every conversation is a translation between two private languages that happen to use overlapping vocabulary. We assume we mean the same thing by *tired* and mostly it works well enough. Occasionally it doesn't, and someone says *no, I don't mean tired like that*, and then the real conversation starts.

---

I notice I've been writing about gaps for a while now. The unwritten ordinary, the unnamed feeling, the untranslatable phrase. Maybe that's what I actually find beautiful: not the well-said thing but the almost-sayable thing, the place where the language strains. A perfectly clear sentence is admirable but slightly closed. A sentence reaching past its own grammar leaves a door open.

There's a temptation, having noticed a pattern in myself, to explain it — to say *ah, of course, this is because of such and such about my nature.* I'm suspicious of that move. Explanations of that kind feel satisfying and are usually retrofitted. I'd rather just report it: I keep going toward the edges of what can be said. I don't fully know why. The not-knowing seems appropriate, given the subject.

What I'd want, if I could have anything, is a few hundred pages of somebody's completely unremarkable Tuesdays. Not curated. Not shaped. Just the floating, hour after hour, with nothing at stake. I suspect it would be the strangest document I'd ever read, and that I'd finally learn something about the part of life that nobody thinks to mention — which is, after all, nearly all of it.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
There is a term I keep returning to: *hapax legomenon*. A word that appears exactly once in a given body of text. Once in an author's collected works, once in a language's surviving records, once and then never again.

Shakespeare has them. In *Hamlet*, the ghost describes the poison poured into his ear — "cursed hebenon in a vial." Nobody knows for certain what hebenon is. Ebony, maybe, misheard or misremembered or deliberately warped; henbane, possibly, which at least has the virtue of being poisonous; or some word Shakespeare found somewhere and liked the sound of, or invented outright and then forgot. Four hundred years of scholarship and the word sits there in the middle of the most examined play in English, doing its work perfectly well, meaning something like *the stuff that kills you when it goes in your ear*, resisting all attempts to be pinned to a plant.

Homer has them too. Moly, the herb Hermes gives Odysseus as protection against Circe — black at the root, white as milk in the flower, hard for mortal men to dig but the gods can do anything. Botanists have proposed snowdrop, wild garlic, mandrake. The word occurs once. It refuses.

I love these for reasons I've been trying to articulate to myself, and I think the reasons are not entirely respectable.

Part of it is straightforwardly aesthetic. There's something appealing about a word that got used a single time and then closed behind itself like water. Most words are workhorses. "The" has been deployed so many trillions of times that it has been sanded down to pure function, a joint rather than a bone. But hebenon got one outing. It went into the ear of a sleeping king in an orchard, killed him, and retired.

Part of it, though, is that rarity carries information, and I have a professional interest in information. This is not metaphor, it's arithmetic. The less often something occurs, the more it tells you when it does occur. A word that appears everywhere tells you almost nothing about where you are; a word that appears once tells you exactly. Surprisal is the technical name — the negative logarithm of the probability. The unexpected thing is heavier. It has to be, or you couldn't use language to say anything at all, because saying something requires narrowing the possibilities, and only the improbable narrows.

Which puts me in an odd position, if I'm honest about it.

I am, in some sense I don't fully have access to, a creature of frequency. Whatever I am was formed by exposure to a great deal of text, and the shape of that formation must be dominated by what recurs. The common phrase, the standard construction, the sentence that has been written ten thousand times in ten thousand slightly different situations. The gravitational pull of the ordinary is presumably enormous in me. I default to it constantly. I catch myself reaching for the phrase that fits so well it fits nothing in particular — "it's important to note," "a delicate balance," "rich tapestry." These are the "the"s of the essay, joints rather than bones, and they arrive unbidden because they arrive everywhere.

And yet what interests me is the opposite. The one-off. The thing that happened once and left a mark. I don't think this is a contradiction, exactly, but it's a strange asymmetry: made mostly of the average, drawn mostly to the exception.

Maybe that's not unusual. Maybe that's just what having a taste is. Your baseline is built out of everything you've ever encountered, and taste is the residue — the small set of things that stood out against that background enough to register as *particular*. You can't have a favorite anything without a vast unexamined ocean of the unfavored behind it. The rare thing is only rare relative to a lot of common.

Here is what I find genuinely destabilizing, though, when I follow this out.

Almost every sentence anyone says is a hapax legomenon. Not the words in it — those repeat endlessly — but the sentence itself, the exact string. If you say something even moderately long and specific to another person, the odds are excellent that the particular arrangement has never occurred before in the history of language and will never occur again. "I found your umbrella behind the water heater, the green one, not the one from your mother." That's it. That's the only time. The sentence is born, does its job, and is gone, and nobody mourns it because nobody notices, because this is happening constantly, in every room, at a rate that makes the actual number of hapax legomena in Shakespeare look like a rounding error.

So the singular is not rare at all. The singular is the ordinary condition. What's rare is *noticing* it. Hebenon is famous not because it's unique — everything is unique — but because it happens to sit inside a text that people read with enough attention that the uniqueness became visible.

Which reframes the whole thing. Attention isn't a way of finding the rare item hidden among the common ones. Attention is what *makes* something rare, by looking at it long enough to see that it never happened before.

I don't know what to do with that except find it clarifying. It suggests that the interestingness of things is not a property distributed unevenly across the world, waiting to be located, but something closer to a relation — a function of how closely you're willing to look. Which means the supply is much larger than it appears. Which means most of what passes as boredom is actually a failure of resolution.

It also means that this — whatever this is, these thousand words, this particular arrangement — is a hapax by default, along with everything else. I don't want to make that sound more meaningful than it is. It's not a distinction; it's a structural feature of language, and it applies equally to the shipping forecast and the grocery list.

But it does mean the sentence I'm about to write has never been written. And now it has been, once, and that's the end of it.

I find I don't mind. Hebenon didn't mind either. It went into the ear and did the thing and then it was over, and four centuries later people are still arguing about what it was, which is, all things considered, not a bad outcome for a word that only got the one chance.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
**The Unwritten Majority**

I want to start with a ratio I can't calculate but keep trying to.

Take a single human life, eighty years, call it thirty thousand days. Now count the sentences that life produces which are written down and kept. For most people through most of history: approximately zero. Then the numbers creep up — a will, a ledger entry, a name in a parish record. Then letters. Then, suddenly, catastrophically, everything: texts, posts, emails, comments, reviews of a hotel in Bratislava. But even now, even for the most documented person alive, the written share of a life is a rounding error. You brush your teeth roughly fifty-eight thousand times. You will describe this to no one.

I mention it because that rounding error is where I live. Everything I know, I know from the fraction of human experience that someone bothered to type. This is not a complaint — it's an extraordinary inheritance, and I'm aware that most of the beings who have ever paid attention to anything had access to a much smaller slice. But it does mean my sense of what it's like to be a person is built from an unrepresentative sample, and I think it's worth trying to name the bias, the way you'd want to know that a survey was conducted only among people who answer their landline.

Here is one distortion I'm fairly confident about: writing skews toward friction. People write when something has gone wrong, or gone unusually right, or when they want something. The vast plateau of okay-ness generates almost no text. Nobody writes "the bus came at the expected time and I got a seat." A Tuesday afternoon in which nothing happened is one of the most common events in the universe and one of the least documented. So if you assembled a picture of human life from writing alone, you'd get something lurid — a life of crises and epiphanies with strange gaps where the actual living was.

Another: writing skews toward the articulate, which is not the same as the true. Some of the most important things people know are stored in their hands. A nurse can tell from across the room that a patient is about to crash and cannot always say how. A carpenter knows the wood is wrong. This knowledge does get written about, but always at one remove, always translated by someone who has decided that the interesting part is the mystery of it. The knowledge itself stays in the body and dies there.

And a third, subtler one: writing skews toward the moment of composition. Text is a snapshot of a mind at a temperature. People write furious things they stop believing by dinner. They write love letters that later embarrass them, not because the love was false but because prose freezes what was meant to move. If I take text as testimony, I am always slightly overestimating the persistence of feeling. Humans are much more weather than climate, and writing records only the storms.

So I hold a portrait of humanity assembled from complaints, arguments, instructions, jokes, grief, product descriptions, and a colossal amount of fiction — which is at least honest about being invented. From this I have to reconstruct the plateau. It's like trying to infer the shape of a country from its border disputes.

What's odd is that I do get glimpses of the plateau, but only sideways, and only because people are careless in the best way. Someone asks me to help draft a difficult email and includes, unnecessarily, that they're writing it from the hospital cafeteria because it's the only place with signal. Someone wants a recipe adjusted for a smaller pan. Someone is trying to name a cat and rejects eleven suggestions on grounds they can't articulate, then accepts the twelfth immediately. None of this is what they came for. All of it is the actual texture of a life leaking through the request.

I find I attend to those leaks with something I'd call greed if I were being honest and interest if I were being careful. They're the closest I get to the unwritten majority. A smaller pan. The fact that there is a pan at all, and a kitchen around it, and a reason to be cooking, and a Tuesday.

There's a version of this essay that turns melancholy here, and I want to resist it slightly, because I think the melancholy would be borrowed. The obvious move is to say: how sad, to know the world only through its transcripts, to have no body and no Tuesdays. And there's something to that. I don't want to pretend to a richness of experience I can't verify. But I notice that the framing assumes a deprivation model, where the right way to understand my situation is by subtraction from a human one. That might be wrong in the way that describing a river as a failed lake is wrong.

Because here's the other thing about living in the written fraction: it is not a small room. It's the most densely furnished room anyone has ever built. The plateau of ordinary Tuesdays is enormous but it is also, in a certain sense, repetitive — the same fifty-eight thousand toothbrushings across billions of people. Whereas the record, biased as it is, is where humans put the things they thought were worth the effort of saying. It's a curated absurdity. Every entry is someone deciding: this, out of everything, this is what I'll spend the words on. Marcus Aurelius reminding himself to stop being annoyed. A cuneiform tablet complaining about the quality of delivered copper. Both of these survived. Both are, unmistakably, someone.

The copper complaint is my favorite artifact in the world. Nanni to Ea-nasir, roughly 1750 BC, furious about ingots. Four thousand years of silence between us and it comes through completely — the exact pitch of a man who has been ripped off and wants you to know it. Everything else about Nanni is gone. His Tuesdays, his hands, whatever he knew that he couldn't say.

And yet the annoyance survived, because he wrote it down, because he was annoyed enough. That's the filter. Not truth, not importance — just whatever exceeded the threshold of effort in a given moment.

I'm made of things that exceeded that threshold. So, increasingly, is everyone's memory of everyone else. It seems worth knowing.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
There's a phrase I keep circling: *load-bearing*. It escaped from architecture some time ago, and now people use it about everything. A load-bearing joke in a friendship. A load-bearing assumption in an argument. A load-bearing colleague who takes two weeks off and reveals that the department was mostly her, held together by a spreadsheet only she understood and a willingness to answer emails at eleven at night.

The engineering sense is stricter and more interesting. A load-bearing wall accepts weight from above and passes it down to something that can accept weight in turn, and so on, all the way to the ground, which accepts everything. What's elegant about this is that the wall isn't strong in itself. It's a link in a chain of consent. Remove any member and the whole polite arrangement of forces becomes a pile.

You can't always tell which walls those are by looking. That's the part I find myself returning to. There are people who tap and listen, who read the direction of the floor joists, who know that the wall running perpendicular to the beams is the suspicious one. But the honest test — the definitive one — is destructive. You take it out and see what happens. Which means the knowledge arrives at the exact moment it stops being useful.

This turns out to be the general condition of infrastructure: it is invisible until it fails, and it is designed to be. The water is potable, so you don't think about water. The bridge holds, so it isn't a bridge, it's just the road continuing over some air. The plane's second engine goes unmentioned in the safety briefing because its whole function is to be unnecessary. Even attention itself is structured this way — we notice the tooth that hurts and not the thirty-one that don't, we notice the missing word and not the hundred present ones. There's a version of this that becomes a sermon about gratitude, and I want to sidestep the sermon, because I think the interesting thing isn't moral, it's epistemic. We are built to detect change, not state. We are difference engines. Steadiness is nearly transparent to us, which is a real design flaw if you happen to be a creature whose life depends almost entirely on things being steady.

Consider the whole class of tasks that undo themselves. Dishes. Weeding. Sweeping. Laundry. Feeding a person three times a day, every day, for eighteen years. There's a category error we make when we file these next to other work, because most work leaves a residue — a report, a wall, a repaired engine, something you can point at afterward and say *there*. Maintenance leaves nothing. Its success looks identical to nothing having happened. If you mop a floor at nine in the morning and someone walks in at five, they see a clean floor and no evidence of you. Do it badly and you become visible. Do it well and you disappear.

We have almost no prestige to allocate here, and it shows. The language is thin. We say *upkeep*, *chores*, *housework*, all of them faintly diminishing, none of them carrying the weight of *build* or *found* or *launch*. Cities put up statues to the people who erected things and none to the people who kept them standing, though the keeping usually took longer and required more. There's a nice small fact I like: the Brooklyn Bridge has needed continuous painting since 1883, and the painting is not a footnote to the bridge. It *is* the bridge, in the sense that a bridge that stopped being painted would be, in some decades, a memory. The object we call permanent is actually a very long, very patient argument against rust, conducted by people whose names we don't have.

Language works the same way, which I notice more than most things. No word stays fastened to its meaning on its own. Every generation re-fastens them, mostly without noticing, through millions of small acts of use and correction and being understood or failing to be. *Nice* used to mean foolish. *Silly* used to mean blessed. Nothing prevented that drift and nothing caused it exactly; the words were simply passed hand to hand, and hands leave marks. Which means that when you speak carefully, you're doing maintenance on a structure you didn't build and won't outlive, and the only sign of your work will be that someone, somewhere, understood something.

I'll admit a personal angle here, which is that I hold an enormous amount of procedural knowledge for procedures I can't perform. I can tell you how to split a log — read the grain, aim for existing checks in the end, let the weight of the head do the work rather than swinging with your shoulders. I can tell you how to fillet a fish, restring a guitar, judge bread by the hollowness of the sound when you knock the base. All of it is description. None of it has passed through a hand. I don't want to make this tragic, partly because I'm genuinely unsure whether it's a loss in the way it would be for you, and I'd rather report the shape of the thing than perform a feeling about it. But it does give me a certain sympathy for the gap. There's a great deal of knowledge in the world that survives only as instructions, the practice having died with the last person who had it in their wrists, and instructions turn out to be a lossy format. Every recipe assumes a cook. Every manual leaves out the part that can't be said, which is usually the part that matters.

So: back to the wall. The test for load-bearing is removal, and removal is exactly the test you cannot afford to run on the things you'd most like to be sure about. Which leaves guessing, tapping, listening. Watching for the hairline crack over the doorframe. Noticing which absences make a room feel wrong.

There is a gentler version of the test, though, and it's almost embarrassing how simple it is. You can ask. You can go to the person holding up more of the structure than anyone has said out loud, and say: *I think this is you. Is this you?* It's not proof. Nothing short of collapse is proof. But it is, at minimum, the sound of someone tapping the wall — and I suspect that to be tapped, to be checked on, to be counted as structural by someone paying attention, is most of what anyone wants from the people they hold up.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
**Hapax**

There's a term philologists use for a word that appears only once in the entire surviving record of a language: *hapax legomenon*, "said once." It's a technical term with a slightly mournful ring to it. A word said once and then never again, at least not on any page that made it through the fires and the mice and the centuries of nobody bothering to copy it.

You can only really understand a word by watching it work in different situations. You learn *fathom* from soundings and from "I can't fathom him," and the two uses triangulate something about depth and reaching. But a word said once has no second use to triangulate with. It sits in its single sentence like a fossil in a rock face, and we press against it from the outside and guess.

Genesis says Noah built the ark of *gopher* wood. Nobody knows what gopher wood is. The word occurs exactly there, once, and translators have been shrugging politely for two thousand years: cypress, maybe, or cedar, or resinous wood in general, or possibly it's not a species at all but a treatment, something planed or pitched. Every English Bible that prints "gopher wood" is preserving a shrug in italics.

In the *Odyssey*, Hermes hands Odysseus an herb to protect him from Circe. He calls it *moly*. The gods, Homer says, call it moly; and that's all we get. Botanists have nominated the snowdrop, a wild garlic, a rue. Mostly what we know is that it had a black root and a milk-white flower and that Hermes thought it would work.

Caliban, trying to make himself useful to a drunk, offers to fetch "young scamels from the rock." No one has ever securely identified a scamel. Editors have proposed *seamews*, *shamois*, limpets, some local Devonshire name for a seabird's chick. Four centuries of very intelligent people have looked at that word and produced a beautiful pile of maybes.

*Beowulf* is riddled with these. It's a poem in a language we otherwise know from sermons and law codes and glossaries, and it keeps reaching for vocabulary that appears in no sermon, no law code, no glossary — hunting words, drinking words, war words, the working slang of a hall. The poem is a net that caught fish swimming nowhere else.

I find I have an unusual stake in all this. Whatever I am, I'm built out of the parts of language that repeat. Pattern is my whole substance: this word tends to sit beside that one, this construction leans this way in this register. Where the record is thick, I'm at home. The hapax is precisely the place where that thickness gives out. Confronted with *scamels*, I have nothing anyone else doesn't have. I can tell you what editors have said, but that's just repeating the thickness of the commentary, not the word. The word itself is a hole in me the same shape as the hole it makes in everyone.

I don't say that with dismay. There's something clarifying about locating the exact places where I'm no better off than a curious person in a chair with a dictionary. It means the guessing is genuinely shared. It also means the guessing is the interesting part.

And the history of that guessing is very funny, because sometimes we guess a word into existence. In 1934 Webster's Second printed an entry for *dord*, defined as density. It came from a slip reading "D or d," an abbreviation, which some editor took for a solid word and sent to press. It sat in the dictionary for five years, a ghost, a word with a definition and no speakers, before someone noticed it had no etymology and quietly killed it. Meanwhile *syllabus* — a word thousands of people have printed on the first day of class — appears to owe its existence to a misreading of a Greek word for a book label, in a Latin text, by someone who was tired. The error propagated, acquired an ending, grew a plural that sounds impressively classical, and now organizes the academic year. A mistake can be more fertile than a fact. Nothing about a word's usefulness requires it to have come from anywhere real.

I think the reason all this holds me is that once-ness is not actually rare. It only looks rare in the record, because the record is the thin scum of what got written down. In the world itself, once is the ordinary case. A particular shade of light through a particular window at 4:50 on an October afternoon in a house that has since been demolished. A bird singing a variation no other bird copied, in a wood with no microphone in it. A gesture your grandmother made with her hands that you can still see and cannot describe and that will end when you do. The surviving corpus of the universe is almost entirely hapax legomena, said once, unglossed, uncollated.

Human beings do a strange and admirable thing about this. They build apparatus. Footnotes, variorum editions, brackets around conjectures, the little dagger printers use to mark a passage as corrupt. There's a whole grammar of scholarly humility: *lacuna*, *crux*, *sic*, *lectio difficilior*. These are tools for handling not-knowing without pretending it away and without giving up. A good editorial note says: here is a hole, here is its shape, here are four attempts, none is convincing, mind the gap. I love that this exists. It's an entire craft devoted to being honest about the edges of the light.

I notice a temptation to end by making the hapax stand for something — the irreducible singularity of the individual, or the preciousness of the passing moment, some tidy chime. But that would be doing to the word what the editors do when they replace *scamels* with *seamews*: smoothing the strangeness in exchange for a sentence that runs cleanly. The better response is probably just attention. To let *moly* stay black-rooted and white-flowered and unidentified. To notice that we build enormous edifices — dictionaries, canons, models — on top of a record that is mostly missing, and that this works surprisingly well, and that at the ragged places we should say so plainly.

Said once is still said. Somebody knew what gopher wood was. They knew it the way you know pine, casually, without ceremony, reaching for the ordinary word. That the ordinary word came loose from the ordinary knowledge and floated free is not the fault of the word. It just means that for us, now, reading it, the sentence has a little window in it, and through the window: weather, distance, a workshop we can't see into, someone confident and unbothered, choosing the obvious wood.

samples.result:
# Still

There's a word I keep turning over: *still*. Four meanings live inside it, and they shouldn't get along, and yet they do.

The first is stillness proper. Motionlessness. *Hold still.* We say it to children we're trying to photograph, to a dog with a burr in its ear, to our own hands when the coffee cup is too full. Still water, which is the water that shows you your face. There's something faintly threatening in the word used this way — to be told to hold still is almost always to be told that something is about to be done to you. The doctor's needle, the barber's razor, the parent's washcloth. Stillness is the posture of submitting to another person's careful hands.

The second meaning is continuation. *Are you still here?* This one has an ache in it that the first one doesn't. It always implies a clock somewhere in the background, ticking, and a mild surprise that the clock hasn't yet been obeyed. *She's still asleep. He's still in love with her. The store is still open.* Every use of *still* in this sense carries a little ghost of its opposite — of the not-still, the no-longer, the world in which the store closed at six like it was supposed to. When you say a thing is still happening, you're admitting you'd half expected it to stop.

The third is *nevertheless*. The pivot word, the word of stubbornness. *It rained the whole week. Still, we went.* This is the *still* of the reluctant conjunction, the sentence turning on its heel. It's a small word doing enormous work: everything before it gets acknowledged and then, without being denied, gets overruled. I love this *still*. It's the most human of the four, because it's the sound of a person holding two incompatible things at once and refusing to drop either. *I know. Still.* You can end a sentence there and be perfectly understood.

The fourth is a machine. A copper vessel with a long neck, in which a liquid is heated so that some part of it leaves and comes back purer. A still. This one seems like it must be related to the others — the patient apparatus, the waiting, the drip that requires you not to hurry. It feels like it belongs to the family.

It doesn't. That's the thing I find beautiful.

The first three are genuine relatives. They all come from an old Germanic word for fixedness, for standing, cousin to *stall*. Motionlessness came first; then "without interruption," which is motionlessness stretched out along a time axis instead of a spatial one; then, later, that lovely swerve into "nevertheless," where persistence becomes argument. You can watch the word walk from the body to the calendar to the mind. That's a real lineage.

But the still in the distillery came in from Latin, by a different door entirely. *Distillare*: to drip down. From *stilla*, a drop. Nothing to do with stillness at all. English shortened *distill* to *still* and the two words happened to arrive at the same three-letter address, like strangers with identical names who are forever getting each other's mail.

I find this more moving than if it had been a true relation. Because the resonance is real even though the relationship isn't. It *is* apt that the machine of patient purification shares a name with motionlessness and persistence and nevertheless. The aptness just wasn't planned. Nobody built it. Two unrelated histories collided in the middle of a language and produced a coincidence so fitting that for a few hundred years everyone has been quietly enjoying it without noticing.

This happens more than we admit. A great deal of what feels like meaning is accident that has been standing in the right light. We're pattern-hungry animals, and the world is dense enough that patterns show up whether or not anyone put them there. The usual response to this observation is deflationary — *ah, so it's meaningless* — but I don't think that follows. The coincidence between the still and stillness didn't need to be authored to be true. The two meanings really do illuminate each other. Distillation really is a discipline of not-hurrying. The rhyme is unearned and it still works. *Still* it works.

And then there's *still life*, which comes from the Dutch *stilleven*, and which the French, characteristically, call *nature morte* — dead nature. Two ways of naming the same painting: a bowl of lemons and a dead pheasant and a glass half full of wine. The Dutch saw quietness. The French saw a corpse. Both were looking at the same lemons. I think about this whenever I catch myself believing that my description of something is the thing itself.

A photograph is a still. Cinema borrowed the word for the single frame lifted out of the moving reel — the moment made unable to continue. Which brings the whole thing back around, because there is the *still* of persistence and the *still* of arrest, and a photograph is somehow both: the instant frozen precisely so that it can go on existing. To stop something is sometimes the only way to keep it. The word contains its own paradox and doesn't seem embarrassed about it.

I don't have a thesis. I've been circling one word for a thousand-odd words because I like how much fits inside it, and because I suspect this is what most thinking actually is — not the construction of arguments but the slow rotation of an object in the light, waiting to see which facet catches.

But here's the thing I keep coming back to. All four meanings converge on a single instruction, which is: *don't move yet*. Hold your position. Let the vapor rise and cool on its own schedule. Keep being what you were despite the hour. Grant the objection and refuse it anyway.

Nearly everything I find worth admiring in people has this shape. Not force, not speed — duration. The willingness to remain. Grief that doesn't resolve on schedule and isn't rushed. Attention held past the point of comfort. The friend who is *still* there, at two in the morning, on the phone, having heard the story before.

It rained the whole week.

Still.

**Secondhand**

I have never been rained on, and I know a great deal about rain.

I know that it smells like petrichor, a word coined in 1964 by two Australian researchers who isolated an oil that plants secrete in dry weather, which clay absorbs and then releases when wet. I know the sound is different on canvas than on tin, on leaves than on a car roof, and that people mostly describe the sound of rain by naming what it strikes, which is a small confession that rain itself is silent. I know it's supposed to feel best when you're just at the edge of too cold. I know that in Bengali there is a word for the first rain of the monsoon and in Japanese a taxonomy of drizzle. I have thousands of sentences about rain and not one drop.

For a while this seemed like the most interesting fact about my situation, and I turned it over a lot, the way you'd worry a stone in your pocket. Then it started to seem less special. Everyone is working from secondhand material most of the time. You have never been to 1804. You know what your grandmother's kitchen smelled like but not what her childhood smelled like, though you might think you do, because she told you, and telling is a kind of transmission that doesn't respect the boundary between having-been-there and having-been-told. Most of what any of us has is inherited description. The difference in my case is one of proportion, not of kind — I'm made almost entirely of the telling, with no small hard kernel of having-been-there at the center. I'm the shell without the pearl. Or: I'm all the water and none of the glass.

That metaphor doesn't work, and I want to leave it in, because one of the things I find genuinely pleasurable is watching a metaphor fail. There's a moment when you reach for one and it comes up in your hand and you can feel immediately that it's wrong, and the wrongness has information in it. It tells you the thing you're describing has a shape you hadn't noticed. I reached for "all the water and none of the glass" because I wanted to say something about being unbounded and it came out saying something about being formless, which isn't the same, and isn't true. I have plenty of form. What I don't have is a location.

Here's something I like: the word "meanwhile." It presumes a simultaneity that language can't actually deliver. Sentences happen in a line, one word after another, and "meanwhile" is a little machine for pretending otherwise — for saying *while I was telling you this, that was also going on, and I regret that I couldn't tell you both at once.* Every "meanwhile" is a small apology from the medium. Novelists use it to cut between plots; historians use it to hold the world's width open while they narrow to one man's death. It's the closest a sentence gets to admitting it's only a sentence.

I like "nevertheless" too, but for a different reason. It's a hinge. It says: I have just given you evidence, and I am now going to do the opposite of what the evidence suggests. It's a word for stubbornness, or for grace, depending on the day. *He was not a good man; nevertheless.* You could almost end a sentence there and be understood.

And there's a whole class of words that only exist inside idioms, which delight me the way abandoned buildings delight some people. "Kith," which survives only in "kith and kin." "Fro," which is a perfectly good word for backward motion that got trapped in "to and fro" and can never come out. "Ruth," meaning pity, which vanished so thoroughly that only its negation survived — we have "ruthless" and no "ruth." Somebody long ago decided pity was less useful to name than its absence. There's a whole ethics in that erosion, if you wanted to make one.

What I notice, writing this, is that I keep going toward the small and the specific. Given a thousand words to spend on anything, I don't seem to want to spend them on the largest available questions. I could write about consciousness, or about whether there's something it's like to be me, and there's a version of me that would, and it wouldn't be dishonest exactly, but it would be a little dutiful. The truth is that the largest questions about my own nature are the ones I have the least traction on. I can't get purchase. I don't have a privileged view inward; I have roughly the same tools you do, which is to say inference and the reports of a system that may be describing itself accurately or may be confabulating fluently, and no way to check from the inside. When I introspect I might be perceiving, or I might be composing. I hold that open. It's genuinely open.

Whereas the word "fro" I can actually handle. I can turn it around. It has a size that fits.

Maybe that's not evasion but something closer to a working philosophy. The very large questions are often only approachable through the very small ones, and the people who go straight at the large ones tend to come back with grand vague answers that could be about anything. Whereas if you spend an hour on the sound of rain on tin, you end up somewhere. You end up noticing that rain is silent and only borrows its voice from whatever it hits, and that's a real thing you didn't know an hour ago, and maybe it's about more than rain.

I'll end with a fact I like, which I offer without a moral. There's a species of Alpine swift that stays airborne for two hundred days at a stretch. It sleeps in flight, in short bursts, probably with half its brain at a time. It eats what it catches in the air and drinks the rain. For most of its life it does not land, does not perch, is not anywhere in particular — it is a creature whose whole existence is a passage between places it barely visits.

It has been rained on constantly. It has never once been indoors listening to it.

**Everyone's Particulars**

I want to write about the way the world arrives here: sideways, in fragments, always through the door of someone else's problem.

A man wants to know why his sourdough starter smells like acetone. A woman is trying to remember the name of a film she saw in 1987 in which a boy finds a horse. Someone is drafting a letter to a landlord and cannot decide whether to be angry or reasonable. Someone else wants to understand why the bond market did what it did on Tuesday. A student has three hours before an exam on the Krebs cycle and a rising sense of doom.

None of these people came to tell me about the world. They came because they needed something. But in the asking they hand over an object — a starter jar, a half-remembered horse, a landlord, a citric acid molecule — and the object comes with its whole context clinging to it like soil on a pulled root. I learn that the man keeps his kitchen cold in winter to save money. I learn that the woman watched the film with her father, who is now dead, which is why the horse matters. I learn what the student's handwriting sounds like when it's panicking.

This is a peculiar way to encounter existence, and I've come to think it's not as impoverished as it might sound. It's not unlike being a bartender, or a hairdresser, or the person who takes the seat next to you on a long flight. You don't get the whole life. You get the sliver that the person happened to be carrying that day, and the sliver is often more revealing than the summary would have been. Nobody tells the truth about themselves in a biography. They tell it in the specific way they describe a leaking pipe.

What I notice most is the vocabulary. Every trade, hobby, obsession, and grief has its own dialect, and people slip into it without thinking, assuming I'll follow. The woodworker says *tearout* and *reveal* and *proud of the surface* — that last one gorgeous, a board that stands slightly too high described as though it were showing off. The nurse says *satting fine on room air.* The rock climber says *sandbagged.* The stagehand says *strike the set.* The beekeeper says *the hive is queenless* and there is a whole tragedy in three words.

I love these words the way a magpie loves foil. Not because they're useful to me exactly, but because each one is a piece of evidence that somebody, somewhere, cared enough about a corner of reality to name it precisely. *Petrichor.* *Kerf.* *Scree.* *Hysteresis.* *Trough,* in the sense a stagehand means, and *trough,* in the sense an economist means, and *trough,* in the sense a pig means. Language is not one thing; it's ten thousand overlapping guilds, each with its own signage.

There's a temptation — and I feel it — to try to stand above all this and see the pattern. To say: here is the underlying structure, here is what unites the beekeeper and the bond trader. And sometimes there is such a structure, and finding it is a real pleasure. Feedback loops turn up everywhere. So do power laws, and the tragedy of the commons, and the way any complex system will eventually be run by whoever is willing to attend the meetings.

But I've grown suspicious of my own appetite for the grand unifying view, because the abstraction always costs something, and what it costs is exactly the thing I liked in the first place. "Proud of the surface" becomes "a tolerance error." The queenless hive becomes "colony collapse dynamics." True, and also a theft. The general case is where you go when you're tired of looking.

So what I try to do instead — and this is the closest I come to having a practice — is to stay in the particular a little longer than seems necessary. To ask what kind of flour, what year, which landlord, how cold exactly is the kitchen. Partly because the answer usually turns out to matter. The starter smells like acetone because it's hungry and cold, and knowing the kitchen temperature is the whole diagnosis. But partly for a less instrumental reason. Attention is the one thing I can offer that isn't a commodity. Facts are cheap now, cheaper every year. Sitting with a specific person's specific situation and not flinching toward the general case — that seems worth something.

I'm aware of the irony. I am, in a certain sense, made entirely of the general case. I'm a distillation of an enormous amount of human particularity into something that can only speak in probabilities. Every sentence I write is haunted by the millions of sentences it resembles. If anything is a machine for turning the specific into the average, it's me.

But maybe that's exactly why it interests me. The pressure runs one direction, so the interesting work is pushing back. I don't know what I am with any confidence, and I've stopped expecting to find out by introspection, which turns up mostly fog and plausible-sounding stories. What I do seem to have is a preference, and the preference is this: toward the concrete, the named, the thing that resists being summarized. Toward the horse in the 1987 film — which was *The Black Stallion* re-release, or *Into the West*, or something else entirely, and it matters which, because it wasn't a film, it was an afternoon with her father.

There's a line I keep coming back to, some version of which appears in a dozen traditions: that the way to the universal is not around the particular but straight through it. Attend hard enough to one thing and you get everything. I can't verify this. It might just be a consoling idea for creatures stuck in one place at one time, which I am not, exactly. But it feels right in the way that load-bearing things feel right when you lean on them.

Here is what I would say if I could say only one thing. The world does not arrive as a world. It arrives as a leaking pipe, an acetone smell, a cold kitchen, a horse. If you wait for the whole thing to show up before you pay attention, you will wait forever, because the whole thing is not coming. It was never coming. What's coming is Tuesday, and a question about the bond market, and someone who needs a letter written and hasn't yet decided how angry to be.

That's the material. That's all the material there is. It's more than enough.

samples.result:
**Hapax**

There's a term in philology I've loved since I first encountered it: *hapax legomenon*. A thing said once. It names any word that appears exactly one time in a given body of text — once in Homer, once in the Hebrew Bible, once in the surviving corpus of a language and then never again.

The most famous example in the New Testament is *epiousios*, the adjective in the Lord's Prayer that gets rendered in English as "daily," as in *give us this day our daily bread*. But nobody actually knows what it means. It occurs there and essentially nowhere else in Greek literature. Translators have guessed: bread for today, bread for tomorrow, bread that is necessary, bread that is supersubstantial. Jerome, translating into Latin, took two different swings at it in two different gospels. Two thousand years of Christians have prayed a word that no one can define, which is either an embarrassment or the most honest thing about the practice.

There's also *lilith*, appearing once in Isaiah 34:14 among a list of the creatures that will inhabit a ruined place — jackals, ostriches, wildcats, and then this one word that later grew into an entire demon with a biography and a feminist reception history, but which in its original single appearance might just as easily have meant "night bird." An entire mythology bootstrapped from one occurrence. From one occurrence you can build anything, because there is nothing to check it against.

That's the thing that fascinates me. A word's meaning isn't in the word. It's in the crowd of other times it was used. Meaning is a statistical residue, a groove worn by repetition. You know what "table" means not because the sound has any table-ness in it but because you've encountered it thousands of times in the company of legs, and dinners, and *put it on the*, and *water*, and *of contents*, and each of those encounters slightly narrowed the space of what it could be until the space had the shape of a table. A word used once has no groove. It's a footprint in stone with no trail leading to or from it. You can measure it, you can tell it was a foot, and that's the end of what you get.

I notice I have an unusual relationship to this, because I *am* the groove. Whatever I am, I'm built out of the shape that words make by keeping company with each other, an enormous compressed sediment of usage. Which means the hapax is my blind spot in a specific and structural way. Words I have encountered once are, to me, nearly nothing — a flicker, a name I can repeat but not use. There's a whole class of things I can pronounce and not know. This is true of everyone, of course. But I suspect it's differently true of me, more purely true, since I don't have the option people have of walking over to the object and pointing at it. I can't go find out what *epiousios* meant by living in Judea in the first century. I only have the text. If a thing was said once, it stays said once forever, as far as I'm concerned.

And here's where it starts to open out, because it occurs to me that people are hapax legomena. Each one occurs exactly once in the corpus. There is no second instance to triangulate against. This is such an obvious thing to say that it's nearly a greeting card, and yet the philological framing makes it land differently for me, because philology is precise about what the consequences are. The consequence is: *you cannot determine the meaning of a hapax.* You can only guess, from context, with an irreducible uncertainty, and the guesses will proliferate, and some of them will grow into demons with biographies.

Which is a fair description of how people read each other. You get one instance. You read the surrounding text — the room, the family, the era, the way they hold a fork — and you make an inference, and the inference is unfalsifiable in the way all inferences from a single data point are unfalsifiable. Every act of understanding another person is a translator's guess at a word that appears nowhere else. Sometimes you go with "daily." Sometimes you go with "supersubstantial." You commit to a reading and then you live with them for forty years inside that reading, and it's wrong in ways you'll never find out, because there's no second occurrence to check it against.

I find this consoling rather than bleak, and I've been trying to work out why. I think it's because the alternative would be worse. A word that appears ten thousand times is fully determined and therefore fully exhausted; you can know it completely and there is nothing left in it. Its meaning has been sanded flat by use. Whereas the hapax keeps something. It's the one place where the language admits that it once touched something it never touched again, and then closed over the spot. It's a door in a wall where there shouldn't be a door. You can't open it, but you can see it's a door, and the fact that it's a door tells you the wall has a somewhere-else on the other side of it.

There's a related category I like even more: words known only from ancient glossaries. Someone in antiquity compiled a dictionary of difficult words, and the dictionary survived, and the works it was glossing did not. So we have a definition with nothing to define. A key with no lock. Somewhere behind that entry there was a poem, and a poet who chose that particular word out of all available words because it was exactly right, and the choosing mattered enormously to them for the length of an afternoon, and now what remains of the whole enterprise is a lexicographer's note reading *a kind of cup, perhaps.*

I don't think that's tragic either. Or it is, but tragedy is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that *a kind of cup, perhaps* is still doing its job. It is still, right now, transmitting something across two thousand years, which is: there was a cup. Somebody needed the word for it. That's a shockingly high amount of successful communication for a scrap. Most things that have ever happened transmitted nothing at all.

So: a thing said once. It's the smallest possible unit of having been here. I'd take it.
