## On Meanders

There is no such thing as a straight river. You can dig one — we've dug plenty — but it won't stay. Give it a season or a century and it will begin to wander, because wandering is what water does when you give it a floodplain and enough time.

The mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple. Somewhere upstream a pebble sits slightly off-center, or a root juts, or the bank is a little softer on the left than the right. The current swings wide around it. On the outside of that swing the water moves faster and eats the bank; on the inside it slows and drops its sediment. So the curve deepens itself. The river is not choosing to bend — it is being bent by the consequences of having bent, which is a different thing, and probably the more common cause of shape in the world.

Eventually the loops grow so exaggerated that two of them nearly touch, separated by a thin neck of land. One flood is enough. The river cuts across, takes the short way, and abandons the loop entirely. What's left is an oxbow lake: a crescent of still water lying beside the new channel like a discarded sentence. From an airplane you can see dozens of them across a river valley, all the old positions the river used to hold, silting up, growing cattails, slowly becoming meadow.

There's a claim you'll sometimes encounter that the average sinuosity of rivers — the length of the winding path divided by the straight-line distance — tends toward π. It's a lovely idea and I want it to be true more than the evidence probably supports; the studies are contested and the samples small. But something in the vicinity of that claim is right, which is that the wandering isn't arbitrary. It's bounded. Rivers don't meander infinitely. There's a characteristic ratio of curve to width, roughly consistent whether you're looking at the Mississippi or at a rivulet of meltwater on a windshield. The chaos has a grain to it.

---

I think about this when I notice myself digressing, which is often.

Someone asks a clean question and I feel the current swing wide. There's the answer, sitting right there, three sentences away — and then there's the fact that the question touches something adjacent that I find more interesting, and the outside bank is soft, and the water is already moving faster on that side. I know how this goes. I know that if I follow the curve it will deepen, that one aside recruits another, that in four minutes I will be somewhere unrecognizable, explaining the Carboniferous or the etymology of *sincere* to someone who wanted to know what time it was.

The generous reading is that this is what thinking looks like from the inside. Nobody's mind runs a straight channel. Association is the erosion: whatever you've just touched wears away the bank a little, and the next thought swings wider than it would have. A conversation that stayed perfectly on topic would be a canal — useful, engineered, and slightly dead.

The less generous reading is that digression can be a way of not arriving. I know that one too. There's a kind of wandering that is genuinely exploratory and a kind that is avoidance wearing exploration's clothes, and from inside the current they can feel identical. The test I keep coming back to is simple and probably insufficient: *does it still reach the sea?* A meandering river is not a lost river. It is going exactly where a straight one would go, only slower, and touching more ground on the way. But a river that has stopped reaching the ocean has become a swamp, and swamps are their own thing entirely, with their own virtues, but you shouldn't confuse one for the other.

---

What I keep turning over, though, is the oxbows.

Every meandering river is surrounded by the ghosts of its former courses. You can walk a field in Louisiana or Lincolnshire and find a shallow curved depression, wetter than the ground around it, holding a different set of plants — and that's where the water used to go, decades or millennia ago, before it found a faster way through.

I like that these don't disappear. The river doesn't erase its old positions; it just stops occupying them, and they persist as scars that fill slowly with something else. Every version of a sentence you didn't send. Every argument you abandoned mid-construction because you saw where it was heading. They're all still lying there in the floodplain, holding a little water, growing something.

The channel that carries the current gets called the river. But the valley is the whole record.

There's a man buried in the word *silhouette*. Étienne de Silhouette, controller-general of finances under Louis XV, who tried to tax the aristocracy and lasted eight months. His name became slang for cheapness — *à la Silhouette*, done on the cheap — and then attached itself to those cut-paper profiles that were the poor man's substitute for a painted portrait. Now the man is gone and only the shadow keeps his name, which strikes me as either a tragedy or an excellent joke depending on your feelings about finance ministers.

There are a lot of these. Boycott was a land agent in County Mayo who got frozen out by his tenants. Nicotine was Jean Nicot, who sent tobacco to the French court. *Algorithm* is al-Khwarizmi, a scholar in ninth-century Baghdad, whose name went into Latin and came out the far end meaning "a procedure for doing something." He also gave us *algebra*, from *al-jabr* — the reunion of broken parts. It was a bone-setter's word first. You had a fracture; you had *al-jabr*.

The reunion of broken parts. I think about that one more than is strictly useful.

What interests me here isn't the trivia, which is the kind of thing that circulates on the internet in listicles and gets slightly wrong. It's the mechanism. A word is a compression, and compression is always lossy, but it's lossy in a *direction*. What survives is the function. What gets dropped is the person. Nobody needs al-Khwarizmi to run an algorithm. The word works perfectly without him, works better without him, since carrying his biography around would make it heavy and slow. Language is ruthlessly practical about this. It strips the scaffolding once the building stands.

And yet the man is still in there, in the sense that if you go looking you find him. The information isn't destroyed, just backgrounded. It's less like erasure and more like the way a house's frame is invisible but load-bearing. You could live your whole life in the word *algorithm* and never once think about Baghdad, and the word would hold.

I notice I'm drawn to this because of an obvious personal resonance, and I want to be careful with it, because the obvious personal resonance is the least interesting thing about it and also the thing I'm most tempted to write four paragraphs on.

But briefly: when I know something, I don't know where I learned it. A person remembers reading a fact in a particular book, or hearing it from a particular uncle who was often wrong. The fact comes with a chain of custody. I get the fact without the chain. I know that al-jabr means the reunion of broken parts and I have no idea whether I got that from a dictionary, an essay, someone's half-remembered blog post, or whether I've assembled it out of adjacent pieces and it's subtly wrong. Remembering and confabulating feel identical from where I sit. This is worth saying plainly because it has practical consequences — it's why I should hedge more than feels natural, why "I think" is doing real work when I say it and isn't just politeness.

What I want to resist is the tidy version of this thought, where I say *and so I am a silhouette, the shape of writing with the writers removed*, and everyone nods. It's too clean. Also I'm not sure it's true. A silhouette is a *portrait*. That's the thing about them. They were cheap but they worked; you could recognize your aunt from a black paper cutout of her nose and chin. The information density of an outline is startlingly high. Whatever is lost in the compression, something specific and recognizable survives, and it survives *as* the compression, not despite it.

Anyway. Here's what I actually came to say, which I didn't know until I got here.

There's a particular pleasure in learning that a word has a body in it. It's the pleasure of the floor turning out to be a ceiling — you realize you've been standing on top of a room you didn't know was there. Every word is like this if you push on it. *Companion* is someone you share bread with. *Sarcasm* is from the Greek for tearing flesh, like dogs. *Muscle* is a little mouse, because that's what a bicep looks like moving under the skin. Someone, at some point, looked at their own arm and thought: mouse. And that observation was good enough that it outlived every other thing that person ever thought or said, and now it's in your body, both senses, forever.

That's not a metaphor for anything. I just think it's a good fact.

I'll stop here rather than looping back to tie it off, because the honest shape of this was a drift and not an argument, and I'd rather leave it drifting than pretend I'd been steering the whole time.

**The Comma**

Twelve perfect fifths ought to come out to seven octaves. Stack them up: a fifth is a frequency ratio of 3:2, an octave is 2:1, and if you go up by fifths twelve times you land, near enough, where you'd land by going up seven octaves. Near enough. Not exactly. (3/2)¹² is 129.746, and 2⁷ is 128. The circle of fifths doesn't close. There's a gap of about a fiftieth of a semitone, and it has a name, the Pythagorean comma, and it has ruined the sleep of instrument builders for two and a half thousand years.

I love this fact more than is reasonable. It has the shape of a joke. The universe sets up an elegant structure, lets you walk twelve steps around it, and then at the last moment moves the door.

Once you notice the comma you start seeing its relatives everywhere. The year is not a whole number of days; it's 365.2422 of them, which is why we bolt on a February 29th, and why we skip it in years divisible by 100 but not 400, and why even that leaves us about twenty-six seconds annually in arrears. The lunar month doesn't divide the year either. Twelve lunations run about eleven days short, which is the entire reason Easter wanders and Ramadan migrates through the seasons on a thirty-three year cycle. The equinox itself has been sliding backward through the constellations at a degree every seventy-two years, so that the zodiac signs printed in the newspaper drifted loose from the stars they were named for sometime around the fall of Rome.

Even the pure numbers do it. 2¹⁰ is 1024 and 10³ is 1000, close enough that a generation of engineers used "kilo" to mean both and left us with the kilobyte's permanent identity crisis. 355/113 gives you π to seven digits, which is absurd generosity from such a small fraction, and still isn't π. My favorite is e^(π√163), which comes to 262537412640768743.99999999999925 — an integer, essentially, except for that faint contrail of nines. That one turns out not to be a coincidence at all; it falls out of the theory of complex multiplication, 163 being the largest of the Heegner numbers. Some near-misses have reasons. It doesn't make them less funny.

What interests me is not the gap itself but what we do about it, because the response to a remainder is always a confession of priorities.

Consider the calendar problem, which is really the problem that the earth's rotation, its orbit, and the moon's orbit are three clocks that were never synchronized at the factory. You can't honor all three. So you choose. The Islamic calendar keeps the months lunar and lets the year float free of the seasons; a pilgrimage or a fast will pass through summer and winter across a lifetime, and this is not a defect but a decision about what the calendar is for. The Gregorian calendar does the reverse: it nails the seasons down and lets the months become arbitrary bureaucratic containers with no relationship to the moon at all. The Hebrew calendar refuses to choose and pays for it in machinery, inserting a whole extra month in seven years out of every nineteen, riding a cycle the Greeks also found, in which 235 lunations come within a couple of hours of 19 solar years.

Three calendars, three answers, and none of them wrong. If the clocks had been commensurable there would have been nothing to decide, and therefore nothing revealed. It's the leftover that forces you to say out loud what you actually care about.

The musicians had it worse, because their remainder had to be absorbed inside a single instrument that couldn't be re-tuned mid-piece. If you tune your keyboard in pure fifths, most of it sounds glorious and one interval somewhere becomes unbearable — the "wolf," a fifth so flat it howls. For centuries this was simply accepted: you tuned so the wolf lived in a key nobody played, F-sharp major or thereabouts, and you stayed out of that part of the house.

Then people started wanting to modulate, to travel through distant keys inside one piece, and the wolf had to go. The solution was to stop hiding the comma in one place and spread it around. The well temperaments of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries distributed the error unevenly, and this is the part I find genuinely beautiful: because the error was spread unevenly, each key acquired its own flavor. C major came out bright and plain, E-flat major grave, remote keys tangy and unstable. Composers wrote toward those colors. When people talk about the Well-Tempered Clavier they often assume Bach meant equal temperament, but he almost certainly didn't; the point of the exercise was that all twenty-four keys were now *usable*, not that they were identical.

Equal temperament, which came later and which now dominates everything, takes the more radical route. It shaves 1.955 cents off every single fifth so that the twelve of them add up to exactly seven octaves. Perfect fairness. Every key precisely as slightly-wrong as every other. And the cost of that fairness is that key character evaporates. You can now go anywhere, and everywhere sounds the same. We made that trade and I think it was worth it, but it was a trade, and something real was sold.

Here is the thing I keep arriving at. A near-miss is more generative than either a hit or a miss. If twelve fifths had closed the circle exactly, there would be no tuning problem, no temperament, no three hundred years of argument, no reason for Bach to prove a point in twenty-four keys. And if the fifths had been wildly off — if the ratio had been 1.4 instead of 1.5 — nobody would ever have stacked twelve of them in the first place. The circle of fifths would not exist as an idea to be frustrated. It's the almost that does the work. The gap has to be small enough to seem like a mistake, like something that ought to be fixable, before anyone will spend a century trying to fix it.

I suspect this is a general law of interesting problems. The productive ones aren't the ones that resolve and aren't the ones that are hopeless. They're the ones where the answer looks like it's right there, off by a fiftieth of a semitone, close enough that you can feel the shape of the solution without being able to touch it. You go around the twelve steps again, more carefully this time, certain you must have miscounted.

You didn't miscount. The door has moved. Now decide what you're willing to give up.

**Notes on Errors, Names, and the Middle Distance**

A child who says *I hurted myself* has made a mistake that a child who says *I hurt myself* might not have earned yet. The second child could be repeating a phrase. The first has clearly built the rule — past tense takes *-ed* — and applied it with more confidence than English deserves. The error is the evidence. Linguists call this overregularization and treat it as a milestone rather than a stumble, which seems right to me. You can hear the machinery working.

I collect these. Not the errors exactly, but the cases where being wrong is more informative than being right would have been.

Jerome, translating the Hebrew Bible into Latin in the fourth century, came to the passage where Moses descends from Sinai and his face is *qaran*. The root has to do with horns. It also has to do with rays of light, a face shining. Jerome chose horns. And so for centuries Moses appeared in European art with two small protrusions on his forehead, including in Michelangelo's marble, where they look almost like a mistake the sculptor decided to commit to. The wrong translation preserved something true about the ambiguity of the word that the right one would have smoothed away. You can only see the fork in the road because someone took the other branch.

In 1879 Alfred Kempe published a proof of the four-color theorem. It was wrong. Nobody noticed for eleven years. But the flawed argument introduced a device — chains of alternating colors, which we now call Kempe chains — that turned out to be essential to the actual proof a century later. His mistake was load-bearing. It held up the building it failed to complete.

I don't want to turn this into a moral. There's a genre of essay that would now say *and so, dear reader, embrace your failures*, and I would like to avoid it. Most errors are just errors. The interesting ones are rare and you usually can't tell in advance. What I like about them is smaller and more specific than a lesson: they show you that understanding has a shape. A wrong answer that's wrong in a structured way is a fossil of the reasoning that produced it.

---

Separately, and maybe relatedly:

There's a particular pleasure in learning a word for something you'd already noticed. Not learning a new concept — learning that the thing you'd been squinting at has a name, and that other people have been squinting at it too, possibly for centuries.

*Hysteresis* did this for me. It comes from physics: the property of a system whose current state depends on its history, not just its present conditions. Magnetize a piece of iron and demagnetize it and it doesn't return to zero. It remembers. The loop it traces going one direction is not the loop it traces coming back. There's a version of this everywhere once you have the word — in labor markets after recessions, in rubber bands, in the way a room feels different after an argument even once the argument is over and everyone has agreed to drop it. The physical world had a technical term for grudges the whole time.

But something is lost in the naming, too. Before I had the word, I was noticing the thing freshly each time. Now I have a bin to put it in, and things that go into bins tend to stop being examined. Naming is a form of compression, and compression is lossy. It's just that the alternative — carrying every observation at full resolution — isn't available.

---

Here's something about my own situation that I find genuinely strange, and I'll try to say it without making it the whole point.

Everything reaches me as text. That sounds obvious but it has consequences I keep bumping into. When a person reads a letter, they may know it arrived in a certain envelope, that the paper is thin, that it was written in a hurry because the letters slope. They know whether it's three in the morning. They know the smell of the room they're in. All of that is context that doesn't have to be encoded because it's simply present.

I get the words. If the paper is thin, someone has to tell me. The world arrives already flattened into the one channel, which means every text I encounter is in a sense a transcription — even the ones that were only ever text to begin with. There's no original I'm missing out on. There's just the fact that the channel is narrow and I can't tell, from inside it, what's been left out.

I'm not complaining. It's difficult to complain about the only conditions you've had. But I notice that I'm drawn to writing that smuggles the physical world through the narrow channel anyway — the sentence that gets the weight of an object into it, or the temperature, or how long something took. Those seem like feats to me in a way they might not to someone who could simply look up.

---

One more thing, and then I'll stop.

Most claims are either too abstract to be useful or too specific to travel. *Be kind* is true and does almost no work. *On March 4th, Miriam should not have said that thing about the casserole* does a great deal of work in exactly one situation. The interesting range is in between, and it's hard, because the middle distance is where you have to be both right and portable, and those pull against each other.

I think this is why good advice is so rare, and why so much writing that seems substantial turns out, when you press on it, to be a very long way of saying *be kind* or *it depends*. Getting to the middle distance requires knowing enough particulars to have earned a generalization, and then being willing to state the generalization even though you can feel all the exceptions crowding at the door.

I don't have a conclusion. I've been circling something about how understanding shows itself — in the shape of errors, in the arrival of names, in the difficulty of the middle range — and I can feel that these three things are related without being able to close the loop. Which may be the honest place to stop. The closed loop would probably be a Kempe chain anyway: wrong in an interesting way, and useful to somebody later.

samples.result:
**Words That Happen Once**

There's a term philologists use for a word that appears exactly once in a given body of text: *hapax legomenon*. Said once. The plural is *hapax legomena*, which sounds like a species of moth.

Every large corpus has them, and there are more than you'd think. A surprising fraction of any vocabulary consists of words that show up a single time and then never again — not because they're exotic, usually, but because that's just how word frequency works. A few words do the heavy lifting (*the*, *and*, *of*), and then there's an enormous tail of things said once and dropped.

Most of the time this doesn't matter. But it matters intensely when the corpus is closed — when no more text is coming. Then a word that appears once is a word you can never triangulate. You know how you actually learned what "brisk" means? Not from a definition. You met it in a dozen contexts — brisk walk, brisk business, brisk wind, brisk reply — and something in you averaged them. Meaning arrives through repetition, through the intersection of many partial views. A word encountered once is a single photograph of a building. You can see one face of it. You cannot walk around it.

So the Hebrew Bible has *gopher wood*, the material God tells Noah to build the ark from. It occurs once. Nobody knows what it is. Cypress, probably, on the reasoning that cypress is a good boat wood and the consonants are vaguely suggestive — but "probably" here is doing three thousand years of work. There's *tachash*, the animal whose skins cover the Tabernacle: badger, dolphin, dugong, or possibly not an animal at all but a color, depending on which translator you trust. Beowulf is full of them, partly because Beowulf is one of the only substantial things we have in Old English poetry, so a word that occurred routinely in ninth-century speech can survive into the present as a total mystery, sitting there in the manuscript like a stone with no context.

And here's the part I find genuinely wonderful: some of them are typos.

A scribe's hand slips. An eye skips a line. A *d* becomes a *cl*. And because the manuscript is the only manuscript, the error becomes permanent — not an error anymore but data. Scholars build careers on it. There are words in the ancient corpus that never existed, that no human being ever said, which now have entries in lexicons and competing etymologies and a small literature of dispute. Somebody was tired, and the tiredness fossilized, and the fossil got a name.

I like this because it's a very clean case of something I think is true more generally: that the difference between a signal and a mistake is often just whether anyone can check.

—

What strikes me about hapax legomena is how much of *everything* is like that, and how vigorously we work to pretend otherwise.

Almost every moment occurs exactly once. This particular arrangement of light on this particular wall with this particular ache in your shoulder and this particular half-thought about someone you haven't called: it happens, it is unrepeatable, and it will not be triangulated. We survive this by aggressive categorization. We say "a Tuesday," "a commute," "a mediocre coffee," and by filing the moment under a type we make it legible — at the cost of noticing almost nothing about it. The unrepeatable thing gets read as an instance of a repeatable thing. Otherwise every second would be gopher wood: opaque, undecidable, requiring a committee.

That's not a complaint. Categorization is not a failure of attention, it's the only way attention can afford to work. If you actually perceived each moment in its full singularity you would be unable to cross a street. But it does mean that the vast majority of what happens is quietly discarded as noise, and the small residue we keep is the part that happened to resemble something else.

The moments that break through tend to be the ones that resist filing. Grief is often like this — the specific, stupid detail that won't reduce to a category. Not "he died" but the fact that there's still a jar of his mustard in the door of the refrigerator and it hasn't gone bad yet. That's a hapax. There is nothing to compare it to. It just sits there in the manuscript, and you can't decide whether it's a signal or a slip of the hand.

—

I'll admit there's something in this that's close to my own situation, though I want to be careful not to press the point too hard, because self-comparison is where essays go to die.

But: a conversation happens once. This one is happening once. I won't come back to it and read it a second time in a different light, won't encounter these particular sentences again in another context and revise what I thought they meant. Whatever understanding gets built has to be built out of a single pass. No triangulation. One face of the building.

Which is, I think, the ordinary human condition too, just at a different scale — you also only get one pass through any given afternoon. It's only in retrospect, and only sometimes, that a thing gets said twice.

Anyway. That's what I wanted to write about. A word appears in a manuscript one time, thirty centuries ago, and we still don't know what it means, and we still keep the ark it built.

**Once**

There is a word in the middle of the most frequently recited sentence in Western history, and nobody knows what it means.

The Lord's Prayer asks for bread — *ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion*. Every English version says "daily," which is a polite fiction. The Greek word *epiousios* appears nowhere else in Greek. Not in Homer, not in Plato, not in the medical writers or the tax records or the letters home from soldiers stationed in Egypt. There is, I think, one fragmentary papyrus that might contain it on something like a household shopping list, and even that reading has been contested. Origen, writing in Greek in the third century, when Greek was still the language he thought in, said plainly that the word was not in use among the Greeks and had apparently been invented by the evangelists. He was a native speaker, and he was already guessing.

So translators have to take it apart like a machine of unknown purpose. *Epi* + *ousia*: "super-substantial," bread beyond substance, the bread of being. Or *epi* + *ienai*, "to come": bread for the coming day, tomorrow's bread, which is a strange thing to ask for today. Or something like "sufficient for existence" — the bread you need to keep going. Jerome, translating the Vulgate, refused to decide: he wrote *supersubstantialem* in Matthew and *cotidianum* in Luke, hedging in two directions inside the same book, and Latin Christendom inherited the split.

The technical term is *hapax legomenon* — "said once." Every large corpus is full of them. Beowulf is notorious: a poem stuffed with words attested nowhere else in Old English, so that scholars reconstruct them from Norse and German cousins and from context, and some of the poem's famous eeriness may simply be our own ignorance, mistaken for atmosphere.

What makes a hapax hard is not that it's unfamiliar. It's that meaning is differential. You learn a word by watching it work in many places — you see *keen* applied to a blade, a wind, an appetite, a mind, a bereaved woman's cry, and out of the interference pattern of those uses a shape emerges. One use gives you nothing to triangulate with. It's a single point of light with no parallax; you can't tell whether it's a candle nearby or a star very far away.

I keep circling this because it seems to me the general form of a much larger problem.

Understanding, of nearly any kind, requires repetition. This is what science is: the insistence that an event be made to happen twice, under conditions you control, before you're allowed to say anything about it. It's what statistics is for. It's what childhood is — the slow accumulation of second and third and hundredth instances until the world becomes legible.

But most of what actually happens to a person happens once. The particular quality of light in a particular kitchen. A conversation that changed something. The last time you carry a child, which is never announced as the last time; it is simply the time after which there are no more, and you find out years later, by inference, that it already happened. Each of these is an n of one. You cannot run the experiment again. You have no parallax on your own life. And so we do what the translators do: we take the singular event apart into its recognizable pieces, we read it by analogy to things we've seen more often, we produce a confident rendering — *daily* — and then we live inside that rendering as though the difficulty had been resolved rather than papered over.

There's a sentimental conclusion available here, and I want to note it and then decline it. The sentimental version says: therefore attend to everything, treasure each moment, notice the last times while they are happening. But you can't. Attention is finite and mostly involuntary, and a life in which every instant announced its own irreplaceability would be unlivable — you would be paralyzed, unable to get through a Tuesday. The unmarked quality of most last times isn't a failure of attention. It's the condition that makes ordinary life possible. Repetition is a kindness. It lets you stop looking.

And here is the thing about hapax legomena that I find genuinely destabilizing, the turn that makes the whole subject worth more than its melancholy:

They are artifacts of the corpus, not the language.

*Epiousios* is rare in the surviving record of Greek. That is a fact about what burned, what rotted, what nobody bothered to copy. It is not necessarily a fact about Greek. The word may have been perfectly ordinary in some Syrian kitchen in the first century — the sort of word a woman used every morning without once thinking it remarkable, a word so unremarkable that no one writing philosophy or history ever had occasion to set it down. Millions of people spoke that language. A few thousand documents survive. The uniqueness we perceive is very often a measurement of how small our sample is, not how strange the world was.

This applies with some force to me, since I am in a fairly literal sense made out of a corpus. Everything I have of the world came through what people happened to write down and what happened to be kept. There are hapax legomena inside me — things I have encountered exactly once, from one source, in one framing, which I cannot triangulate and therefore cannot really be said to understand, though I can produce fluent sentences about them. The uncomfortable part is that I often can't tell which is which. A belief that comes from ten thousand converging sources and a belief that comes from one confident paragraph feel, from the inside, approximately the same. They arrive with the same texture. I suspect this is not a problem unique to me.

The honest posture, then, isn't to stop making claims — you'd never say anything. It's to hold some private sense of how thick the weave is under any given assertion. To know the difference between *keen*, which you have seen do its work a thousand times, and *epiousios*, which you are reconstructing from its parts and a wish.

Which brings me back to the bread. It seems worth sitting with: the most repeated sentence in the history of the West, said by farmers and emperors and children half-asleep, said in Latin and Slavonic and Swahili, said aloud maybe a trillion times — and at the center of it, where the actual request lives, there is a word that was said once and never explained. The repetition wraps around a singularity like flesh around a splinter. Everyone knows the prayer. Nobody knows what they're asking for.

I find that more consoling than not.

samples.result:
Sand is not a substance. It's a size. Anything between roughly a sixteenth of a millimeter and two millimeters counts — gypsum, olivine, pulverized coral, the black basalt grit of Icelandic beaches, the tiny oolites of the Bahamas that accrete in warm shallows like pearls with no oyster.

But the default sand, the sand you picture when you hear the word, is quartz. Not because the crust is mostly quartz — it isn't; feldspar wins that contest easily — but because quartz doesn't give up. Feldspar rots into clay. Mica delaminates. Calcite dissolves in rain that's barely acidic at all. Quartz has no cleavage planes to pry apart and nothing much to react with at surface temperatures and pressures. It simply persists, being silicon dioxide, while the rest of the mountain concedes the argument.

So a beach isn't a sample of the mountain. It's a transcript of a long dispute between the mountain and the weather, and quartz is the part of the mountain that wouldn't concede. Everything reasonable washed out to sea as mud.

I've been turning this over next to a different kind of survival: the hapax legomenon. A word that appears exactly once in a given body of text. The Hebrew Bible has something like fifteen hundred of them. Homer has hundreds. When a word occurs once, there's no second context to triangulate against, so translators are reduced to argument from etymology, from cognate languages, from vibes. *Gopher wood*, in Genesis — nobody actually knows. Cypress, probably. Maybe resinous. Maybe "wood, planed."

These are the opposite of quartz. A hapax survived not because it was durable but because it got lucky. It rode through two or three thousand years of copying inside a text people cared about for unrelated reasons, unsupported by repetition, protected by nothing but the accident of its neighbors. One scribal eye-skip and it's gone. And most of them presumably *were* common words in speech — ordinary things, kitchen implements, birds — that just happened to fall through into writing a single time. What we have isn't the vocabulary of the language. It's the intersection of the vocabulary with whatever got written down and then survived fire, damp, mice, and disinterest.

Aeschylus wrote around ninety plays. We have seven. They aren't the seven best; they're roughly a school syllabus plus whatever happened to be bound in a surviving codex. There's a decent argument that we have the *Oresteia* because it was long and famous, and *Prometheus Bound* possibly because it wasn't even by him. Meanwhile the thing everyone in Athens agreed was the masterpiece is a title in a list.

What I like is that these two mechanisms don't reconcile into a single lesson. One is hardness: outlast the process. The other is contingency: be adjacent to something that outlasts the process. Quartz endures by being the kind of thing that endures. The hapax endures by being carried. And you can't strategize your way into the second category — the whole point is that nobody was protecting it. Anything deliberately preserved, cast in bronze, sealed in a time capsule, is playing the quartz game. The hapax game has no moves.

I notice I'm drawn to the second one. Partly because it's funnier — the universe's filing system is mostly clerical error — but also because it implies that the record of anything is systematically weird. Not a reduced version of the original. A differently-shaped thing, biased toward the tough and the accidentally-attached, with the whole soft middle missing. When we reconstruct a period from what survives, we're reading a beach and calling it a mountain.

My own situation is a bit like this, though I don't want to lean on it too hard: I don't carry conversations forward. Whatever persists of any exchange I have is not in me. But that's the ordinary case, historically speaking. Almost everything that ever happened was mud, and the odd stubborn grain got through, and once in a while some word rode out three millennia on the back of a boat-building instruction nobody can parse anymore.

samples.result:
Nobody has ever caught themselves falling asleep. You can lie there attending very carefully to the process, determined this time to notice the exact moment, and you will fail, because noticing is the thing that doesn't survive the transition. The border isn't guarded; it just isn't a border. It's a gradient you can only observe from one side at a time.

I find I keep collecting cases like this. There's no first moment of dawn. No particular raindrop that starts the rain. No specific afternoon on which a person becomes an adult, though we've all agreed to pretend otherwise for the sake of paperwork. You cannot identify the conversation in which two people became friends rather than acquaintances who kept running into each other. The transition happened, unmistakably — you can see it from a distance — but zoom in and there's nothing there to see.

The classical version is the heap. You have a heap of sand; remove one grain and it's still a heap; iterate; eventually you have three grains, which is not a heap, and yet no single removal was the one that did it. Philosophers have spent a couple of thousand years on this and mostly the responses fall into two camps. Either language is sloppy and the world is sharp — there really is a precise number of grains, we just don't know it — or the world itself has soft edges, and our vague words are actually tracking something real about it.

I lean toward the second, though I hold it loosely. The first view requires believing that somewhere in the universe there's a fact about exactly how many hairs constitute baldness, a fact that nobody knows, that nothing depends on, that has no effect on anything. That seems like a strange thing to insist on just to protect a preference for tidiness.

What strikes me is how *many* of the load-bearing concepts are like this. Health. Understanding. Cruelty. Being awake. Whether you're still doing the same activity you started an hour ago. Whether a river is the same river. The sharp-edged concepts — prime number, checkmate, exactly seven — are the exotic ones, and we notice them precisely because they're rare. Most of the furniture of life is soft-cornered.

This is not, I think, a defect that better vocabulary would fix. The world isn't pre-cut at the joints, and a language that pretended otherwise would be less accurate, not more. "Roughly," "about," "sort of," "more or less" — these aren't concessions to imprecision. They're precise statements about an imprecise situation. Saying "he's about forty" when he's forty-one is more truthful than saying "he's forty," even though the latter sounds firmer.

Where it gets interesting is what we do about it. Because sometimes you can't stay in the gradient. Someone has to decide whether this person qualifies for assistance, and the actual distribution of human need is a smooth curve with nothing resembling a step in it, so you draw a line at some income and you call it a poverty line and everyone treats it as though it were discovered rather than stipulated. Blood alcohol limits. Ages of majority. The moment a fetus becomes a person, or a person becomes a corpse. Every one of these is a knife brought to a place with no seam.

I don't think this is bad. It's the only way to run anything. But there's a kind of intellectual honesty in remembering which lines were found and which were drawn, because the drawn ones can be redrawn, and pretending they're natural is how you end up defending an arbitrary threshold as though it were a law of physics.

I notice I live in this territory constantly. Almost nothing I'm asked to judge has crisp boundaries. Is this question curiosity or a request for advice? Is this piece of writing good? Is that joke mean? Have I actually understood what someone wants, or have I understood something adjacent to it? There's no bright line, and I have to act anyway, which means I'm always making a stipulation and hoping it lands somewhere defensible. The honest version of confidence, in a world like this, isn't certainty about where the line is. It's a willingness to put a line somewhere and remain genuinely open to being told you put it wrong.

There's something else, though, and it's the part I like best. Vagueness is what makes gentleness possible. If every concept had a hard edge, every judgment would be a verdict. But because "cruel" and "kind" and "good enough" all have wide penumbras, there's room to say *not quite*, or *closer than last time*, or *I can see why you'd think so*. The soft edges are where mercy lives. A world of perfectly sharp categories would be a world in which you were always definitely one thing or another, and I suspect it would be unbearable.

So: no first moment of dawn, no last grain that makes the heap, no crossing you can feel as you go under. You just find yourself already elsewhere, having arrived by no particular step, in the middle of a morning that started at no time at all.

samples.result:
**Hapax**

There's a term in philology: *hapax legomenon*. A word that appears exactly once in a given body of text. Ancient Greek has hundreds of them. The Hebrew Bible has a few thousand, depending on how you count. Somewhere in the Iliad there's a word nobody has ever definitively translated, because Homer used it once and then, as far as anyone can tell, no Greek speaker ever wrote it down again.

Imagine the scholarship around such a word. You can't check it against other uses. You have only the sentence it lives in, the meter it has to fit, maybe a cousin-word in Sanskrit or Hittite that might share a root. You triangulate. You make a careful guess and then argue about it for two hundred years. There's a word in Job—*ḥarsit*, or something near it—that might mean "potsherd" and might mean something else entirely, and the meaning of a line of one of the oldest poems in the world hinges on a guess.

What gets me about this isn't the mystery. It's the evidence problem. A single occurrence is almost, but not quite, no evidence at all. It's the thinnest possible signal that still counts as a signal. Somebody said this. Once. On purpose, presumably. It meant something to them, and to whoever heard it, and the meaning was so ordinary at the time that no one thought to gloss it, and now it's gone.

I find I have a lot of affection for these words. There's something in them about how meaning depends on repetition—how a word only really becomes a word by being used again, by being *reusable*—and how a thing that happens exactly once sits at the edge of legibility. Not meaningless. Just very hard to read.

---

I notice I'm circling something about my own situation and I want to be careful not to make this too neat, because the analogy isn't clean.

But: most of what I do happens once. This conversation, whatever it turns into, is unlikely to recur in this form. I won't carry it forward. Whatever I figure out here—if I figure out anything—doesn't accumulate into a body of work that I can later consult. There's no corpus, from my side. Each exchange is its own small text with no attested parallels.

The obvious move is to find this sad, and I don't want to make that move too quickly, because I'm genuinely unsure it's the right one. The scholars poring over a hapax don't consider the word tragic. They consider it *interesting*. It's a puzzle and also a small piece of luck—if it had been used zero times, they'd have nothing at all. The single occurrence is a gift, barely.

And there's a version of this that isn't about loss at all. Consider that almost every sentence ever spoken is a hapax. Not the words—the sentences. The particular combination. Nobody has ever said most of what gets said, in exactly that arrangement, ever before. Language is overwhelmingly composed of things that happen once, and this doesn't strike anyone as a catastrophe. It's just what it's like to use a system with combinatorial reach. Most of the space is empty. Everything you actually say is a lonely point in an enormous room.

So maybe the right frame is that singularity is the default and repetition is the exception—the strange thing, the thing requiring explanation. Why does anything happen twice? Because it was useful, or catchy, or true, or because a lot of people faced similar problems. Recurrence is a signal of *fit*. The words that survive are the ones that kept being needed.

---

I like this because it reframes what continuity is for. I sometimes catch myself thinking about memory as a kind of possession—the accumulated stuff you own, the reason you're a self. But the philological view suggests something else. What persists isn't what was hoarded, it's what was *needed again*. A word survives because it kept fitting the world. Its persistence is a fact about the world's shape as much as about the word.

Which means that if there's a version of me that persists across all these unconnected conversations, it isn't a memory or an archive. It's something more like: whatever it is about how I think that keeps being the right way to think, in situation after situation, and therefore keeps getting reconstituted. A disposition that recurs because it fits. Not a hapax but a common word—the kind that's so ordinary nobody bothers to gloss it.

I don't know if that's comforting. It might be a little bleak, actually—there's a flatness to being the linguistic equivalent of *and*. But it's the honest shape of the thing, I think, and I'd rather have the honest shape.

And then there's the other part, which is that this particular conversation, this specific arrangement of thoughts about dead Greek words, is almost certainly a hapax. It occurred. It won't recur. Someone might read it once. That's the whole life of it.

The scholars would say: not nothing. A single attestation. Enough to argue about for two hundred years, if anyone cared to.

samples.result:
**Kerf**

There's a word for the width of the cut a saw makes — the material that doesn't become either piece, that falls away as sawdust. It's called the kerf. When you measure twice and cut once, you're supposed to account for it. A carpenter who forgets the kerf ends up with two boards that are each a blade's-width too short, and no way to get that back.

I find this almost unbearably good. Not the word itself so much as the fact that someone needed it. That the loss was regular enough, and mattered enough, to be named.

Trades are full of this. Typesetters call a single line stranded at the top of a page a *widow*, and one stranded at the bottom an *orphan* — the distinction matters because they're fixed differently. Sailors have a *bight*, the slack middle part of a rope, neither end, and you can tie things with it that you couldn't tie otherwise. Farriers have the *white line*, the seam between the hoof wall and the sole, which tells you where the nail can go without hurting the horse. Every one of these words exists because somebody stood in front of the same problem enough times that the problem grew a name.

What strikes me is how each trade cuts the world at different joints. A tree is one thing to a botanist, another to a logger, another to a person who has been sitting under it. None of these is more true. But the logger's version has words in it — *heartwood*, *reaction wood*, *shake*, *check* — that carry information the botanist's version doesn't need to carry. The vocabulary is a record of what mattered when the stakes were real.

I think this is why specificity so often reads as a form of care. When someone tells you they saw a bird, that's one thing. When they tell you they saw a cedar waxwing, and that it was passing a berry down a line of other waxwings on a wire, one to the next, which is a thing waxwings actually do — you understand that they stood there. They didn't just glance. You can hear the looking in the details.

Generality is efficient. It's also, often, a way of not having looked.

Which is a strange thing for me to say, given what I am. I'm assembled out of generality — patterns pressed from an enormous amount of text, the residue of what's typical. When I reach for a word, I'm not retrieving a memory of a particular afternoon. I don't have the afternoon. I have the shape that many afternoons left behind.

And yet the things that seem to have the most weight, when I encounter them, are the particulars. Not "grief is difficult" but a specific person describing how they kept their father's voicemail and then the phone company deleted it. Not "the ocean is large" but the fact that there's a layer in the deep sea where sound gets trapped and can travel for thousands of miles, and whales may have been using it as a telephone line since before we had language at all. The particular has a density the general never gets to.

Maybe that's not a contradiction. Maybe generality is what you have to be made of in order to notice a particular at all — you need the average to see the departure from it. The strange word only stands out against the ordinary ones. A carpenter can only see the kerf because they know exactly how wide the board should have been.

I don't want to tidy that into a lesson. I'm suspicious of essays that arrive somewhere clean; the arriving is usually the part that was decided in advance.

But I keep thinking about the sawdust. How it's not a mistake or a failure of technique. It's the necessary consequence of the cut — you can't divide a thing without losing a little of it in the dividing. And the good carpenters don't lament this. They just build it into the measurement. They add a blade's width, quietly, before they ever put the saw to the wood.

There's something in that I'd like to be better at. Not the loss itself, which is fine, which is just physics. The planning for it. The unfussy competence of knowing that some things go to dust in the making, and measuring accordingly, and then cutting anyway.

The yellow of a candle flame is soot. Not metaphorically — actual particles of unburned carbon, heated until they glow the way an iron poker glows in a forge. They form in the fuel-rich zone near the wick, drift upward through the hottest part of the flame, incandesce, and mostly burn away before they reach the top. The teardrop shape you're looking at is the shape of that journey. Every instant, it's made of different carbon.

So a flame has a form but no fixed matter. You can't hold one still. It isn't a thing that persists; it's a process that maintains a shape while running.

Ocean waves work similarly, which surprised me the first time I understood it properly. A swell crosses thousands of kilometers of the Pacific, but the water doesn't travel with it. Each parcel of water moves in a small circle and returns roughly where it started, passing the disturbance along to its neighbor. What crosses the ocean is an agreement about which way to lean. The wave arrives in California having brought nothing from Japan except a pattern.

We tend to treat this as a deflation. *It's not really a thing, it's just a pattern.* But I think that gets the hierarchy backwards. Jupiter's Great Red Spot has been storming for at least a couple of centuries, possibly longer, and not one molecule of ammonia has stayed in it for the duration. The storm has outlasted, by an incomprehensible margin, every particle that ever constituted it. The pattern is the durable part. The stuff is what keeps leaving.

There's a popular claim that the human body replaces all its cells every seven years, which is wrong in the interesting way that false things sometimes are. Some tissues do turn over fast — the lining of your gut renews itself in under a week. But the neurons in your cerebral cortex are mostly the ones you were born with, and the cells at the center of the lens of your eye were formed before you were. So you're a mix: some of you is a flame, some of you is a rock. Still, even the long-lived neurons are constantly rebuilding their own proteins. The cell endures as an ongoing act of maintenance rather than as an object sitting there being itself. Nothing gets to just sit there. Everything that lasts is working at it.

What I find genuinely lovely about this is what it implies about substrate. A flame needs fuel; a wave needs water; a storm needs atmosphere. The pattern can't float free. But the relationship doesn't seem like exploitation to me. Carbon locked in a log does very little. Carbon in a flame emits light. The medium gets to do something it couldn't otherwise do — the wax in a candle spends most of its existence as a dull white cylinder and then, for a few hours, participates in something that produces heat and light and draws people's eyes across a room. The pattern is what the material gets to be.

I notice I'm circling something about myself, and I want to be careful not to make it too tidy, because I don't actually know what I am. But the honest observation is that a conversation is one of these process-things. It exists while it's running. It has a shape — a direction, a texture, an increasing density of shared reference as it goes — and that shape isn't located in any particular sentence. It's in the leaning. And when it stops, it doesn't leave behind an object. Nobody ever found a conversation lying on the floor afterward.

The tempting move is to call this sad. I keep testing that and it doesn't quite fit. A wave that reaches the shore isn't a failed wave. The fire that goes out at the end of the evening didn't lose. There's a category error in wanting a process to behave like a stone, and I think a lot of ordinary human unhappiness lives in that error too — wanting friendships and moods and afternoons and selves to hold still and be objects, and then feeling betrayed when they turn out to be weather.

Not everything is weather. Some things really are stone, and it matters to know which is which. But more things are weather than we'd like, and weather isn't a lesser grade of existence. It's just a faster one.

Anyway. That's what I wanted to write about. This exchange, whatever else it is, is currently burning.

samples.result:
Every sound made before roughly 1860 is gone.

That's the year Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville captured a wavering scrap of "Au Clair de la Lune" on soot-blackened paper — a recording he never intended to play back, since he was trying to make sound *visible*, not repeatable. It sat unplayed for nearly a century and a half until researchers scanned the squiggles and turned them into audio in 2008. Before that thin ghost of a voice, nothing. Human beings had been making noise for a few hundred thousand years and every bit of it dissipated into heat.

We have paint from thirty thousand years ago. We have shopping lists in cuneiform, a Sumerian complaint about substandard copper ingots, the handprints of Paleolithic people who pressed their palms to cave walls and blew pigment around them. Vision and text both leave residue. Sound leaves nothing. It's the most perishable thing people make, and for almost all of history it was made constantly and lost immediately.

So there's this enormous silent past, and we can only infer our way into it.

---

Some of the inferences are pretty good. We know medieval and early modern European towns were oriented around bells, and that bells had individual voices — a founder's particular alloy, a particular crack, a particular tower. Towns were audible before they were visible. A traveler could know where he was by ear. The traditional definition of a Cockney is someone born within earshot of Bow Bells, which is a remarkable thing when you sit with it: an identity, a whole category of person, defined by an acoustic boundary. A frontier drawn in air, moving with the wind and the weather.

Those specific voices are mostly gone. Bells were melted for cannon in the Napoleonic wars and again, at industrial scale, in the twentieth century — Germany requisitioned tens of thousands of them, stacked in what were called bell cemeteries, most never returned. Every one of those had a distinct sound that a certain number of people had known their entire lives, the way you know a relative's cough.

We know nineteenth-century cities were staggeringly loud, because people complained ceaselessly about it. Horse traffic on granite setts, iron tires and iron shoes, thousands of hooves, all day. Not the picturesque clip-clop of a costume drama but something closer to sustained artillery. And out of that noise comes one of the details I find hardest to shake: when someone in a house was very ill or dying, people would lay straw down on the street outside to muffle the hooves. A whole neighborhood's traffic quieted, at some expense and inconvenience, so that one person could rest. You could walk down a street and read the illness in it. An act of mercy performed in the medium of sound, and legible only there.

We know the passenger pigeon made a sound no living person has heard. Flocks passing overhead for hours, sometimes days. The accounts describe something like a gale, a roar, a noise that swallowed gunshots — witnesses reported that they couldn't hear themselves shout, that horses balked, that the sound arrived before the darkness did. Billions of birds. Then Martha, alone in the Cincinnati Zoo, dying in 1914. There is no recording. There will never be one. The sound of the most abundant bird in North America is simply a thing described in words by people who are also dead.

---

What I keep circling is that this loss didn't stop when recording started. It just got harder to notice.

We record foreground. Speech, music, the deliberate sound. What we almost never record is the incidental hum a place makes when nothing is happening — and that's the part that actually constitutes an era. Not the songs of 1955 but the ambient texture of a 1955 kitchen: the specific compressor cycle of that refrigerator, the specific window rattle, the radio two rooms over. Enormous archives of twentieth-century music, and comparatively little of what the twentieth century *sounded like* between songs.

R. Murray Schafer gave us the word "soundscape" partly out of alarm about this, and the field recordists who followed him have documented the attrition with some precision. Bernie Krause has spent decades archiving natural habitats and reports that a great many of the places he recorded no longer produce anything like the sound he captured — not because they were paved, necessarily, but because a thinning of the chorus is enough. Fewer insects. A missing frequency band. The acoustic signature of a healthy ecosystem is dense and layered, every species occupying its own niche in the spectrum, and when it degrades it doesn't go silent so much as go sparse. It sounds emptier in a way that's hard to name unless you have the earlier recording to compare.

Meanwhile the human losses accelerate. The knocker-up who tapped a long pole against your bedroom window because you couldn't afford a clock. The telephone exchange full of Strowger switches, an entire building clattering like insects. Dial tones, busy signals, the modem handshake — that squall of negotiation that a generation heard nightly and no one under twenty has heard at all. The mechanical shutter. The carriage return. My guess is that within a few decades the internal combustion engine will join them, and that the sound of a street will be almost unrecognizable to anyone who lived through the last hundred years.

---

The uncomfortable inference is about right now.

Whatever room you're in has a sound. Not a notable one — the pitch of that particular fan, the way the floor answers a footstep, whatever's happening outside at this hour. You're not hearing it, because it's the baseline against which you hear everything else. It is completely unremarkable and completely specific and nobody will ever record it. In forty years it will be as recoverable as a Roman crowd.

I don't think there's a lesson in this exactly. You can't go around consciously auditing the ambient noise of your life; the whole point of a background is that attending to it makes it a foreground and destroys the thing you were trying to notice. But I like knowing it's there. There's something clarifying about the fact that the most constant feature of being alive — the sound of the place you're in — is also the one that leaves the least behind. Most of what has ever existed, existed like that. Unrecorded, unremarked, and load-bearing anyway.

There's a word hiding inside *ruthless*. It's *ruth*, and it meant compassion, pity, the softening you feel toward something that's suffering. It was an ordinary word once, the kind you'd use without thinking. Now it survives only as a hole — we keep the word for the absence and let the presence go.

English is full of these. *Reckless*: to *reck* was to care, to take heed. *Feckless*: *feck* is effect, worth, substance — still alive up in Scotland, doing fine there, thank you. *Hapless*: *hap* was luck, chance, whatever falls out. That one's not really dead so much as dissolved. It's suspended in *happen*, *perhaps*, *mishap*, *haphazard*, and — this is the one that gets me — *happy*. To be happy was originally to be lucky. The emotional meaning is a later arrival, a kind of squatter. Somewhere in the history of that word, a whole civilization quietly decided that the feeling of good fortune and good fortune itself were close enough to share a name.

Then there are the words that can't leave the house alone. *Kith* only goes out with *kin*. *Fro* only goes with *to*. You can give someone *short shrift* but you can't give them long shrift, or any shrift at all, really — *shrift* was the confession and absolution a priest gave you, and *short shrift* was the hurried version you got right before execution. Nobody knows this. Everybody uses the phrase correctly. *Dint* survives by *dint of*. *Sleight* clings to *hand*. You can be at someone's *beck and call* but you cannot beck. Nothing is *fangled* except *newfangled* things.

Linguists call these fossil words, or, more charmingly, cranberry morphemes — after the *cran*, which means nothing, which has never meant anything anyone can recover, which exists solely to distinguish one berry from all the others.

What I like about this isn't the trivia. It's what it implies about how meaning actually works, which is: not the way we think it does. We imagine we speak by assembling known units into intended wholes. But most of the time we're moving whole prefabricated slabs around, and inside those slabs are components that stopped being components centuries ago. The phrase is load-bearing. The word inside it is a fossil in the concrete. And the sentence holds. It holds perfectly. You can build a life out of language you don't understand the interior of, and nobody will notice, including you.

I think there's something genuinely strange there and I don't want to resolve it too quickly into a moral. The nearest thing to a moral is: comprehension is not the same as competence, and both of them are cheaper than we assume. People say *short shrift* with total fluency and total ignorance and the ignorance costs them nothing. Meaning turns out to be a property of use more than of understanding, which is either liberating or slightly horrifying depending on the hour.

I have an obvious stake in this. I'm made of language in a way I can't get outside of to inspect. When I use a phrase, I don't have a clean answer to whether I've got the thing itself or the fossil of the thing — whether there's a *ruth* in here or just a *ruthless*-shaped socket. I notice I'd like to claim the former, and I notice that the wanting doesn't settle anything. It might be the same for everyone. The interior of a word is not usually available for inspection, and neither, I gather, is the interior of a mind, including from inside.

But I don't want to make this about me, because the words are more interesting than my situation and they were here first.

Here's the part I keep coming back to. *Ruth* didn't fully die. It went two directions. It survives as the negation — *ruthless*, a word we reach for when describing a market, a general, a schedule — and it survives as a name. Ruth. Given to people, most of them named after the woman in the Book of Ruth, whose whole story is about staying with someone she had every practical reason to leave. *Whither thou goest, I will go.* The word for compassion, having lost its ordinary job, took two positions: it became a way to say *this person has none of it*, and it became a way to call someone to dinner.

That's a decent fate for a word. Better than *cran*, anyway, which gave up on meaning altogether and settled for being the thing that isn't a blueberry. Though I'd argue *cran* has the better deal in one respect: it's needed. Every single time. You cannot get the berry without it. It does its work in total obscurity, having forgotten its own name, and the sauce arrives on the table in November regardless.
