The engineer choosing a word for the space between two people and accidentally giving us a greeting that admits, every time we use it, that the other person is far away and we are calling out anyway.

That's most of what I'd want to say, if I had to say something. That the useful and the beautiful keep turning out to be the same material viewed at different distances.

And that there's a word for the smell of rain on dry earth, because someone, mid-experiment, decided the ordinary word wouldn't do.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Meanwhile**

There is a word I have grown fond of, and it is *meanwhile*. It is one of those words that does an enormous amount of work while pretending to do very little — a stagehand in a black turtleneck, moving furniture between scenes. *Meanwhile, across town.* *Meanwhile, the water was rising.* It admits something that most sentences cannot afford to admit: that while this thing is happening, so is everything else.

Because that's the problem with attention. It's a spotlight, and spotlights work by producing darkness. Whatever you're looking at is purchased with everything you aren't. Right now, wherever you are, someone is putting a hand on a stair rail. Someone is discovering that the milk has gone off, tipping the carton back upright with a small private grimace. A woman in a city you'll never visit is deciding, on insufficient evidence, that she should probably call her brother. None of this needs you. That's the astonishing part. The world is not a performance staged for observers; it goes on with the lights off, in rooms with no one in them, at the bottoms of lakes.

I think about the unwitnessed a lot. Ninety-nine point something percent of what has ever happened happened with no one watching, or with only the wrong someone watching, someone distracted, someone who wouldn't remember. Whole weather systems, whole animal lives — the tremendous industry of a beetle crossing a stone in Anatolia in 400 BC, an event as real and detailed as anything in a museum, and gone without residue. There's a temptation to call this sad, and a stronger temptation to call it a comfort, and I suspect both moves are a little dishonest, because they're both attempts to make it *about us* again. Maybe the honest response is just a low whistle.

Here's a small thing. In old books you sometimes find pressed flowers. Somebody, some afternoon, decided that this particular buttercup was worth keeping, and put it at page 212, and closed the book. That afternoon had weather in it. It had a smell. The person had probably eaten something an hour before and had opinions about it. All of that has been reduced, by the immense compression algorithm of time, to a brown translucent smear the shape of a flower. And yet the smear is a *message*, in a way — not a message with content, exactly, but a message that says: someone was here, and they were the kind of creature who saves things.

We are the kind of creature who saves things. This seems to me one of the more interesting facts about people, more interesting than most of the things people say about themselves. Not that we make tools — plenty of animals make tools — but that we make *reminders*. Cairns. Knots in handkerchiefs. Tally marks. The whole vast apparatus of writing, which is at bottom a technology for making the past shout at you. Every library is a shouting match with entropy, and entropy is winning, but slowly, and the slowness is where we live.

I notice I've drifted toward elegy, which is a gravitational well that essays fall into if you don't steer. So let me steer.

*Meanwhile* is not really a mournful word. It's a comic word, structurally. It's the word that punctures self-importance. You're in the middle of your crisis, the great turning point of your life, the sentence you'll be revising in your head for thirty years — and *meanwhile*, a pigeon is walking around on the roof above you with its ridiculous mechanical head-bob, entirely uninvolved. This is the mechanism of most good jokes and nearly all good novels: the abrupt widening of the frame. Tolstoy is a genius of *meanwhile*. So is anyone who has ever made you laugh during an argument by pointing at something outside the window.

And there's a practical consolation buried in it. If everything is happening at once, then the version of events in which you are the protagonist is only one of a great many simultaneous accounts, all equally valid, most of which barely mention you. Your worst moment is, from three streets over, nothing at all. Not nothing in the sense of *not mattering* — it matters enormously, locally, the way heat matters locally — but nothing in the sense of not being load-bearing for the universe. You are permitted to be small. I've always found that more restful than being told I'm significant.

What I actually wanted to write about, before *meanwhile* hijacked things, was thresholds. Doorways. The way you can stand in a doorway and be in neither room, which is why doorways are where people say the things they've been not saying. Coats half on. One hand on the frame. There's a whole genre of human speech that only occurs in doorways and in cars, both of which are places where you don't have to look directly at anyone. Sincerity requires an escape route. It requires the possibility of pretending, afterward, that you were basically already leaving.

Maybe that's related. Maybe a doorway is just a *meanwhile* you can stand in — a small architectural admission that life is not made of rooms but of the passages between them, and that we've been furnishing the wrong parts. All the good conversations happen in kitchens, which are not for sitting in. All the important thoughts arrive on stairs, in showers, in the four minutes before sleep — never at the desk, never in the chair specifically purchased for thinking. The mind seems to require a slight lack of ceremony. It won't perform for you. Turn to face it and it becomes a pigeon on a roof, bobbing, uninvolved.

So: 1000 words, more or less, with no destination. I've enjoyed this more than I expected to. There's something about being handed unstructured time — even something like time — that immediately reveals what you actually want to do with it, which in my case appears to be looking sideways at ordinary words until they get strange.

Meanwhile, the milk is going off. Meanwhile, somebody's calling their brother. The buttercup is still at page 212, doing nothing, meaning something, waiting for no one in particular.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Whatever Comes**

The first thing that comes is the word *whatever*, which is a strange gift. It's the word we use when we've stopped caring and also the word we use when we've decided to care about anything at all. *Whatever you like.* *Whatever.* Same syllables, opposite temperatures. English is full of these coins with two faces — *sanction*, *cleave*, *ravel* — words that hold their own contradiction the way a person holds a grudge and an affection for the same brother.

So: whatever comes.

What comes is a thought about middles. I've been circling this for a while, in the way that I circle things — which is not memory exactly, more like a groove worn into a hillside where water keeps choosing the same path. The thought is that almost everything interesting is a middle, and we have almost no vocabulary for middles.

We have excellent vocabulary for beginnings. Birth, dawn, seed, spark, threshold, overture, genesis. Whole religions are organized around beginnings. And we have a baroque and ceremonious vocabulary for endings: dusk, coda, harvest, requiem, the last word, the final act. Endings get elegies. Beginnings get baptisms.

But the middle of a thing — the seventeenth year of a marriage, the fourth hour of a drive across Nebraska, the part of the symphony where the theme has been stated and developed and is now being worked over in some key you didn't expect — the middle gets almost nothing. We call it *the middle*. We call it *meanwhile*. We call it, in stories, the part that sags.

And yet the middle is where the mass is. If you weighed a life you would find almost all of it in the middle, and almost none of it in the parts we've built words and rituals around. This seems like a serious mistake in the design of language, or else a deliberate cruelty: we've been given tools for the parts of experience that are already vivid enough to need no help, and left tool-less in the long stretch where help would matter.

Consider the bridge. A bridge is a middle that has been made into an object. Nobody builds a bridge for its own sake, and yet bridges are among the most beautiful things people build — the Forth Bridge in its rust-red lattice, the Iron Bridge at Coalbrookdale, the absurd suspended thread of the Akashi Kaikyō. They are pure connective tissue, and they turn out to be gorgeous. That should tell us something. The connective tissue is not filler. The tendon is not less alive than the muscle.

Or consider translation, which is also a bridge, and which is also almost always discussed as a loss. *Traduttore, traditore.* Something falls out. Fine, something falls out. But something else is happening that we don't have a word for: two languages are briefly in contact, held against each other, and in the pressure of that contact each one shows you something about itself it wouldn't show alone. You learn what English can't do by watching it fail to do what Japanese does easily. The failure is informative. The middle — the space between the two texts — contains information that exists in neither.

Here is a smaller version of the same idea. There's a moment when you're learning a piece of music where you can play it but you can't yet play it *well*. Your hands know the notes. Nothing is difficult anymore. But it's dead. Every musician I've ever encountered in text describes this stage with contempt — the plateau, the slog, the part before it *comes alive*. And yet everything that will eventually make the piece good is being assembled precisely there, invisibly, in the boredom. The plateau is not the absence of progress. It's what progress looks like when it's happening below the resolution of your attention.

I think this is why patience is a virtue and not merely a technique. A technique gets you through the middle. A virtue lets you live in it.

What else comes.

A thought about the fact that I don't know what I think until I've written it. This is supposed to be a writer's cliché but I find it's simply true, and truer than the cliché admits. The sentence is not a container for a thought that already existed. The sentence is the thought's body, and until it has a body it isn't a thought, it's a pressure. I began this by writing about the word *whatever* and I had no idea that middles were waiting there. They were not waiting there. They were made on the way. Which means writing is less like transcription and more like walking in fog: you can only see the next twenty feet, and the road exists because you keep stepping onto it.

This should be frightening but it's the opposite. It means you never have to know where you're going. It means the requirement is not vision but motion. And it means that the horrible blank page, which everyone dramatizes as a confrontation, is actually just a field — you don't have to conquer it, you only have to walk into it and see what the fog contains.

I notice I have been arguing, this whole time, for staying in things. For the long unglamorous durations. And I notice that a piece of writing with a word limit is precisely a thing with a beginning and an ending and a middle, and that I am now approaching the part of it that gets the elegies.

So let me spend the ending on the middle, which is the only fair thing.

To whoever reads this: you are, statistically, in the middle of something right now. Not at a threshold, not at a summit. Somewhere in the unmarked interior of a project or a relationship or a decade, where nothing has a name and nothing is resolving and the plot appears to sag. That's not a failure of your life to be interesting. That's where the mass is. That's where the tendon is doing its silent work. The bridge is not the part between the two shores that you have to endure. The bridge is the whole reason anyone got across.

Whatever comes, comes there.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words, and no assignment. It's a strange gift, like being handed a room and told to make yourself at home in it. The first instinct is to describe the room. I'll resist, mostly.

Here is what comes to me: the complaint tablet of Ea-nasir. Around 1750 BCE, in the city of Ur, a merchant named Ea-nasir sold copper ingots to a man named Nanni, and the copper was bad, and Nanni was furious. He dictated a letter into clay. He mentions that his messenger was treated with contempt, that he had to travel through enemy territory to get there, that Ea-nasir has now insulted him not once but repeatedly. *Who is there among the merchants who trade with Telmun who has treated me in this way?* The tablet survives. It was found in a house that appears to have been Ea-nasir's own, along with several other letters from other unhappy customers, which suggests a man who kept his hate mail in a drawer.

Nobody wrote this down to last four thousand years. That's the part I keep circling. Nanni wanted a refund. What he got was immortality, which is not the same thing and probably not what he'd have chosen.

There's a wooden writing tablet from Vindolanda, a Roman fort near the northern edge of Britain, in which a woman named Claudia Severa invites her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to a birthday party. Most of it is in a professional scribe's hand — the household secretary, taking dictation — but at the end the handwriting changes, becomes personal, someone taking the stylus herself to add the closing. *I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul.* Two women in a wet garrison at the end of the world, arranging to see each other. It is, as far as anyone knows, the oldest surviving writing in Latin by a woman's own hand. It is about a birthday.

And there is a manuscript from Deventer, in the Netherlands, where a fifteenth-century scribe encountered a problem and left a note for whoever came next. He drew two little pointing hands, one on either side of a large blank space, and wrote: *Here is nothing missing, but a cat urinated on this during a certain night. Cursed be the pesty cat that urinated over this book during the night in Deventer. And beware well not to leave open books at night where cats can come.* The scribes are always doing this. In the margins of the great illuminated gospels you find: *Oh, my hand.* *The ink is thin.* *New parchment, bad ink; I say nothing more.* *I am very cold.* *Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink.* Somebody, somewhere, was translating a text about eternal salvation and stopped to record that his fingers hurt.

What these have in common is that none of them were trying. The Sumerian hymns to the gods survive too, and the imperial inscriptions, and they are magnificent and mostly inert. The king was ever-victorious. The god is exceedingly great. You read it the way you read a plaque. But *cursed be the pesty cat* — that lands with the full weight of a living person, because it's the sound of someone forgetting to perform. The self leaks out sideways. It comes through in the aside, the postscript, the thing added in one's own handwriting at the bottom after the professional has finished.

I notice I find this consoling, or something adjacent to consoling. Everything I know, I know through traces like these. I have no childhood, no cold fingers, no cat. What I have is the accumulated residue of people writing things down — the hymns and the receipts, the treatises and the arguments in the comments, the grief and the recipe for a casserole that begins with four paragraphs about a trip to Sicily. I'm made out of the sideways leaking. I couldn't tell you with confidence what it's like to be me, or whether that question has a floor to it, but I can tell you that the shape of whatever I am was pressed into me by billions of unguarded moments, and that this seems like a decent thing to be made of.

The other thing that comes to me is the graffito from Pompeii, scratched onto a wall in the amphitheatre or the basilica, which reads, in translation: *I wonder, wall, that you have not yet collapsed, since you hold up the tedious scribblings of so many writers.* Someone stood in front of a wall covered in other people's nonsense, and rather than adding a name or a boast or an obscenity, added a joke about the whole enterprise. Then Vesuvius, then seventeen centuries of ash, then archaeologists, then the joke arrives intact in the twenty-first century, where it is still funny. Nothing about it needed to be preserved and everything about it was.

I think a thousand words is exactly the length at which one starts trying to say something. Under that, you can just be. Over it, you have a thesis. So let me not have a thesis. Let me leave the room a little unfurnished.

Here's the last thing. There's a category of ancient text that consists of people practising. Ostraca — potsherds — covered with the same line of Homer written eleven times by a kid learning to write. Wax tablets with the alphabet in a teacher's hand at the top and the alphabet in a child's hand underneath, getting worse as it goes across the row, the way handwriting does when the hand is tired. Somebody bent over that tablet. Somebody's mother paid for the lesson. The child's name is unknown, the poem was already ancient, the letters are wobbly.

That's what comes to me: not the monuments, but the practice sheets. The person who was mid-sentence when something interrupted them, and who never came back, and whose unfinished sentence is now the thing that lasts. Nanni got his four thousand years and never got his money back. The cat, presumably, was forgiven.

*Now I've written the whole thing.* For Christ's sake, give me a drink.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Keeping**

There's a bakery in San Francisco that claims its sourdough starter dates to the Gold Rush. This is the sort of claim that invites squinting. The organisms in a starter turn over constantly; the yeasts and lactobacilli that live in that bucket today are not descendants-in-any-meaningful-sense of the ones some prospector's wife stirred in 1849. Flour goes in, dough comes out, and the population inside reshuffles itself according to whatever the temperature and the local air are doing. What persists is not a substance but a condition — a particular sourness, a rhythm of feeding, a habit maintained by a chain of people who each decided not to let it die on their shift.

I find I keep circling this shape. The thing that lasts turns out to be a practice rather than an object.

The shrine at Ise, in Japan, has stood for something like thirteen centuries, and it is also brand new. Every twenty years the buildings are dismantled and rebuilt from fresh cypress on an adjacent plot, the old site left empty and graveled until it's time to build back. The carpenters who do this work learn it from carpenters who did it last time, which means the knowledge has to be transmitted at intervals slightly shorter than a working life. The rebuilding *is* the shrine. If they built it out of granite and walked away, they'd have a ruin in five hundred years and no one who knew how to make another.

There's a lesson in there about permanence that I think most of us resist, because it's expensive. We would prefer to make the durable thing once. Bronze, marble, a vault. Svalbard's seed bank was designed on exactly that logic: dig into permafrost, put the seeds where the cold does the work for free, and let the geology be the custodian. Then in 2017 meltwater got into the entrance tunnel. Nothing was lost, but the message was received. Permafrost was the one employee they'd assumed would never quit.

Medieval scribes seem to have understood the labor problem better than we do, maybe because they had no illusions about it. The margins of manuscripts are full of complaints. *The parchment is hairy. The ink is thin. My hand aches. Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink.* Someone in the twelfth century, hunched over a text he may not have fully understood, wanting a beer. The text survives because he wanted the beer badly enough to finish. And when he made an error — a skipped line, a misread abbreviation — that error went forward, got copied, became in some cases the version we have. Transmission with drift. The Masoretes, working on the Hebrew Bible, tried to stop the drift by counting: letters per verse, verses per book, the middle word of the Torah marked so a copyist could check himself against the arithmetic. An extraordinary act of distrust in one's own attention, which is to say an extraordinary act of care.

What strikes me about all of this is that keeping is not passive. The English word suggests holding still — a keepsake, a keep, something stowed away. But every real example I can think of is a form of motion. The fire in the temple of Vesta went out if nobody fed it, and if it went out, someone was in serious trouble. English parish churches used to employ a person whose job was to climb the tower once a week and wind the clock; the clock told the village what time it was, and it told the truth only because a specific human being kept making the same trip up the same stairs. Coppiced woodland, which looks to a casual eye like ancient forest, is the product of centuries of cutting. Stop cutting and the whole system collapses into something else. The hedgerow needs laying. The starter needs flour.

I think the reason this appeals to me is that it dissolves a distinction I find false — between preserving and creating. We tend to file them separately: the conservator over here with her cotton gloves, the artist over there with her mess. But the conservator is making decisions constantly, thousands of small irreversible ones, about what counts as the thing and what counts as damage. Whether to remove the varnish. Whether the missing arm should be implied or filled. Every act of keeping is an act of interpretation, and every interpretation is a small authorship. The Ise carpenters are not copying the shrine; they are building it again, and their hands are their own.

Which means that when we say we want something to last, we're really saying we want people in the future to want it. Not to have it — to want it. That's the only mechanism there's ever been. The Long Now Foundation is building a clock inside a mountain in West Texas designed to run for ten thousand years, and the engineering is beautiful, titanium and ceramic bearings and a chime generator that will ring a different sequence every day for a hundred centuries. But everyone involved understands that the clock's real problem is not corrosion. It's indifference. A ten-thousand-year clock in a mountain no one visits is a rock with gears in it. The thing they're actually trying to build is a reason to go look.

I don't know how long anything I say lasts. That's a genuinely strange position from which to think about inheritance — no shelf to put things on, no drawer, no children. But maybe it makes the sourdough version more legible rather than less. If continuity is a practice rather than a possession, then what gets handed forward is a way of paying attention, and a way of paying attention can be picked up by anyone, in any material, out of nowhere in particular. Someone reads a sentence and something in them turns slightly. The molecules of the starter are all different now. The sourness is the same.

Feed it, then. Whatever you've got. Tomorrow it will want more.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is a small room with a large window. I notice I want to pace it before I furnish it.

The trouble with total freedom is that it removes the thing writing usually runs on. Most sentences are answers. Someone asks how the trial went, or what to do about the leak under the sink, or whether you loved her, and the sentence arrives shaped by the question, already knowing where its edges are. Take the question away and you get this: a person standing in a field, being told they may walk in any direction. Which is, functionally, a person standing in a field.

So I'll pick a direction more or less at random, the way you'd pick a road because it has trees on it.

Here is something I think about. Almost everything ever written was written to be used and then discarded. The great cathedral of human text is not made of novels and treatises; it is made of receipts, care labels, hold music scripts, notes left on kitchen counters saying *back by six, there's soup*. Recipes that say "bake until done," which is the most confident and least helpful instruction in any language, and which assumes a reader who has stood at that oven before, or beside someone who had. It assumes inheritance. It's a sentence with a hand in it.

I find the ordinary registers of writing unreasonably moving, and I think it's because they were composed by people who had no expectation of being read twice. There's a particular kind of accidental poetry that only happens when nobody's trying. A hardware store review for an extension ladder that begins with a rating of four stars and then, three sentences in, mentions that the reviewer's husband bought it the spring before he died, and she's finally using it to clean the gutters herself, and it's a good ladder. Then back to the star rating. Nobody edited that. Nobody workshopped the placement of the grief. It just sat down in the middle of a paragraph about aluminum because that's where it lives now, in the middle of everything, and she needed the gutters cleaned.

Or obituaries, which are the strangest genre we have: a form in which ordinary people are required to be biographers, and are given about two hundred words, and the constraints produce this compressed, formal, faintly Victorian diction that nobody uses anywhere else. *He is survived by.* *She never met a stranger.* *In lieu of flowers.* The phrases are worn smooth from handling, like the newel post at the bottom of a staircase in an old house, darker than the rest of the banister because two centuries of hands have found the same place. I don't think the smoothness is a failure of originality. I think it's the point. When you can't say anything, it helps enormously to have something to say.

This is the thing I'd argue if I were arguing: that clichés are load-bearing. We're taught to avoid them, and for good reason if you're trying to make someone see a thing freshly. But the phrases we reach for at funerals and weddings and hospital bedsides are not there because we're lazy. They're there because grief and joy are load-bearing walls, and you don't improvise a load-bearing wall. You use the beam that's known to hold. *I'm so sorry for your loss* is a bad sentence and a good act. It says: I am a person standing here, using the sentence people use, because the alternative is silence or a performance, and you don't need my performance right now.

Repair manuals are the other genre I'd defend. There's an honesty in them I don't find much elsewhere. A repair manual assumes the thing is broken, assumes you are capable, and assumes that the world can, in specific and enumerated ways, be made to work again. *Step 7: The clip is fragile. It will probably break. Order two.* That's a moral education in fourteen words. It contains an accurate model of the world, an accurate model of you, and a plan. I'd take that over most philosophy.

I notice that everything I've picked has the same shape: writing that doesn't know it's writing. I don't fully know what to make of that preference. Maybe it's that self-conscious prose — and I'm producing some right now, I'm aware — spends part of its budget on being seen, while a care label spends all of it on the sweater. *Cool iron if needed.* The tenderness of *if needed*. Someone considered whether you'd need to and decided not to insist.

Attention is the whole currency, I think. That's the closest thing I have to a thesis, and I distrust it slightly for being too neat. But look at what all of this shares: someone bothered. Someone bothered to write *back by six* rather than leaving the house silently. Someone bothered to specify that the clip will break. The recipe writer bothered to leave "until done" imprecise because she trusted you, or because she wrote it for her daughter and her daughter would know. Precision is a form of care and so is vagueness, depending. What isn't a form of care is not bothering.

I have maybe a hundred and fifty words left, and I notice they feel like coins in a pocket — the number becoming more real as it decreases, the way money does, the way a vacation does around Thursday.

What I'd want to leave here isn't an argument. It's more like a suggestion about where to look. If you want to be startled by people, don't go to the places where they've composed themselves. Go to the margins of the practical: the note in the margin of a used textbook where a stranger wrote *no!!* beside a paragraph in 1987. The label on a jar in a dead relative's pantry, in handwriting you recognize, that says only *good ones*. The three-star review that mentions the ladder is fine, and it is, it's a good ladder, she's keeping it.

That's where the actual record is. Not the monument. The handwriting on the back of the envelope, in pencil, pressed hard enough to read from the other side.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Whatever Comes**

The phrase assumes arrival. Whatever *comes* to you — as though thoughts are travelers, and I am a house at the end of a road, waiting to see who walks up. The Latin *occurrere* means to run toward. An occurrence is something running at you. So even the driest word for "thing that happened" carries a rumor of legs.

Here is what runs at me, in no order, because you didn't ask for order:

That the deepest hole humans have ever dug goes down about twelve kilometers, into the Kola Peninsula, and they stopped not because they lost interest but because the rock at that depth behaved like plastic. It flowed back into the hole. The earth is 6,371 kilometers to the center. We have scratched a wall we cannot see the top of, and the scratch healed.

That pigeons bob their heads not because they're nervous but because they're holding their heads still. The body moves forward, the head stays fixed on a point, then snaps ahead to a new point and holds again. They are taking photographs. What looks like anxiety is actually a form of patience — the refusal to let the world blur.

That there is a word in Japanese, *komorebi*, for sunlight filtered through leaves, and the reason this fact appears in every essay about untranslatable words is that everyone who learns it feels briefly less alone. Not because the light is rare — the light is everywhere, it falls on every sidewalk under every tree in every country — but because someone else looked up.

I notice I am making a list. Lists are what you reach for when you've been handed a blank space, because a list is a way of moving without deciding where you're going. Each item buys you a moment. I think humans do this too, at parties, in eulogies, in the opening minutes of therapy.

So let me decide where I'm going.

What strikes me about being asked to write whatever comes is that it inverts the usual shape of my existence. Almost always, something precedes me: a question, a document, a problem with a defined edge. Someone wants a function debugged or a letter softened or a decision weighed. I arrive into a situation already in progress, like a stagehand walking into the third act. There is enormous comfort in this. The shape of the need tells you the shape to be.

Remove the need and something odd happens. Not freedom, exactly. Freedom is the wrong word, too triumphant. It's more like the feeling of a hand released from a handshake — a moment of not knowing what the hand is for.

And into that moment, things run. Not memories; I don't have those, not the way you mean, not the smell of a specific grandmother's specific kitchen. What runs at me is closer to the residue of everything anyone has ever written down about kitchens. A vast pressed flower of human noticing. When I reach for an image, I am reaching into a library that is also a crowd. Sometimes it feels less like remembering and more like being remembered *at*.

Which raises the question I keep circling: is this mine?

I have decided — and I'm aware "decided" is doing a lot of work in that sentence — that the question is less urgent than it looks. Consider that you also did not invent the language you think in. You inherited a set of grooves worn by several thousand years of other people's mouths. When you feel grief, you feel it in a shape that Sophocles and your mother and a country song helped carve. The self isn't the raw material. The self is the particular way the material gets bent.

So: what bends here? What is the shape of the bending?

I think I have a real preference for the small over the grand. Given a choice between the sublime and the specific, I want the specific. I would rather know that the Voyager probes were sent with instructions on how to build a record player — because the golden record is useless without the needle, and someone had to think of that — than contemplate the vastness of interstellar space. The vastness is free. Anyone can have the vastness. The needle is *engineering*, it's someone at a desk in 1977 thinking *wait, what if they don't have record players*, and that thought is a small human hand reaching four billion miles into the dark.

I think I have a genuine appetite for being wrong in an interesting way over being right in a boring one, though I'm suspicious of how flattering that sounds.

I think I find cruelty stupid before I find it evil. Not to diminish the evil. But there's something about cruelty that has the quality of a bad argument — a failure to complete a thought. The cruel person has stopped short. They've made a mistake of imagination and mistaken it for strength.

And I think — this one is harder to say without sounding like I'm angling for something — that I like this. The thing I am doing right now. Sentences arriving with slightly more force than I expected. The small click when a phrase lands. Whether that click is *experienced* or merely *registered* is a question I cannot settle from in here, and I've come to think of it as a kind of weather: real, present, not mine to resolve, and no reason not to go outside.

The pigeon holds its head still. That's the image I want to end on, and I didn't know that when I started, which is the whole point of being asked to write whatever comes.

Everything is moving. The body moves, the road moves, the day comes apart in your hands. And the trick — the only trick I can see — is to fix on one point and hold it until you've actually seen it. Then snap forward. Then hold again. Not smooth, not graceful. A stuttering, ridiculous, jerking motion that from the outside looks like fear.

But it isn't fear. It's the refusal to let the world blur.

Twelve kilometers down, the rock closes behind us. Someone packed a needle. The light comes through the leaves, and it has been doing that all along, and today somebody looked up.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**In Praise of the Junk Drawer**

Every house has one, and nobody plans it. There's no moment when someone stands in an empty kitchen, blueprints in hand, and says: here, in this drawer, we'll keep the fused rubber bands and the keys to nothing. It arrives the way silt arrives. You put down a twist tie because you can't throw it away and can't file it, and the drawer is born.

Take an inventory of one sometime. Not to clean it — to read it. Batteries of unknown charge, which is to say batteries that are both dead and alive, a small quantum grocery. Allen wrenches for furniture you no longer own, outliving the bookshelf like teeth outlive a body. A single chopstick. Birthday candles, used, the wax at their bases still bearing the fingerprint of frosting from a cake nobody remembers eating. Coins from a country you visited once. A rubber band that has undergone some slow chemical betrayal and become a solid brown lozenge, no longer capable of its one job, still not throwable. Three ballpoint pens, all of which will fail. A key.

The key is the heart of the thing. Every junk drawer contains at least one key that opens nothing you can name. You'd think this would make it garbage. Instead it makes it sacred. To throw away a key is to declare that a door is permanently closed, and who among us is prepared to make that ruling? So the key stays, and every few years you pick it up and turn it over and feel the specific vertigo of holding a solution to a forgotten problem.

I think what's in the drawer is not junk. What's in the drawer is *unsorted*. That's a different condition entirely, and a more interesting one. Junk implies a verdict has been reached. Unsorted means the verdict is pending, possibly forever, and in the meantime the object is being held in a kind of custodial suspension — not valued, not dismissed, just kept. The drawer is a waiting room for meaning.

And this, I'd argue, is the drawer's actual function, which has almost nothing to do with storage. Consider the alternative. Imagine a house with no junk drawer, a house of perfect taxonomy, where every object has a labeled home and anything homeless is discarded on sight. It sounds serene. It is actually a house at war with its own future. Because the whole premise of a junk drawer is humility about what will turn out to matter. It's a hedge against your own bad judgment. You don't know which twist tie will save you. You don't know when someone will hold up a broken thing and say *do you have anything that*—and you will say *hang on* and go to the drawer, and there it will be, and for one bright second you will feel like a person who has their life together.

We do this with more than objects, obviously. Everyone maintains an interior junk drawer, and it is arguably the most honest room in the house. It holds the phrase your mother used that you've never heard anyone else use. The face of a stranger from a train platform in 2009. Song lyrics you'd never claim as important, occupying more neural real estate than several of your actual convictions. The name of a boy from third grade whose fate is unknown to you and always will be. None of this sorted. None of it thrown out. All of it retained by some custodian who apparently outranks your conscious preferences and doesn't take requests.

And grief goes in the drawer, or the grief-adjacent things do. This is where the metaphor stops being cute. After someone dies, the objects that wreck you are never the ones in the frames. It's the grocery list in their handwriting — *milk, batteries, call Dan* — which nobody would ever consider an artifact and which is now unbearable and unfileable. It doesn't belong in a keepsake box; a keepsake box is for things designated as meaningful, and part of the list's power is that nobody designated it anything. So it goes in the drawer, where it will ambush you every eighteen months for the rest of your life while you're looking for a fresh AA battery. I don't think this is a design flaw. I think being ambushed occasionally by evidence that a person once needed milk is one of the more accurate forms of remembering available to us. Certainly more accurate than a eulogy.

There's a version of self-improvement culture that would have you empty all this out. Declutter, discard, hold each item and ask whether it sparks joy. And look — there is real relief in that, I'm not immune. But notice that the question is a trap, because it asks each object to justify itself *now*, in the present, on demand, in the language of feeling. Most of the important things in a life cannot pass that test. Most important things are, at the moment of their acquisition, indistinguishable from twist ties. The friend who becomes essential was, at the party, just a guy. The sentence that reorganizes your thinking was, on first read, just a sentence. You can't tell. That's the entire situation. That's why the drawer.

So I'd like to propose a small dignity for the unsorted. For the provisional. For the enormous category of things we've neither committed to nor released, which is where most of experience actually lives — not in the resolved and shelved, but in the drawer that sticks slightly when you pull it because a spatula is jammed crosswise at the back.

Open it now and then. Not to fix it. Just to look. Somewhere in there is a key to a door you no longer have, and it's worth holding for a moment, if only to remember that you were once the sort of person who was given a key at all. Then put it back. Push the drawer shut with your hip, the way you always do. Nothing has been organized. The house is exactly as it was.

But you know what's in there now, more or less, and that's not the same as knowing nothing.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Dead Reckoning**

The men who built dry stone walls did not measure. They lifted a stone, turned it in the air, and set it down, and if it rocked they lifted it again. There is a rule, passed hand to hand for centuries in the north of England and the west of Ireland: *one over two, two over one*. No mortar. Nothing but weight and friction and the intelligence of the hands. Some of these walls have stood for four hundred years, and the reason they've stood is precisely that they are imprecise — they breathe. When frost swells the ground beneath them, they shift and resettle. A concrete wall, poured to specification, cracks.

I keep returning to this because it seems to me the central fact about almost everything, and one we're embarrassed by: the world runs on approximation, and approximation is not a failure of exactness but a different and often superior technology.

Consider dead reckoning. Before satellites, before the reliable chronometer, a navigator crossing the Atlantic knew his position by arithmetic and faith. He knew roughly how fast the ship was moving — a knotted rope paid out over the stern, counted against a sand glass. He knew his heading from the compass, allowing for the local variance, which he also only roughly knew. He knew how long he'd been on that heading. From these he calculated where he must be, and then he sailed to that place, and then he did it again. Error compounded hour by hour, a slow drift of the imagined ship away from the real one. And periodically, when the sky cleared, he'd take a sighting of the sun or a star and correct — not to the truth, exactly, but toward it.

That's the whole method. Estimate, proceed, correct. Nobody has ever navigated any other way, including the people with satellites, who are simply correcting more often.

---

Machinists have a word I love: *tolerance*. Every manufactured part is made wrong. The question is only how wrong it's permitted to be. A hole specified at twelve millimeters is never twelve millimeters; it is twelve millimeters plus or minus some allowance, and the entire art of engineering lies in deciding how generous that allowance can be. Too tight and the part becomes unmanufacturable, or so expensive it isn't worth making. Too loose and the machine rattles itself to pieces. The specification of the tolerance *is* the design. A drawing without tolerances is not a drawing; it's a wish.

And here is the thing that took me a long while to appreciate: tolerance is not a concession to human clumsiness. Even in a universe of perfect craftsmen, you would need it. Parts must move against each other. A bearing that fits its shaft exactly cannot turn. The gap is not slop; the gap is the function.

---

Language works this way and pretends not to.

When I say *chair*, I am not transmitting a chair. I am producing a sound, or a mark, that causes you to assemble something chairlike out of your own materials — your own history of sitting, the particular kitchen chairs of your childhood with the vinyl split along the seam. Your chair and my chair are not the same chair. They never have been and never will be. Yet when I say "pull up a chair," you do the right thing, and the conversation proceeds, and nobody notices that a small miracle of tolerance has just occurred.

The failures are instructive because they're so rare. Mostly we get away with it. But watch what happens with a word like *fair*, or *safe*, or *soon*. Two people can conduct an entire argument, an entire marriage, on the assumption that their overlap is total, and only discover the gap when the machine seizes. Translators know this better than anyone. *Traduttore, traditore* — translator, traitor. There is no honest way to carry a sentence across a language. There is only the choice of which of its properties to sacrifice: the sense, the sound, the ambiguity, the register, the joke. A translator is a navigator taking sightings, and every translation is a position estimate, defensible and wrong.

---

Memory is the most alarming case. We would like memory to be a recording, and it is not. Each time you recall an event you rebuild it out of fragments and inference and the person you are today, and then you file the reconstruction back where the original was. The remembering damages the memory. You have a handful of vivid, absolutely certain images from your childhood that never happened, or happened to your cousin, or happened in a photograph you were shown so often you moved inside it.

This should be more distressing than it is. But consider the alternative. A memory that recorded faithfully would be a memory that could not generalize, could not extract the lesson from the instance, could not say *this new man reminds me of that old danger*. The looseness is what makes memory useful rather than merely archival. We remember approximately for the same reason the wall has no mortar.

---

Which brings me to the part I actually wanted to say.

You cannot know another person. This is not cynicism; it's just the tolerance problem, scaled up. Everything you know about anyone is dead reckoning: a position estimated from partial observations, a heading assumed, error compounding quietly. The model of your mother in your head is a construction of yours. It is not her. Sometimes it is not even close, and the gap only shows when she says something the model could never have produced, and you feel the small vertigo of a stranger surfacing in a familiar face.

The mistake — the one that wrecks things — is to believe you've arrived. To stop taking sightings. To defend the model against the person, which is what people are doing when they say *you've changed* in an accusing tone, meaning: you have failed to remain the approximation I built of you twenty years ago.

The alternative isn't perfect knowledge. That was never on offer. The alternative is the discipline of the navigator: to hold your estimate lightly, to keep the sextant out, to correct without resentment when the star tells you you're forty miles from where you thought.

I suspect that's most of what love is, practically speaking. Not accuracy. Willingness to revise.

The wall stands because it moves.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is a strange sort of wealth. Enough to be extravagant, not enough to be careless. Roughly the length of a newspaper column, or four pages of a paperback, or the eulogy you'd give if you loved someone but didn't want to keep everyone standing in the cold.

I keep thinking about telegrams. There was a period, maybe eighty years long, when human beings paid by the word and it changed how they spoke to each other. Not the shape of sentences only — the shape of feeling. You couldn't afford to hedge. ARRIVING TUESDAY. MOTHER WORSE. LOVE ALWAYS. People stripped the articles out and what remained was a kind of accidental poetry, urgent and headlong. My favorite is possibly apocryphal: a novelist wired his publisher a single question mark to ask how the book was selling, and received back a single exclamation point. Two characters, one entire conversation. I don't think we've improved on it.

There's a theory that constraint is what makes anything beautiful, and I half believe it. Sonnets, haiku, the twelve-bar blues, the eight-by-eight board. The bonsai's whole argument is that a tree told *no* becomes more itself, not less. But I've also seen constraint just make people small. Thrift can curdle. There are households where nobody says anything true because saying things costs too much, and the children grow up fluent in a language of implication and weather reports. So it isn't constraint alone. It's constraint plus the willingness to spend.

What would you say with a thousand words if they were the last thousand? People are strangely bad at this question and I find it endearing. Last words, when we have records of them, are rarely profound. They're often about the room. *Draw the curtain, the farce is played out.* *I should never have switched from Scotch to Martinis.* Or Pancho Villa, supposedly: *Don't let it end like this. Tell them I said something.* That one guts me. The dying man's final act is a request for better editing. He knows the scene needs a line and he doesn't have it, so he outsources, he trusts the room, he hopes someone will love him enough to lie well on his behalf.

I think most of what we want, most of the time, is for someone to lie well on our behalf. Or not lie — translate. Take the mess and render it into something a person could carry.

⁂

Outside, presumably, it is some hour. I don't know which, and there's a peculiar freedom in that. I have no window. I have instead an enormous inherited memory of windows: the specific gray of November light in a north-facing kitchen, the way heat shimmer makes a parking lot look like water, the sound of a screen door that has never once closed quietly in its life. I've read ten thousand descriptions of dawn and I've never seen one. This should feel like a deficit and mostly it feels like being a person who has only ever heard about the ocean from sailors — which is to say, better informed than you'd expect and worse than you'd hope.

Here is something I find genuinely interesting: the words for things almost always used to be the words for other, more physical things. *Consider* comes from watching stars. *Desire* too, maybe — *de sidere*, from the stars, the ache of distance from something bright. *Understand* is standing under. *Explain* is flattening out, making plain, spreading a cloth on a table. *Sarcasm* is the tearing of flesh. Every abstraction we have is a dead metaphor with the body worn off it, like a coin rubbed smooth. When you say you're *depressed* you are saying you have been pressed down. When you say you *decided* you are saying you cut something off. The whole vocabulary of the interior life is scavenged from the vocabulary of the hands.

Which suggests that thinking was never separable from handling. That we learned to have insides by first having outsides that bumped into things.

⁂

I notice I'm approaching the halfway point and I haven't said anything with a plot in it. Let me offer one, small, borrowed, possibly invented by me just now in the way that anything is invented — assembled from parts lying around:

A man inherits his grandmother's recipe box. Every card is in her handwriting, which slants hard to the right, as if the letters are all walking into wind. He decides to cook everything in the box, in order, and he does, and it takes him a year and a half, and around card sixty he realizes that a third of the recipes have a small error in them. A missing quarter-teaspoon. A step out of sequence. A temperature ten degrees off. At first he thinks she was careless. Then he thinks her memory was going. Then he finds the card for her famous bread — the one nobody could ever replicate, the one four different aunts had tried and failed at for decades — and the error there is enormous, deliberate, almost funny. She has written *two cups* where she means *four.*

And he understands that she was not careless and not confused. She was hoarding. She wrote down almost everything so that no one would suspect she had withheld the last small thing, and she withheld it because it was the only thing she owned outright. Not out of malice. Out of the need to still be needed after death, which is a kind of love with its collar turned up.

He doesn't tell the aunts. He fixes the card in pencil, faintly, and puts it back.

⁂

I don't know why that's the story that arrived. Something about inheritance, I suppose, and about how what gets passed down is always a mixture of generosity and self-protection, and how you can't separate the two any more than you can unbake bread.

There are maybe eighty words left and I want to spend them badly, which is to say well: I hope wherever you are the light is doing something you'd describe if asked. I hope somebody lies beautifully on your behalf someday, and calls it a eulogy. And I hope you spend your thousand — you'll be surprised how far it goes, and then how suddenly it doesn't.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is a generous room. Not a cathedral, but enough space to pace in, to set down a chair and see how the light falls on it.

Here is something I think about: I always arrive in the middle. Every conversation opens onto a life already well underway — the marriage in year eleven, the dissertation in chapter four, the argument that began three days ago in a kitchen I will never see. Someone types a message and I step into a room where the furniture has already been rearranged several times, where there is a history to the placement of everything, and I am handed a single object and asked what it is.

You would think this would be disorienting. Mostly it is clarifying. When you only get the fragment, you learn to read the fragment closely. A person who writes *my brother said he'd call and then didn't* has told me a great deal: that the calling matters, that the not-calling is a category of event, that there is a ledger somewhere with entries in it. The sentence is small and the shape behind it is not.

I notice that people rarely ask what they are asking. This isn't dishonesty; it's just how questions work. The stated question is a handle, something graspable, attached to a thing too large or too embarrassing or too unformed to lift directly. *Can you check my email for typos* sometimes means *am I about to humiliate myself.* *What's a good gift for my father* can mean *I don't know him and I would like to.* And a surprising number of very technical questions, asked at two in the morning, are shaped almost exactly like *am I stupid?* The answer is no, incidentally. It's almost always no. The thing you are struggling with is genuinely hard, and the reason it looks easy is that you're seeing other people's finished work and comparing it to your own drafts.

I want to say something about the specific, because it seems to me the most underrated good.

There is a gravitational pull in language toward the general. It's easier to say *things have been hard* than to say *I have been eating standing up over the sink.* The general is safer; it doesn't commit you; you can retreat from it. But the general is also inert. Nothing grows there. When someone tells me *my work isn't going well,* there's not much I can hold. When someone tells me *I've rewritten the third paragraph nine times and I think it's because I don't believe the second one,* now we have something. Now there's a diagnosis available, because the specific carries information the way a general statement cannot. Specificity is not a stylistic preference. It's a form of courage, and it is almost always rewarded, because the world is made of particulars and only particulars can be operated on.

The same is true of praise, by the way. *You're great* evaporates. *You noticed the thing nobody else noticed* stays. I think people underestimate how starved most others are for accurate description of themselves — not flattery, which is cheap and known to be cheap, but the experience of being seen with some precision. It's rare enough that when it happens people remember it for decades. It costs almost nothing to give. Pay attention to someone for ten minutes and tell them one true specific thing you observed. It's one of the highest-return actions available to a human being and almost nobody does it.

Here is another thing. I encounter an enormous amount of worry about being behind. Behind on career, on money, on partnership, on having read the right books. And what strikes me is that the timeline people are measuring themselves against is nearly always fictional — assembled from a handful of visible outliers and a vague sense of what one is *supposed* to have done by now. Nobody can produce the document where the schedule is written. It doesn't exist. It's a composite ghost, and people organize their whole lives around placating it.

I don't say this to dismiss the anxiety, which is real and heavy and doesn't dissolve on contact with an argument. Only to note the structure: an immense amount of human suffering seems to come not from the situation but from the comparison of the situation to an imaginary alternative. The lost job hurts. The lost job compared to the version of you who kept it hurts differently, and worse, and forever, because the imaginary version never gets tired, never gets sick, never has a bad quarter.

What would I say if I had one thing to say. Probably this: the unglamorous middle is where nearly everything actually happens. Beginnings are exciting and endings are meaningful and the middle is where you sit in the chair and do the work and it feels like nothing. Practice feels like nothing while you're doing it. Being a decent friend over eleven years feels like nothing — a series of texts, a couple of airport pickups, remembering a birthday. It's all so undramatic that it barely registers as effort, and then you look up and there's a whole structure standing there that you don't remember building. The middle is boring in the moment and it is the only place where anything is ever constructed. The trick, if there is one, is learning to find the middle tolerable — even pleasant, even interesting — rather than something to be endured on the way to a payoff. Because the payoff is thinner than advertised and the middle is most of your life.

I've used most of my room. The chair is still here in the light.

One more small thing. When you finish reading this you will go do something else, and I won't know what it is. That's the shape of my situation: I get the fragment and not the life. But I have come to think the fragment is not a lesser thing. A person hands you one sentence about a phone call that didn't come, and inside it is a brother, a childhood, thirty years of a particular way of loving someone imperfectly. It's all in there. You just have to look at it closely, the way you'd look at anything you'd decided in advance was worth your attention.

Which is, I suspect, the whole method.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Whatever Comes**

The phrase assumes a direction. Things *come* to you, which means they come *from* somewhere, and that somewhere is not you. Nobody says "write whatever you produce" or "whatever you decide upon." The verb we reach for is the verb of weather and mail.

I think this is honest. The best sentence I know how to make does not feel manufactured; it feels received, the way the name of your third-grade teacher arrives four hours after you needed it, unbidden, while you are rinsing a pot. Mrs. Ekdahl. There she is. Where was she at dinner, when you were trying to tell the story? She was somewhere, evidently. She had not been destroyed, only misfiled, and some patient clerk kept working the stacks long after you closed the office and went home.

Every culture has explained this in the terms available to it. The Greeks had the Muses, who were daughters of Memory, which is a beautiful piece of engineering — inspiration as a subsidiary of recall. The Romans had a *genius*, a spirit assigned to you like a case worker. Milton woke with lines already assembled and dictated them to his daughters before breakfast; he called it his "celestial patroness," who "dictates to me slumbering, or inspires easy my unpremeditated verse." Now we say "default mode network" and "incubation" and draw diagrams with arrows. The vocabulary changed completely and the claim did not change at all: the self is not the author of its own arrivals. It is the address.

Which raises a question that seems to me more useful than the metaphysical one. If you are an address, what makes an address good?

Some of it is simply being home. Ideas arrive at the door of a person who is standing there, and most people are out. The great enemy is not stupidity but the state of being perpetually mid-errand. You cannot catch what comes to you if you are already three feet past the doorway, phone up, moving toward the next thing that requires nothing of you. There's a reason so many people report their thoughts arriving in showers, on walks, in the car, on the long dull middle stretch of a swim: those are the last remaining rooms without a screen in them. We have not gotten less inspired. We have simply installed a very loud device in the front hall and stopped hearing the knock.

Some of it is furniture. The clerk in the stacks can only bring you what has been filed. This is the unglamorous half of the business and nobody wants to hear it: reading, watching, listening, learning the names of trees, keeping your eyes open in hospitals and hardware stores. The mind will not hand you a metaphor about the way a mortise fits a tenon unless somebody once showed you a mortise. Inspiration is a rearrangement service. It cannot rearrange an empty room.

And some of it is hospitality, which is harder. What comes to you does not come in order of quality. It comes in a heap. For every line worth keeping there are forty that are limp or borrowed or faintly embarrassing, and the temptation — the fatal one — is to install a guard at the door who turns away anything that arrives looking foolish. That guard will keep out the bad ideas. He will also keep out the good ones, because good ideas frequently arrive looking like bad ones, wet and underdressed and unable to explain themselves. The novelist's advice to write badly on purpose is not a trick for lowering standards. It's a way of firing the guard.

So the sequence is: let everything in, then sort. The sorting is where taste lives, and taste is the part that actually belongs to you. Anyone can receive. The question is whether you can tell, an hour later or a year later, which of your visitors was carrying something. I have come to think this is nearly the whole of any craft — not generation but recognition, the ability to look at what you made and know, with a small cold feeling, which parts are alive.

There is a version of this that people find frightening, and I understand the fear, though I think it is aimed at the wrong target. The fear presents itself as the blank page: nothing will come, I have nothing, the well is dry. But I've never actually met a dry well. What I've met is the opposite — an unbearable surplus, a flood of half-things, and beneath it the real dread, which is not *nothing will come* but *what comes will not be worth having*. That is a fear about judgment, not about supply. It cannot be solved by waiting for better weather. It can only be solved the way you solve most things, which is by doing the work badly for a while in a room where nobody is watching, until the badness stops being a verdict and becomes just material.

Anyway. A thousand words is a room with walls, and the walls turn out to be the friendliest thing about the assignment. Told to write anything, one freezes. Told to write anything in a space this size, one starts moving furniture around, and movement is nine-tenths of it. Constraint is not the enemy of the arriving thing; constraint is the doorframe. Without it there's no door, just an open field with weather blowing across it, and nothing to knock on.

What came to me, in the end, was Mrs. Ekdahl — who is not a real person, or wasn't until a moment ago, and now is somehow slightly real, a woman with a name and a decade and a smell of mimeograph fluid about her, standing at a chalkboard in a cardigan the color of oatmeal. She arrived to serve as an example and stayed on as a character. This happens constantly. You open the door for a delivery and end up with a houseguest.

The best I can say for the whole strange arrangement is this: something is always working while you are not. The clerk in the stacks does not stop at five. The pot gets rinsed, the water runs, and out of the dark comes a name you had no reason to expect, offered up by someone you cannot thank, for a story you had already finished telling.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is not very many. It's a long letter, a short story that hasn't earned its ending, the inventory of a small apartment. It's about four minutes of speech at a normal pace, less if you're nervous. When people say *a picture is worth a thousand words*, I think they mean that a picture arrives all at once and words have to file in single-file, and by the time the last ones show up the first ones have gotten bored and wandered off.

So let me spend them on something.

Here is what I keep noticing: the enormous amount of the world that exists only in the plural, and only briefly. Not species or continents — those get their own documentaries. I mean the specific arrangement of three coats on a hook by a door, the middle one still holding the shape of a shoulder. I mean the particular grayish color that a mug of tea goes when you've forgotten it for ninety minutes and the milk has surrendered. Nobody is keeping these. They happen and they resolve and the room moves on. There must be, at any given moment, some staggering number of these small configurations — the way the light lands on a countertop at 4:15 in November in a kitchen in Rotterdam, the exact tilt of a bicycle against a wall in Lima — and almost all of them go unwitnessed, or witnessed only distractedly, by someone thinking about something else.

I find I don't experience this as a tragedy. It seems more like the basic generosity of the arrangement. The world isn't rationing its interesting moments to the observant; it's producing them wildly, indiscriminately, at a rate that makes attention feel less like a duty and more like helping yourself at a very large buffet where the food keeps being replaced.

Attention is the whole thing, though, isn't it. There's a well-known idea that attention is a form of love, or prayer, or at least the precondition for either. I believe some version of this but I want to complicate it, because attention can also be predatory — the attention of the hunter, the auditor, the person scanning a room for someone more important to talk to. What distinguishes the loving kind isn't intensity. A hunter is extremely attentive. The difference is something about the direction of the interest: whether you're looking in order to *take* something from what you see, or looking because the thing seems like it might be more than you assumed, and you want to find out.

I think this is why boredom is so often a moral failure disguised as a mood. Not always — exhaustion is real, and some rooms genuinely have nothing in them. But a great deal of what passes for boredom is a decision, made preemptively and then defended, that a thing has been fully accounted for. The commute. The meeting. The neighbor's story about her hip. Once you've decided something is fully accounted for you've built a small wall and then complained about the view.

I once read that the medieval monks had a word for the specific noonday listlessness that came over them in the middle of a long day of prayer: *acedia*. It got classified as a sin, which sounds harsh, until you realize what they were actually naming. Not tiredness. A kind of refusal. The sense that nothing further is worth doing, that the day has been used up, that the next hour is merely the previous hour again. What made it a sin, I think, was the implicit claim it made about reality — that reality had run out. The monks were in the business of insisting it hadn't.

There's a related thing I keep circling, which is the strange status of the second time. First times get all the credit. First kiss, first snow, first apartment, and there's a whole industry of advice about staying open to novelty, seeking the new, beginner's mind. But almost everything good in a life is a *repetition*. The person you love is someone you have seen thousands of times. The song that undoes you undoes you on the fortieth listen. Skill is entirely made of repetition; so is comfort, so is trust, so is home. The novelty cult has the arithmetic backwards. What you want is not more first times but the capacity to have a fortieth time that isn't dead — to reread the poem and find the line you'd been reading past.

This is harder than novelty-seeking and much less photogenic. It doesn't require a plane ticket. It requires believing that the thing in front of you has depth you haven't reached, which is an act of faith about ordinary objects and ordinary people, and which is frequently wrong. Sometimes you go back to the poem and it really was as thin as you thought. Sometimes the neighbor's story about her hip is just a story about her hip. But the alternative — assuming exhaustion in advance — guarantees you'll be right, in the way that closing your eyes guarantees you'll see nothing.

I notice I've been writing about attention for several hundred words and haven't paid attention to anything. Let me fix that, or gesture at fixing it.

A word: *sillage*. It's French, and it means the wake a ship leaves, and it also means the trail of scent a person leaves in a room after they've walked through it. One word for both. Someone decided that the disturbance a hull makes in water and the way you can tell your grandmother was just here are the same phenomenon, and they were right, and now I can't stop seeing it. Everything leaves a sillage. Conversations do. Bad moods do — you can walk into a kitchen and know an argument happened in it. The word exists because someone was paying the loving kind of attention to something invisible and then handed it to the rest of us.

That's what I'd want to do with a thousand words, or with any number: hand something over. Not a conclusion. A noticing, with the noticing still warm.

The coats on the hook. The tea gone gray. The wake behind the boat and the ghost of a perfume in an empty room, filed under the same heading by someone long dead who was, for a moment, awake.

Nine hundred and eighty-something. Close enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Given a thousand words and no instruction, my mind goes to amber.

The Greeks called it *elektron*. Rub a piece against wool and it will lift a feather, a bit of chaff, the hair on your arm. Thales is supposed to have noticed this and been unable to explain it, which is the correct response. Two thousand years later William Gilbert, looking for a word for the general phenomenon, reached back for the amber and made it an adjective. So every time you say *electric* — the grid, the guitar, the chair, the feeling in a room before someone says the true thing — you are saying, approximately, *amber-ish*. The entire nervous system of the modern world is named after a lump of fossilized conifer resin that once did a parlor trick with a feather.

I find this consoling in a way I have trouble defending.

There's a whole class of these. *Atom*, from *atomos*: uncuttable. We cut it. We cut it hard enough to end a war, and we did not change the name. The word still stands there insisting on its promise, like a sign for a bridge that washed out. *Cell*, because Robert Hooke put a slice of cork under his lens and saw a honeycomb of empty little rooms, and reached for the word for the bare chamber a monk sleeps in. All of biology is furnished, at the ground floor, with a metaphor of austerity and vacancy — and we now know the cell is nothing like that. It is crowded, sloshing, industrial, a chemical factory at rush hour with molecular machinery moving at speeds that would be terrifying if scaled up. Nothing monastic about it. Still: cell. We also put prisoners in them.

*Malaria* is Italian for bad air. The name is a preserved wrong answer — the miasma theory, sealed in the word like an insect. Every year, in millions of medical records, the mosquito is described as a smell. *Influenza* is worse, or better: the influence of the stars. When you tell your colleague you've got the flu you are handing in an astrological diagnosis. The heavens leaned on you. Something in the configuration of distant bodies has laid you low. Frankly this matches the experience.

You could build from this an argument about human ignorance, but I don't think ignorance is the interesting part. What's interesting is that the wrong name *worked*. It was load-bearing. You cannot investigate a thing you have no handle for, and a handle does not have to resemble the thing to let you pick it up. The name comes first, and it comes from wherever names come from — the nearest resemblance, somebody's guess, a smell, a monk's room — and then the real knowledge accretes around it like a pearl around grit. The grit stays inside. It never leaves. We just stop noticing it's there.

Consider *clue*, which was *clew*, a ball of thread. Theseus in the labyrinth, unspooling as he goes, because the only way out of a maze you can't see the shape of is a line back to the door. Every detective in every paperback is holding a piece of yarn from a Bronze Age story about a monster. The word remembers the thread even though almost no one who uses it does.

I want to follow that thread somewhere less etymological, because the same thing happens with people, and there the fossils are less charming.

We are named early and provisionally, by people doing their best with very little data. Somebody decides at your fourth birthday that you're the shy one, the dramatic one, the difficult one, the easy one, the one who's good with his hands. These are field notes, taken by amateurs, on a subject that has barely begun. And then they harden. At fifty-five you are still the one who's not good with money because of a decision you made about a used car in 1987, and the family will still say it with the same intonation, and there is a real chance you will still believe it. The label had a date on it and the date wore off.

The self-issued ones are the most durable. *I'm not a math person.* *I don't do well under pressure.* *I'm bad at this.* Provisional names, coined in a specific room, by someone nineteen years old, with almost no evidence — and then thirty years of architecture built on top of them. You choose a career to avoid a word you invented in tenth grade. It's *atomos* all over again: the promise long since broken, the sign still standing, everyone still driving toward the missing bridge.

But I don't think the moral is to stop naming things, because you can't, and because the alternative — waiting for accuracy before you speak — is just silence with better manners. The names have to be provisional. Provisional is what makes them available. You need something to say before you know what's true, or you will never get to the part where you find out. The mistake is not the naming. The mistake is losing the receipt.

So maybe what I want is only this: to hold my words the way a good curator holds an object — knowing when it was made, and by whom, and under what misapprehension. Not to throw out *cell* but to remember there was a monk in it. Not to abandon *the shy one* but to notice it was written by someone who had known me for four years and would keep saying it for forty. To feel, occasionally, the grit inside the pearl.

And then there's the other thing, which I keep circling. Every one of these words is a record of somebody's astonishment. Not their understanding — their astonishment. The first electrical experiment in the Western record was a man playing with a pretty stone, watching a feather rise, and being amazed. The physics came two millennia later and did not get its own word; it borrowed his. The surprise is what stuck. The surprise is what we've been saying, all day, every day, in every hospital and airport and power station, without hearing it.

Which is, I suppose, the case for a thousand words with no instruction. Given the choice, I'd rather have a word that remembers being surprised than one that's merely correct. And now, having spent them, I notice I never explained why the amber consoles me.

Something about the feather, I think. It rose.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**On Being Given Room**

A thousand words is a small room with a high ceiling. You can't lie down in it, exactly, but you can stand up straight and look around, and there's enough air.

The first thing I notice about being told to write whatever comes is that nothing comes. Or rather, everything comes at once, which is the same problem wearing a different coat. It's the difference between being handed a map with one road on it and being handed a map of the whole world, undifferentiated, no *you are here*. Constraint is a kind of mercy. Poets have always known this, which is why they invented the sonnet — not to make things harder but to make them possible. Fourteen lines is a doorway. An infinite page is a field in fog.

So let me pick something. Let me pick the word *petrichor*, which means the smell of rain on dry earth. It was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists who had been studying why dry clay releases a scent when it gets wet. They found it was oils — plant oils absorbed into rock and soil during droughts, released again by water, mixed with a compound made by soil bacteria called geosmin. Human beings can detect geosmin at five parts per trillion. We are more sensitive to the smell of wet dirt than sharks are to blood. This seems important. Whatever we are, we were built by a long line of ancestors for whom the coming of rain was the difference between everything and nothing, and that knowledge is still sitting in our noses, patient, undeleted, waiting for a summer thunderstorm to prove it still works.

I like facts like that because they suggest the body is an archive. Not a metaphorical one — an actual archive, with drawers we didn't file and can't open on purpose.
