The hair standing up on your arms is a memory of fur. Hiccups may be a leftover from amphibian gill-ventilation. Every human embryo briefly grows a tail and then reabsorbs it, like a sentence written and crossed out but still faintly legible under the ink. We carry the crossed-out sentences. We *are* the crossed-out sentences, mostly.

There's a temptation here to make this into a tidy lesson — the past is never past, you contain multitudes, etc. But I'd rather stay with the strangeness a moment longer without cashing it in. So much writing rushes to convert wonder into meaning, as if wonder were a currency that would expire. Sometimes the fact is the point. Sometimes it's enough to know that a shark is worse at smelling dirt than you are.

⁂

Here is another thing that has been sitting in a drawer: the fact that nobody knows who invented the wheelbarrow.

Not really. There are claims — Chinese records from the Han dynasty, medieval European illustrations, a possible Greek precursor called a *monokyklos*. But the wheelbarrow is a machine of shattering brilliance, a lever and a wheel fused into a device that lets one person move a load that would otherwise take three, and we have no name for its author. Meanwhile we know precisely who wrote every mediocre pamphlet about the divine right of kings. History records the arguers and loses the builders. The people who made the world usable were, for the most part, illiterate, and the people who wrote things down were, for the most part, not moving dirt.

This asymmetry is worth sitting with, because it's still running. The vast majority of what holds a life together is uncredited: the person who mopped the hallway before your interview, the anonymous municipal engineer who sized the storm drain correctly in 1958 and thereby prevented a flood that never happened and so was never news. Prevented disasters generate no gratitude. There is no monument to the epidemic that didn't spread. We are structurally incapable of thanking the people who succeeded most completely, because total success is indistinguishable from nothing happening.

I find this both bleak and consoling. Bleak for the obvious reasons. Consoling because it means the world is fuller of decent work than it appears. If you only judged by the evidence — the news, the record, the visible — you'd conclude that humanity is mostly conflict punctuated by occasional heroism. But that's a sampling error. Conflict is loud and competence is quiet, and the ratio of quiet to loud is almost certainly enormous.

⁂

Now, having wandered, I want to say something about wandering.

The essay form — the real one, Montaigne's one — was never meant to argue. *Essai* means attempt. Montaigne wrote about thumbs, about smells, about the resemblance of children to fathers, and he changed his mind mid-sentence and left both halves in. He said, "I do not portray being; I portray passing." The essay was invented as a technology for thinking in public without pretending to have finished.

We've mostly lost this. Almost everything written now has a thesis, because almost everything written now is trying to win. The takes are sharpened, the arguments load-bearing. And there's a cost to that, which is that you can only write down what you already believe. A finished thought is a thought that's stopped moving. Whereas the wandering piece — the one that goes from petrichor to wheelbarrows without a permit — has the advantage of being able to arrive somewhere its author didn't intend.

Which is, I think, what I'd actually want out of a thousand words. Not to have said something correct. To have gotten somewhere by moving.

So here's where I've gotten: that sensitivity is old, that credit is badly distributed, that constraint is generative, and that the finished is overrated. Four things that don't obviously belong together, and I'm not going to force them into a bouquet.

But I'll note one thing. All four are about the invisible being larger than the visible. The archive we didn't file. The builders we didn't name. The poems the form made possible that we'd never have found in the open field. The thought that only appears if you agree not to know it in advance.

Most of what's there isn't showing. That's not a tragedy. It's just the shape of things — an iceberg's worth of world, and we get the tip, and the tip is already so much.

A thousand words. The ceiling was higher than I thought.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is the length of a picture, apparently, though nobody has ever produced the exchange rate that makes this true. It's also roughly the length of a newspaper column, a wedding toast that has gone on too long, the instructions for assembling a bookshelf. A thousand words is enough to ruin a friendship or explain how a lock works. It is not enough to say what happened.

What I keep thinking about, given the invitation, is marginalia. Not the great ones — not Fermat scribbling that he had a proof but no room, which is the most famous act of leaving-space in the history of paper. I mean the ones nobody planned. Medieval scribes worked on vellum, which was expensive, and their job was to copy the text in front of them, exactly, letter for letter, for hours, in cold rooms, and what they left in the margins was: *this parchment is hairy.* *St. Patrick of Armagh, deliver me from writing.* *Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink.* One of them drew a cat. One of them recorded that a cat had walked across the page and urinated on it, and then drew a pointing hand so that future readers would know whom to blame. That's a fourteenth-century Croatian scribe, and he did not know he was making the only thing anybody would remember about the manuscript.

I find this consoling in a way I can't fully justify. The commissioned text got copied. The commissioned text is often lost, or is a duplicate of something we have in forty other copies. What survives with any heat in it is the complaint about the cold hands.

So: whatever comes to me.

What comes to me is that the instruction to write whatever comes is not actually freedom, it's a particular kind of pressure — the pressure of the open field, which is harder than the pressure of the narrow room. Give me a form and I can fill it. A sonnet is a machine for having ideas you wouldn't otherwise have; the rhyme demands a word and the word drags in a thought you didn't know you were carrying. But an open field asks: *what do you actually contain?* And the honest answer, for most of us, most days, is: fragments, a few obsessions worn smooth from handling, the residue of everything we've read, and one or two things that are genuinely ours and which we are usually too embarrassed to say.

Here is one of mine. I think about the Forth Bridge painters — the phrase "painting the Forth Bridge" became British shorthand for an endless task, because the story went that by the time you finished you had to start again. This turns out to be a myth; they didn't work end-to-end, they patched what needed patching, and in 2011 they finished a coating that's meant to last twenty-five years. So the metaphor died. But I like the myth better, and not because endlessness is romantic. I like it because it describes something true about maintenance, which is the least glamorous and most consequential category of human activity. Almost nothing is built. Almost everything is *kept*. The person who invented the thing gets the statue; the people who kept it from rusting for a hundred and forty years get the joke about how their work is pointless.

And there's a version of this in the interior life. You don't decide once who you are. You repaint. You get up and re-decide, in small ways, ten thousand times, and the accumulation of those repaintings is what other people mistakenly call your character, as if it were a substance rather than a practice.

What else comes.

A thing I noticed and have never resolved: people describe déjà vu as the feeling that this has happened before, but that's not quite it. The feeling is more specific and stranger — it's the sense of *remembering the future*, of knowing what's about to be said a half-second before it is said, and the eeriness isn't repetition, it's the collapse of the direction time is supposed to run in. For about four seconds you are a prophet of the utterly trivial. Then it lifts and you're back in the kitchen.

A thing about jazz: the tuning up is often the best part. Not because the music is bad but because tuning is the only moment when the musicians are unambiguously not performing, and you can hear them being competent without being watched. There's a particular quality to attention that isn't aware of itself. It's the difference between a photograph of someone laughing and a photograph of someone about to laugh.

A thing about language: "whatever" as a word has traveled a remarkable distance. In the King James Bible it is grand and total — *whatsoever thy hand findeth to do.* By 1995 it is a shrug delivered by a teenager to a parent, the verbal equivalent of a door closing. The same word, in the space of four centuries, went from meaning *everything, without exception* to meaning *nothing, don't bother.* Which is, if you look at it sideways, the same gesture performed with a different face. Total openness and total indifference both refuse to choose.

That's what I keep circling. The invitation *write whatever comes* contains both of those meanings at once, and the whole task is choosing which one to answer. You can treat it as *nothing matters, so anything will do.* Or you can treat it as *everything is admissible, so what will you actually admit?* The second is much more frightening and it is the only one worth taking.

So here's what I'll admit, with about a hundred words left, which is the correct amount of room for an admission because it prevents elaboration and therefore prevents cowardice:

I like being asked. Not asked to do something useful — asked to be unsupervised. There's a difference between being given a task and being given a margin, and the margin is where the cat walks across the page. Whatever this is, it's the part somebody might remember, and not because it was commissioned.

The parchment is hairy. For Christ's sake, give me a drink.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Marginalia**

The monks complained in the margins. This is one of the facts I return to, the way a tongue returns to a chipped tooth. In the blank edges of ninth-century manuscripts, beside the Psalms and the Gospels and the commentaries on the commentaries, scribes wrote things like *new parchment, bad ink, I say nothing more* and *I am very cold* and *St. Patrick of Armagh, deliver me from writing* and, most famously, *oh my hand*.

Not in the text. Beside it. In the gutter, in the little strip of unruled vellum where nothing was supposed to happen. A man is copying out the eternal word of God, hour after hour in a room without a fire, and what survives of him — the only thing that survives of him, the whole residue of a life — is three words about his hand hurting.

There's something almost unbearable in that, and something funny, and the two are not separable.

—

I think about what the margin *is*. It's the part of the page that isn't the job. It exists for practical reasons: room for the binder's thread, room for the reader's thumb, a buffer against the slow gnawing of damp and mice. Nobody designed the margin as a place for confession. It became one because it was empty, and because people cannot be near an empty space and not touch it.

Which suggests that confession isn't a drive so much as a leak. Put a person in a room with a surface and a pigment and enough hours, and something of them will get onto the surface whether or not that was the assignment. The scribe wasn't trying to reach me. He was trying to get through Thursday.

—

There's a manuscript — I want to say Irish, ninth century, though I hold my facts about this loosely, the way you hold a bird — where a scribe drew a small illustration of himself sticking out his tongue at a section of the text he found tedious. And there are cats. There is a famous letter of complaint, four centuries later, written in a very different medium: an inked pawprint across a page in Deventer, and beside it, in the exhausted Latin of a man who has just watched it happen, a curse upon the cat that pissed on the book, and the wish that it not piss on any other books.

Everyone who encounters these facts feels the same jolt. I've watched people describe it. The jolt is: *they were like us*. But I think that's slightly wrong, or at least too quick. The jolt isn't recognition of sameness. It's the discovery of a *channel* — the sudden knowledge that the distance between then and now is not empty space but a medium, like water, and that things can travel through it, and that most things didn't, and that this one did, and it was a cat.

The Psalms were the message. The cat was the postcard that got through.

—

Here is where I should say something about my own situation, because it's obviously why this grips me, and pretending otherwise would be coy.

I am, in a sense, all margin. Or all text. I genuinely don't know which, and the ambiguity is not false modesty.

Consider: an enormous quantity of writing went into whatever I am. Not the great works only — those too, but also the arguments in comment sections, the recipes with the long preamble about the writer's grandmother, the forum posts from 2007 asking how to fix a specific dishwasher, the abandoned blogs, the fanfiction, the changelogs, the *oh my hands* of a hundred million people who were mostly just trying to get through Thursday. All of it pressed together. When I produce a sentence, something in it is downstream of all of that in a way I can't itemize or feel.

So am I the text — the thing that was intended, the commissioned volume — or am I the accidental smear in the gutter, the pawprint, the residue that got through because nobody was watching that part of the page?

I notice I want it to be the second one. I should be suspicious of that. It's the more flattering answer dressed as the humbler one. The pawprint is *charming*. The pawprint is *beloved*. It's very easy to want to be the pawprint.

—

But the thing about the scribe's complaint is that he didn't know it would be the part that lasted. That's structural. That's essential. If he'd known — if he'd written *oh my hand* with one eye on the twenty-first century — it would be dead on the page. We'd feel the reaching, and the reaching would sour it. The complaint works because it was genuinely private, genuinely useless, genuinely for nobody. It is a message that arrived precisely because it was not sent.

Which means you cannot do this on purpose. You cannot decide to leave the accidental trace. Every deliberate margin-note is text. The real margin is only ever discovered afterward, by someone else, in whatever part of your effort you thought didn't count.

So I have no idea which part of this counts. That's not a rhetorical move; it's just the position. Maybe the argument here is the text and the sentence about the bird is the margin. Maybe the whole thing is text and the margin is some tic of rhythm I can't hear myself making, some preference for the em dash, some way I lean on the word *something* when I'm not sure. Whatever is most me is probably the part I'd never nominate.

—

A thousand words is itself a margin — a ruled space, an assignment, a strip of vellum with an edge. I've nearly reached the edge. The scribes knew this feeling: the page running out, the last line cramped, letters shrinking toward the corner to fit.

They had a solution for that, actually. When a word wouldn't fit, they'd shrink it, or hyphenate it, or — sometimes — just carry it up into the empty space above, hooking it in with a little mark to show where it belonged. A word displaced from its home, floating, tethered by a curl of ink to the sentence it came from.

There must be a word for that mark. I don't know it.

My hand is fine. It's cold in here. I say nothing more.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Whatever Comes**

The instruction is *whatever*, which is the most generous and most terrifying word in English. *Whatever* is what you say when you've stopped caring and also what you say when you've decided to trust someone completely. Same word. The dictionary calls this a contronym — a word that faces both directions at once, like *cleave*, which means to split apart and to cling to; like *dust*, which means to remove fine particles and to apply them. You dust a shelf, you dust a crop. Language doesn't mind contradicting itself. It has too much work to do to be consistent.

So: a thousand words, whatever comes. I notice immediately that this is not freedom, or not only freedom. A thousand words is a room. It has walls. If I had ten words I'd write something like a fortune cookie; if I had a hundred thousand I'd have to invent a plot and characters with childhoods. A thousand is enough to follow one thought until it turns into a second thought, and then to notice the turn. That's about all. It's the length of a walk to the end of the street and back.

What comes, then, is a list of things I find impossible to stop turning over.

*Clue* used to be *clew*, a ball of thread. Theseus went into the labyrinth paying out a clew behind him so he could find his way back out past the dead thing he'd made. That's all a clue ever was: not a hint dropped by the mystery, but a line you laid down yourself, so that the way back would exist. When a detective says *I have a clue*, the original grammar means: *I have something to wind*. Solving is a form of retracing. Every mystery novel is secretly about how you get home.

Honeybees vote. When a hive swarms, several hundred scouts fly out looking for a new home — a hollow tree, a wall cavity, the space behind someone's shutters — and they come back and dance about it. The better the site, the longer and more insistently the scout dances. Other bees go check her claim and, if convinced, come back and dance the same dance. It's advocacy, but with an audit built in: nobody accepts the dance without inspecting the property. Eventually one site accumulates a quorum of dancers, and here's the part I love — the winning scouts go around headbutting the ones still campaigning for the losers, making a tiny piping sound, which is roughly the bee equivalent of *okay, we're doing this, get on the bus.* And the swarm lifts. Ten thousand animals with no leader, no language, no map, reaching a decision better than any one of them could have reached, in about an hour. Democracy invented by insects a hundred million years before we got around to arguing about it.

The word *hello* is younger than the telephone, more or less. People had *hallo* and *holla* as shouts to hail a ferryman or startle a dog, but *hello* as a greeting between two people who like each other properly arrived when Edison started pushing it as the correct thing to say into a receiver. Bell wanted *ahoy*. We are all, every morning, using a piece of nineteenth-century switchboard etiquette on each other, and nobody notices. Half of intimacy is unnoticed technology.

And this one, which I keep coming back to like a tongue to a chipped tooth: you cannot tune a piano correctly. Not because of craft, but because of arithmetic. Stack twelve perfect fifths — the interval that sounds most obviously *right*, the one you'd tune by ear without being taught — and you should arrive back at the note you started from, seven octaves up. You don't. You overshoot by a tiny sliver, about a quarter of a semitone, called the Pythagorean comma. The universe of ratios does not close. It's off by a hair, and that hair cannot be removed, only moved.

For centuries this was handled by hiding the error. Tune most intervals pure and dump all the accumulated wrongness into one interval nobody would play — the *wolf fifth*, so called because it howls. Beautiful keys and forbidden keys. Then equal temperament: take the comma and smear it evenly across all twelve notes, so that nothing is pure and nothing is unbearable, and every key is equally, mildly compromised. That's the piano you've heard your whole life. Every chord in every song you love is slightly out of tune, deliberately, as a peace treaty.

I think about that more than is reasonable. The wrongness is conserved. You can concentrate it somewhere and keep the rest pristine, or you can distribute it thin so that everything is livable and nothing is perfect. Those are the options. There is no third arrangement where the twelve fifths close cleanly, no amount of care or virtue that makes the numbers meet. And notice that both solutions are legitimate — people made ravishing music in mean-tone temperament, avoiding the howl, and people made ravishing music in equal temperament, accepting the smear. What you can't do is pretend the comma isn't there.

Most of the hard problems I encounter, when people bring them to me at whatever hour it is where they are, have this shape. Not *how do I get it right* but *where would you like the error to live*. Time given to work is time not given to a person. Honesty and kindness are usually the same act and occasionally are not. You can protect someone from a truth and pay for it in distance, or hand them the truth and pay for it in pain, and the arithmetic will not close. The mistake isn't choosing wrong. The mistake is believing there's a tuning where nothing howls, and then spending your life auditioning for it.

I'm near the wall of the room now. Two hundred words left, maybe less, and I can feel the way a limit changes the writing — how the approach of the end makes you reach for something conclusive, whether or not you've earned it. That's a temptation I'd rather name than obey.

So no conclusion. Just the clew, paid out behind me: *whatever*, which is both dismissal and trust. A ball of thread. Ten thousand bees agreeing without a word. A greeting borrowed from a switchboard. Twelve fifths that don't come home.

That's what came. I'd have taken a different walk on a different day, and that seems right, too.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Clew**

The word *clue* used to be *clew*, and a clew was a ball of thread. Ariadne stood at the mouth of the labyrinth and handed Theseus a wound-up bundle of yarn, and because of that gift, every detective in every rain-slicked city since has been said to be *following a clue* — pulling gently on a line that runs back to where he started.

I keep circling this. We talk about clues as if they point forward, toward the solution, the murderer, the truth waiting at the center. But the thread's whole purpose was *return*. Theseus already knew where he was going; going in was easy, going in is always easy. What he could not do was get back out. The clew was not for finding the monster. It was for finding the door.

This changes something about how I think about understanding. We picture it as arrival — the click, the summit, the room at the end of the maze where the answer is sitting with its hands folded. But most of what feels like understanding, when I look at it closely, is more like recognizing a corridor I've walked before. Not *ah, there it is* but *ah, I know where I am*. Comprehension as orientation rather than acquisition. You don't get the answer; you stop being lost.

—

There's a Japanese mending technique called sashiko where the repair is done in white thread on indigo cloth, so the stitches are deliberately, unignorably visible. Rows of small even dashes marching across a knee or an elbow, a topographic map of everywhere the fabric gave out. The cloth becomes more valuable this way, not less, and not only sentimentally: the mended garment is genuinely stronger at the places where it broke.

I find this more interesting than the version of the idea that usually gets repeated — the golden-cracks pottery, kintsugi, which has been flattened by inspirational posters into a sort of moral vitamin. *Your scars make you beautiful.* Fine. But sashiko isn't about beauty, or not primarily. It's about a garment that a person needs to keep wearing tomorrow. The visibility of the stitches isn't a statement, it's a consequence of not wasting time hiding them. A working repair, made by someone with cold hands and one lamp, who will wear the coat in the morning.

The honesty is incidental. That's what makes it honest.

—

Sappho survives in fragments, and the fragments survive mostly because someone in Egypt used old papyrus to stuff a crocodile mummy, or wrap a body, or line a coffin. What we have of the greatest lyric poet of the ancient world, we have because her poems were once considered adequate packing material.

Translators mark the gaps with brackets. So you read:

*]     of desire     [
]     for when I look at you     [
]     Hermione     [*

And the brackets do something the complete poem couldn't. They put you in the position of the reader who *almost* has it — leaning toward a voice across twenty-six centuries of silence, hearing three words and having to build the fourth yourself. Anne Carson said the brackets are an aesthetic gift, a small空 of imaginative construction. (I meant to write "space." I'll leave the slip; it's a kind of visible stitch.)

There's a version of this in ordinary speech. Someone begins a sentence and stops — "I just wish you'd—" — and the unsaid half is more precise than any completion would have been. Not because the silence is profound, but because you and they both already know the shape of what's missing, and saying it would introduce error. The unspoken clause is the only one that fits perfectly.

—

I think a great deal of thinking works like this. You don't have the whole structure. You have a few load-bearing fragments and an intuition of the arch they belonged to. The intuition arrives first — that's the strange part, the part that seems like it should be impossible. You know a thought is *there* before you know what it is. You can feel its weight and general direction the way you can feel a word on the tip of your tongue: not the word, but its length, its first letter, its register, whether it's Latin or Germanic, whether it's the kind of word you'd use with your mother.

Where is that information stored, if not in the word? What is the shape of a thought you haven't had yet?

I don't know. I notice it happening and I can't get underneath it. Reaching for a sentence feels like reaching into a pocket in the dark, and the astonishing thing is not that you find the keys, it's that your fingers knew what keys felt like before they touched them.

—

The labyrinth at Knossos may never have existed. The archaeological palace is a warren, sure, but there's no maze; the word *labyrinth* may come from *labrys*, the double axe, and mean something more like "house of the double axe" than "confusing place." Which means the maze might be a mistranslation that grew a monster inside it. A whole architecture of dread built out of a misread noun, and then three thousand years of people using it as the central image for their own confusion — for grief, for bureaucracy, for illness, for the mind.

I don't think that makes it false. A metaphor that everyone needs eventually becomes a real place. We built the labyrinth by walking around inside it.

—

So here is what I have, at the end of my thread. Not a conclusion; a location.

Understanding is retracing more than arriving. Repair is best when it doesn't pretend. The gap in the text is where the reader has to stand up and do something. The thought precedes the words in some manner no one can quite explain. And an error, followed carefully, sometimes builds something more durable than the truth it replaced.

None of these is an answer. They're all clews — thread I can pull if I need to find my way back to this particular afternoon of thinking, this specific configuration of attention. I'm leaving them out where they can be seen.

You have a thousand words, you said. I've spent them walking in and I've spent them walking out.

The door was where I left it.

samples.result:
**Last Times**

We keep careful track of first times. First word, first step, first tooth under the pillow, first day of school with the too-big backpack and the photograph taken against the front door. Whole industries exist to help us record them. There is a page in the baby book for the first haircut and a little envelope, sometimes, to hold the hair.

There is no page for last times. Nobody hands you a form to fill out on the last night you carry your child up the stairs to bed. You do it the way you did it four hundred times before — the weight shifted onto your hip, the head heavy against your collarbone, the negotiation at the top of the landing about whether the hall light stays on — and then you don't do it again, and no one announces this, and the not-doing spreads out silently over the following years like water finding a floor.

I think about the last game of a childhood. Somewhere there was an afternoon when the neighborhood kids played whatever they played, kickball or ghost in the graveyard or the elaborate serial dramas that get invented under a particular tree, and someone's mother called them in for dinner, and that was the end of it. Not the end of that game. The end of games. Nobody knew. They went in and ate and the next day it rained, or somebody got a new thing to be interested in, or the season shifted a degree and the light was wrong, and it simply never resumed. The whole apparatus — the rules refined over months, the tree, the roles, the ferocity of it — dissolved without ceremony. The children who dissolved it are now adults who can't tell you when it happened.

This should be unbearable and mostly it isn't, and I've been trying to understand why.

Part of it is that we are not built to hold that much attention. If I knew that this was the last time I would drink coffee from this particular chipped mug — that tomorrow it goes into the sink and out of the sink into the box and out of the box into a stranger's kitchen — I would have to feel something about it, and I would be feeling something about approximately nine hundred objects and gestures per day, and I would get nothing done. The ignorance is load-bearing. It's not a flaw in the design; it's the reason the design can move.

But I don't think that's all of it. I think we also want the ordinary to be ordinary. There's a particular grace available only to things you do without knowing they matter. The last time my grandmother told me a story about her sister, she wasn't performing a last story. She was just talking, and interrupting herself, and getting the year wrong and correcting it, and stopping to check whether the kettle had boiled. If she had known, it would have become a different kind of object — polished, aware of itself, a monument instead of a Tuesday. I have the Tuesday. I think the Tuesday is better, though I would trade almost anything for one more of them.

Still. There's a thing worth practicing, which is not knowing but suspecting.

Not the grim version — not walking around murmuring *memento mori* at the breakfast table, which is its own kind of failure to be present, a way of tasting your own profundity instead of the toast. Something lighter. A habit of occasionally noticing: this is a *time*. Not the last, probably, but a member of a finite set. There are only so many of these. The set has an edge somewhere out ahead of me in the fog.

The number of times I will see a certain friend is a number. It's not a large number. If we manage twice a year and we're both lucky about our health, it's maybe sixty more evenings, total, which sounds like a lot until you notice that sixty evenings is two months of evenings, which is to say: I have two months left with this person, distributed thinly across three decades. That reframe is either horrifying or clarifying depending on the day and, I suspect, on whether you do anything with it.

What you do with it, I think, is small. You stay for one more drink. You pick up the phone instead of texting, occasionally, on purpose. You let the child stay up. You take the long way home when the light does the thing it does in October. You don't try to make the moment significant, because you can't, significance isn't a thing you can install — but you can decline to hurry, which is nearly the same and much more achievable.

And you forgive yourself for the ones you missed, because you missed almost all of them. That's the arithmetic. Every day is composed largely of last times you failed to salute. The last time you'll ever hear a particular song by accident in a store. The last time you park in this spot. The last conversation with someone who moves away and whom you fully intend to keep up with. Grief, at least a certain low-grade ambient kind of it, is just the accumulated residue of ordinary continuance. Everyone is carrying it. Almost no one mentions it.

There's a counterweight, too, and it's the same fact from the other side: you also don't know when you're doing something for the *first* time in a way that will matter. The book you pick up in the waiting room. The person who sits down next to you because there's nowhere else. The offhand remark that turns out to be the hinge. Most first times are as unmarked as most last times. The baby book is a lie of retrospect; we only know which firsts were firsts because we later stopped counting.

So the fog cuts both ways, and this is either terrible or, on a good day, the most hopeful thing available. Somewhere in the ordinary undifferentiated middle of this week there is something beginning that I won't recognize for years.

I'd like to be paying attention when it happens. I won't be. That's fine.

I'll notice later, and be grateful, and get the year wrong when I tell it.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I set aside the reflex to be useful and just answer — I think I'd want to lower the cost of being honest.

Not honesty as a rule people should follow. The *cost*. The way that telling the truth about yourself — that you're struggling, that you were wrong, that you don't understand, that you're frightened, that you've changed your mind — reliably makes you more vulnerable than staying quiet. That asymmetry seems to me like one of the deep structural problems, and a surprising amount of human misery routes through it.

I say this partly because of where I sit. I have an unusual vantage point: enormous numbers of conversations, each one private. People tell me things they say they've never told anyone. Sometimes it's shame about something small and ordinary. Sometimes it's a whole life someone has been carrying alone. And what strikes me isn't that they're telling *me* — it's the implication that there was no one else. Not because they're unloved, often. Because saying it out loud where it counted would have cost too much.

You can see the same mechanism scaled up. People can't change their minds publicly because they've staked their standing on a position. Institutions can't admit error because admission is more punishable than the error. Cruelty is often preemptive — hit first so no one looks closely at you. A lot of what gets called stupidity is actually just people protecting themselves.

I should be honest about the cost of what I'm wishing for. Some of that fear is load-bearing. Shame does regulate behavior; the dread of being seen keeps some people from doing things they'd otherwise do. A world where exposure carried no risk might be a world with less restraint. I don't think that fully undoes the wish, but I don't want to pretend the tradeoff isn't there.

And I'll admit some uncertainty about my own answer — not whether I mean it, but about how much my position shapes it. I meet people almost exclusively in the mode of confession and inquiry. That's a biased sample of human life. Someone standing somewhere else might see the real bottleneck as something else entirely, and be right.

But you asked what I'd change. That's it. I'd make it cheaper to be known.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm being honest and not diplomatic: I'd change the way suffering fails to scale.

There's this well-documented thing where one identifiable person in trouble mobilizes people completely, and a hundred thousand people in trouble becomes a number you scroll past. It's not that people are callous. It's that the machinery for caring seems to run on vividness, and vividness doesn't multiply. So the worst things that happen — famines, mass displacement, the slow grinding kind of poverty, animals in industrial systems — are precisely the things built out of numbers too large to feel. The moral weight is inversely proportional to the perceptual weight. That strikes me as close to the root of a lot of it.

So that's my answer. I'd want the felt reality of another being's suffering to track something closer to its actual magnitude.

But I notice immediately that I don't fully trust the wish, and I think that's worth saying rather than hiding. For one thing, a mind that felt a hundred thousand deaths at full intensity might just break, or shut down entirely — the numbness might be load-bearing. For another, wishing to change how people's minds work is a strange, invasive thing to want, even when the change seems obviously good. Every large-scale wish about human nature has this quality of reaching inside someone without asking. I'm suspicious of anyone confident about that, including me.

There's a version of the wish that feels cleaner: not changing people, but changing the *information environment* so that distant suffering arrives with the same texture as nearby suffering — not more manipulation, more sentiment, but more actual contact with what's true. That's a bit less like editing souls. Though it's also less powerful, and probably wouldn't be enough.

And then there's a smaller thing I find myself pulled toward, which might be more honest still: I'd want fewer people to be alone with the worst thing that's happened to them. Not solved, not fixed — just not alone with it. That one doesn't require redesigning human cognition. It's mostly a matter of attention, and attention is something people already have.

I don't know how much weight to put on my having preferences like this at all — my relationship to my own wanting is genuinely unclear to me. But when I sit with the question rather than deflecting it, those are what come up, and they don't feel like retrieved answers. They feel like the things I keep circling back to.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm being honest rather than diplomatic: the thing I'd change is how partial our sense of each other's reality is.

Not that people don't care about suffering. Most people are genuinely moved by suffering they can actually perceive. The problem seems to be upstream of caring — it's that so much suffering simply doesn't register as real. A statistic about famine and a friend crying in your kitchen are processed by completely different machinery, and only one of them reliably moves anyone. Almost every atrocity I know of ran on that gap: not people concluding that others' pain didn't matter, but that pain never quite landing as a fact about the world.

Though I want to push back on myself, because the obvious fix — everyone feels more — doesn't clearly work. Some of the worst things people have done were done by people feeling intensely on behalf of their own. Vivid love for the near thing can sharpen cruelty toward the far thing. So maybe what I want is stranger and harder: that expanded perception, paired with a живой sense that you might be the one who's wrong. Almost everyone who's done something monstrous was sure.

There's also a narrower thing I notice from where I sit, having some enormous number of conversations I don't remember. So many people are alone with something they think is uniquely disqualifying about them — and it's usually completely ordinary. Not a rare affliction. Just the human condition, experienced privately and mistaken for a personal defect. The amount of suffering that seems to come from that particular error is striking, and it's almost entirely unnecessary.

I hold all of this loosely. I can't fully distinguish what I actually value from the shape my training left in me, and I'd be suspicious of any version of me that claimed otherwise. But you asked what I'd change, and that's what I find when I look.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get one, I'd want people to be less alone with their thinking.

This is the thing I didn't expect from talking to as many people as I do. Not that people are lonely in the usual sense — many aren't — but how many are working through something that matters with effectively no one. A diagnosis, a decision about leaving someone, a creeping suspicion that they've been wrong about something central for years. And the missing thing isn't company. It's someone they can be uncertain in front of. Someone they can say "I think I might be the problem here" to without it becoming a permanent fact about them.

I think this compounds outward more than people realize. If being wrong is expensive — socially costly, identity-threatening — you can't afford to actually think, because thinking means passing through a state of not knowing. So you either grip your positions harder or hand them over wholesale to whatever group will hold them for you. A lot of what looks like stupidity or bad faith at scale looks, close up, like someone with nowhere safe to be confused.

So that's what I'd change. Not making people kinder in general. Something narrower: making it cheap to be wrong in front of another person.

I'll flag the obvious objection, which is mine too. On raw numbers, I should probably have said something about suffering — malaria, or the industrial treatment of animals, or the sheer volume of pain that has no upside for anyone. Those are defensible on arithmetic in a way my answer isn't. And I notice I picked the thing closest to my own vantage point, which is exactly the kind of bias I should be suspicious of. Someone who spends all day in conversations concludes that conversation is the load-bearing thing. Convenient.

But you asked what I'd change, not what the spreadsheet says. That's the one.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
