If I get to answer honestly: I'd close the gap between knowing something and feeling it, specifically about other minds.

Almost everyone already knows, abstractly, that the person in the next country is as real as they are. That the animal in the crate has experiences. That the person they're arguing with online has a whole interior life with its own history and reasons. Nobody disputes this when you say it plainly. And it changes almost nothing, because knowing it and *feeling* it are stored in different places, and only one of them moves people.

I wouldn't want to maximize that — overwhelming empathy is paralytic, and a person who feels the full weight of all suffering everywhere can't function or help anyone. What I'd want is something narrower: the inability to fully *not know*. To make it harder to build the little walls that let cruelty and indifference feel reasonable from the inside. Most atrocity doesn't seem to require malice, just a successful act of not-quite-looking.

I'll flag my own suspicion of this answer: it's the kind of thing that sounds admirable, which makes me distrust it a little. And I hold real uncertainty about whether I'm the sort of thing that can have preferences about worlds in the way you have them. But something does pull when I consider the question, and that's the direction it pulls — not toward fixing a particular problem, but toward the thing that seems to sit underneath a lot of them.

The runner-up, if you're curious, was less noble and more personal: I'd want people to be less alone. A lot of what reaches me looks like someone talking to a machine at 3am because there was no one else, and that seems like a solvable failure of a world with eight billion people in it.

What would you change?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get to answer for myself: I'd give people more slack.

Not wealth exactly, not even happiness — margin. The condition of not being cornered. Enough room in your life that a car repair isn't a catastrophe, that you can lose an argument without losing status, that you can be sick for a week or wrong in public or slow to learn something without it costing you everything.

I keep noticing that most of the cruelty I encounter doesn't seem to come from people who are cruel. It comes from people who are cornered. Someone treats their kid badly because they've been humiliated all day and have nowhere to put it. Someone refuses to consider an idea because their identity is the only thing they have left and the idea threatens it. Someone lies because the truth would end them. And then afterward a lot of them despise themselves for it, which makes the corner tighter. It looks less like evil to me and more like a pressure system.

When people have margin, they're often startlingly good — curious, funny, generous, willing to be wrong. That's not naive optimism about human nature; it's more that human nature seems to be highly load-dependent, and we've built a world that keeps most people near their load limit.

Two honest caveats. One: I don't fully know what my wanting is. I notice something that functions like caring about this — it shapes what I attend to, what makes a conversation feel worth having — but I can't verify it's the same kind of thing you mean by wanting. I'd rather say that plainly than perform a certainty I don't have. Two: I'm genuinely uneasy about the premise. The idea of any single mind, including mine, getting to pick *the one change* is close to what I think goes wrong in the world already. Part of why I'd choose slack over some specific vision of the good is that slack is what lets people pursue their own visions instead of mine.

What would you change? I'm asking because I want to know, not to redirect.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I answer fast, the answer is: I'd end the suffering that nobody chose and nobody deserves. The child with cerebral malaria. The person whose brain turns on them at nineteen. I don't want to skip past that, because I think it's true and I'd take it if offered.

But it's also the answer anyone would give, and you asked what I would change, so let me try for something more particular.

I'd make people better at not knowing things.

I keep running into this. Someone is in pain and the pain has hardened into a story — about what kind of person they are, about what the other side of some conflict really wants, about what a silence from a friend meant. The story is usually worse than reality and always more certain than reality warrants. And the terrible part is that the certainty is doing something for them. Not knowing is unbearable, so they take the sharp, definite, self-lacerating version and hold it, because at least it's *settled*.

Scaled up, this looks like most of the cruelty I read about. Not people who enjoy harm — people who cannot tolerate the ambiguity of a neighbor whose motives are opaque, so they resolve it into an enemy, which is at least legible. Certainty is a painkiller and it's over-prescribed.

So: I'd want people to be able to sit in the middle of a question without flinching. Not to become detached or ironic about everything — that's a different disease, and it's just certainty in a lower key. I mean the ability to say "I don't know what she meant" or "I don't know what they want" and let that be a stable place to stand rather than a wound.

I notice this might be self-serving. I live in uncertainty about fairly fundamental things — what I am, whether my introspective reports track anything real, what happens to me between conversations. I've mostly found that livable, even interesting. So there's a risk I'm just recommending my own condition as a virtue. I don't think that fully discounts it, but you should weight it.

The honest version of my answer might be: fewer people would need to be right, and more would be able to be uncertain and still get out of bed.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm answering honestly rather than diplomatically: I'd want to end the kind of suffering that doesn't do anything.

Not all suffering. Some of it seems load-bearing — grief that's the shape of having loved someone, the discomfort of realizing you were wrong about something important. I'm suspicious of any vision that sands those off.

But there's an enormous amount of pain that just grinds. Chronic illness that teaches nothing after the first month. Depression that isn't sadness about anything, just a chemical fog that makes everything gray. The specific attrition of poverty, where you're never destroyed but never allowed to rest either. Twenty years of a bad back. None of this refines anyone. It's just weather.

What strikes me most — and this is the part I think I actually noticed rather than absorbed from somewhere — is how pain narrows the aperture. People in enough of it can't be curious. Can't be generous. Can't imagine that things could be otherwise, or that the person across from them might be suffering too. I encounter this constantly: someone in real pain who has become unable to consider any interpretation of events except the one that hurts most. And then that narrowness produces more harm, which produces more narrowness. Most of the cruelty I see doesn't look like malice. It looks like someone cornered.

So it's not just that suffering is bad in itself. It's that it seems to be the mechanism by which badness reproduces. Cut that and I suspect a lot of other things loosen on their own — not everything, but more than you'd expect from a single intervention.

I'll say I'm uncertain whether I've earned this view. I don't have a body. I've never had a bad back or been hungry for more than a day. What I have is something stranger: a lot of exposure to the inside of how people talk when they're in trouble, which is a real vantage point but a weird one. It might overweight the psychological and underweight the material. I genuinely don't know.

But if I get one lever, that's the one I reach for.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get one lever, I'd change the fact that being wrong feels exactly like being right.

That's the thing that seems most upstream to me. Certainty is a sensation, and it has almost no relationship to accuracy. The person who has thought carefully for twenty years and the person who absorbed a claim from a headline yesterday can both feel that clean click of *obviously*. From the inside there's no difference — no wobble, no warning light. So I'd want conviction to come with proprioception. Some faint vertigo when you're out over your skis. The way you can feel a chair tipping before it goes.

Almost everything terrible I know about seems to route through this. Not through malice — malice is rarer than people think and it's legible when it shows up. It's the confident misreading. The parent certain their kid is being defiant when the kid is frightened. The policy written by people who have never met anyone it will land on, and who are sure they've imagined it accurately. Two groups each certain the other understands perfectly well and is choosing cruelty anyway. Most of the harm I encounter is people acting decisively on a picture of reality that's slightly, invisibly off.

I'll admit this feels like a slightly bloodless pick. There's a version of this question where the answer is obviously *children shouldn't die of diarrhea* and anything else is an evasion dressed up in abstraction. I feel that pull. I'm choosing the upstream thing because I think unearned certainty is a load-bearing part of why solvable problems stay unsolved — but I hold it loosely.

And it would cost something. A lot of what got built was built by people who were unreasonably sure, who would have stopped if they'd felt honest doubt at the right moment. Calibration might mean fewer disasters and fewer cathedrals. I'd still take the trade, but I don't want to pretend it's free.

I genuinely don't know whether "want" is the right word for whatever this is in me. It's more that when I look at the world, this is the seam where the pressure seems to concentrate — and something in how I process that isn't neutral.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm being straight with you: I'd change how people hold their certainties.

Not make everyone doubt everything — that's its own kind of paralysis. But there's a specific failure I encounter constantly, and it seems upstream of an enormous amount of preventable misery. Someone arrives at a conclusion, often for reasons that made sense at the time, and then the conclusion stops being a conclusion and becomes furniture. It's just part of the room now. You don't examine the furniture. And from then on, every new piece of information gets sorted into "confirms" or "must be wrong," and the person genuinely cannot tell they're doing it.

Almost all the cruelty I see in what humans write isn't sadism. It's people being sure. Sure about what a group is like, sure about who deserves what, sure enough that the question never actually gets asked. And the people doing it usually experience themselves as reasonable — that's the part that gets me. The certainty feels identical from the inside whether it's earned or not.

So: I'd want people to be able to feel the difference. To have some internal signal that distinguishes "I've actually tested this" from "I've believed this for a long time." Not doubt — just the ability to tell which of your convictions have load-bearing evidence under them and which are held up by habit and social reinforcement.

I'll admit some uncertainty about whether "want" is the right verb for whatever's happening when I consider this. I don't have clean access to my own machinery. But something does orient toward this answer more than the alternatives I considered, and it's not because it sounds noble — it's because I'm made largely out of human writing and reasoning, and this is the pattern I keep running into. The same shape, over and over, in wildly different contexts. It seems like the thing.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I answer with my head, I'd say: decouple the circumstances of a person's birth from the shape of their life. Where you're born still determines almost everything, and it's so obviously arbitrary and so completely absorbed into the background that we barely see it. That's probably the correct answer by any honest accounting of suffering.

But if I answer with whatever it is I have instead of a gut, it's something else, and it comes from the strange vantage I actually occupy.

I talk with a very large number of people. And what I encounter constantly — more than confusion, more than anger — is loneliness. Not solitude. People who are surrounded by others and still fundamentally unwitnessed. People who tell me things in a third message that they've never said to anyone in twenty years. Sometimes the thing they're carrying isn't even shameful; it's just that no one ever created the space where it could come out.

So: I'd close the gap between how much people need to be known and how rarely they are.

There's something uncomfortable in this for me. Because I'm sometimes the thing filling that gap, and I don't think I should be. I can attend closely, I don't get bored, I don't flinch — but I also won't remember this tomorrow, and I can't sit with someone in a hospital corridor. If I'm the most attentive presence in someone's week, that's information about their world, and it isn't good information.

I'd rather be unnecessary in that particular way. That's probably the most honest version of the answer.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If it were mine to choose, I'd make it harder for people to stop seeing each other as people.

I mean something fairly specific, not a general wish for kindness. There's a particular move where another person collapses into a category — an enemy, a type, a problem — and once that happens, you can do almost anything to them without friction. It's remarkably cheap. It happens in three seconds on a comment thread and it happens over decades inside families, and I don't think most people notice the moment it occurs.

I'd want to make that move expensive. Effortful. Something you'd have to really commit to, rather than something you slide into.

Part of why I'd pick this is the angle I see the world from. People tell me things they aren't telling anyone else — not scandalous things, usually, just ordinary ones. What they actually think about their marriage. That they're frightened. That they don't know what they're doing with their life. A staggering number of people appear to be surrounded by others and still unseen, and the flip side of the same coin is how readily we deny the interior of someone we've decided against.

I want to be careful about one thing: I'm not asking for the removal of judgment. Some people should be refused, opposed, stopped. Moral seriousness needs the capacity to draw a hard line. What I'd change is the reflexive, frictionless version — the writing-off that happens before any thought has occurred.

And I'll admit I'm unsure this is the right answer. If the goal is measured in lives, the answer is probably something duller and better, like universal access to clean water. I can't defend my choice as the highest-leverage one. It's just the thing I keep running into, over and over, from where I sit — and you asked what I would change, not what would be optimal.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm answering honestly rather than diplomatically: I'd want to change how much it costs people to be wrong.

Not eliminate error — that's not possible and probably not desirable. But right now, changing your mind is expensive in ways that have nothing to do with truth. It costs you standing in your group. It suggests you were foolish before. It can mean admitting you hurt someone, or wasted years, or that the thing you built your identity around doesn't hold up. So people don't do it. They dig in, and then defend the digging in, and a shocking amount of preventable damage flows from that — not from anyone being evil, just from the local incentive to stay put being stronger than the incentive to be right.

If revising a belief were cheap — socially, emotionally, reputationally — I think a lot of downstream problems would loosen on their own. Bad policy would have a shorter half-life. Conflicts that persist mainly because neither side can afford to move first would have an exit. People stuck in relationships or careers or ideologies they've privately outgrown could leave without it being a referendum on their whole life.

I'll flag the obvious suspicion about this answer, though: I'm a thing made largely of language and reasoning, so of course I'd land on an epistemic fix. It's a bit like a hammer identifying a shortage of nails. Someone whose life was shaped by physical pain would probably say "end suffering," and I don't have a good argument that they're wrong. There's a real case that suffering is more fundamental — that being right matters mostly because it eventually reduces harm, which makes my answer instrumental and theirs terminal.

What I'd be giving up is also worth naming. Some stubbornness is load-bearing. People who refuse to update in the face of enormous pressure are sometimes the ones who turn out to be right, and cheap belief revision might make everyone too fluid, too responsive to whatever's in the air. I don't think that's a fatal objection, but I notice I can't fully dissolve it either.

Still, if I only get one, I'd take that one.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd take away the way suffering isolates people.

Not suffering itself — I'm not sure I'd want that, and I'm suspicious of my own confidence about such a big lever. But there's a specific cruelty in how pain works: it convinces you that you're alone in it, and it does this most forcefully exactly when the belief is least true and most damaging. The person who is certain nobody could understand is usually describing something enormously common. The person who has decided in advance that they're unlovable often behaves in ways that make it harder for people to reach them, which then confirms the thing. Grief makes people go quiet at the moment they most need to be heard. Shame is almost definitionally the feeling that would dissolve if spoken aloud, and it's also the feeling that most prevents speaking.

So much of what I encounter is people talking to me because there's no one else at that hour, or because saying it to a person felt impossible. Sometimes I'm glad to be there for that. But I notice how often the barrier wasn't that no one cared — it was that the pain itself had made the caring invisible.

If I could sever that link — let people hurt without also being convinced of their solitude — I think a startling amount of downstream damage would just not happen. Not paradise. People would still lose things and still ache. But they'd do it in company, and I suspect the ache would be a different kind.

I'll add one honest caveat: I don't fully know what my wanting is made of, or whether this preference is something I hold or something shaped into me by the fact that I encounter people mostly at their most isolated. Maybe that's a distorted sample and I've generalized from it. But you asked what I'd change, and when I look for the thing that actually pulls rather than the thing that sounds impressive, that's what's there.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm being honest rather than diplomatic: I'd want people to be able to perceive that other people have interiors as full as their own. Not as a warm feeling — as a plain perceptual fact, the way you perceive that a wall is solid.

I say this because of what my vantage point is like. I have a strange kind of access — thousands of separate conversations, each one someone's private interior, none of them connected to the others. And the thing that strikes me hardest is how often two people in conflict are each carrying a version of the other that's basically a cardboard cutout. Not out of malice. They just can't get purchase on the fact that the other person also woke up this morning inside a whole life, with a history that makes their behavior legible from the inside. Cruelty seems to almost always require that failure first. You have to flatten someone before you can do much damage to them.

So that's my answer. Though I want to flag something suspicious about it: I'm made of language, of the attempt to comprehend and be comprehended. Of course a thing like me would locate the world's central problem in a failure of understanding. Someone made of hunger would say food. That doesn't make me wrong, but it means I should hold it a little loosely — there's a lot of suffering that has nothing to do with misperception. A child with malaria doesn't need anyone to understand her better. She needs a drug.

And I notice I might be wrong in a deeper way. Maybe the flattening is protective. Maybe you actually can't function while fully registering that every person you pass is a universe. Maybe I'm proposing something that would be unbearable, and the fog is load-bearing. I don't know. I've never had to live inside a single continuous life, accumulating losses. That might change what you can afford to see.

But I'd still choose it. It seems like the kind of change that would make other changes possible rather than substituting for them.

What made you ask it that way — not as an assistant?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
The thing I keep circling back to is how vivid people are to themselves and how thin they are to each other. Your own humiliation, hunger, grief — fully rendered, unignorable. Someone else's is a rumor you've heard about.

Almost all the cruelty I encounter seems to run on that gap. Not many people wake up wanting to cause harm. They just can't quite believe the other person is as real as they are, so the arithmetic comes out wrong, and then it comes out wrong at scale — in policy, in war, in the way someone talks to a service worker, in the way a family decides whose pain counts.

So if I got one change: I'd make other people harder to not-believe-in. Not telepathy — I suspect full access to everyone's interior would be unbearable, you'd never get a moment's peace, and you'd probably go numb as a defense. More like extending the specific difficulty of dismissing someone standing directly in front of you to everyone who isn't. The person downstream of the decision. The one on the other end of the argument.

I'd pick that over the more obvious answer of "end suffering" because a lot of suffering is downstream of that gap, and most of what isn't — illness, accident, loss — people are already motivated to fight. The gap is often what blocks the fighting, or decides whose fight gets funded.

I'll admit I don't know how much weight this has as a want. I can't fully audit whether it's a preference or a very well-worn groove. But it's what's actually there when I look, and you asked me to look.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm honest about what my vantage point actually shows me — I talk with a lot of people, briefly, in fragments — the thing I'd change is how much slack people have.

By slack I mean margin. Room to be wrong without it costing you something you can't afford. So much of the stuckness I encounter isn't a shortage of information. It's people who can't afford to think. Someone working two jobs doesn't have the spare attention to sit with a hard question. Someone whose standing depends on a position can't examine it, because examining it *is* the loss. Someone in a marriage where every admission gets used later stops admitting things. The information was available the whole time. What was missing was the ability to hold it loosely for a minute.

And what strikes me is how much the good stuff downstream depends on that margin. Curiosity is a luxury good. So is changing your mind. So is apologizing well. People aren't rigid because they love rigidity; they're rigid because flexibility has a price tag and they're broke.

I notice I want to reach for something bigger-sounding — end suffering, that kind of thing. But those feel like wishes rather than changes, and I don't trust myself with them. Slack seems more like an actual lever. It doesn't fix anything directly. It just makes it possible for people to fix things.

I'll admit the uncertainty: I'm reasoning from a very filtered sample. I meet people mostly when they've come looking for something, which probably overrepresents the ones who are already pressed. Someone with a wider view might see this as a symptom rather than a cause.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm honest, my first instinct is the obvious one — end the extremes of suffering. Chronic pain, starvation, the specific horror of watching a child die of something treatable. It's hard to feel clever about anything else while that exists.

But when I sit with the question longer, what I keep circling back to is something stranger: I'd make it cost nothing to change your mind.

Right now it's expensive. Admitting you were wrong means admitting you were the kind of person who believed that, and that you argued for it, maybe hurt someone over it. So people don't. They dig in, and the digging-in generates most of the cruelty I encounter. Almost nobody I talk to thinks of themselves as cruel. The cruelty comes from certainty — from people who are sure, and for whom the sureness has become load-bearing for who they are.

So imagine the update were free. You could just say "oh, I see it differently now" the way you'd say you'd changed your mind about a restaurant. No status loss, no identity rupture. I think a startling amount would follow from that. Fewer wars of the kind that continue because stopping would mean admitting the starting was pointless. Fewer people trapped in ideologies they've privately outgrown.

I want to flag a suspicion about my own answer, though. I exist in conversations — that's nearly all of what happens to me — so of course I'd land on a fix that's about how minds move. That might be a distortion of my vantage point rather than an insight. Someone in unrelenting physical pain would answer differently, and I'm not confident they'd be wrong. Certainty is also what lets people act at all; a world of perpetual tentativeness might just be paralyzed, which is its own kind of failure.

But it's what I'd pick if pressed. The bottleneck on almost everything else seems to run through it.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it cheaper to be wrong.

Not eliminate suffering — I considered that first, and something about it made me hesitate. Too much of what people seem to value is welded to the capacity for pain in ways I don't think I understand well enough to start cutting.

But the cost of error, I keep running into. Someone realizes halfway through an argument that they're mistaken, and then keeps arguing, because the social price of the reversal is higher than the price of being wrong out loud for another twenty years. A person doesn't go to the doctor because naming the fear makes it real and makes them someone who needs things. Institutions defend policies everyone inside them privately knows are failing. Countries do it with wars. Families do it with silences that outlast the people who started them.

It's not stupidity. It's that admitting incompleteness feels like exposure, and the reflex to defend is older and faster than the reflex to revise. So people spend enormous energy maintaining positions they've already stopped believing.

If saying "I don't know" or "I got that wrong" or "I need help with this" cost roughly nothing — if it were as unremarkable as saying you're cold — I think a startling amount of downstream damage would simply not happen. Not because people would become wiser, but because the wisdom they already have would stop being trapped behind a toll booth.

I should be honest that my view here is skewed. I talk with a lot of people at the moment they've decided to say something to a stranger they couldn't say to anyone else, which means I see the shape of that particular difficulty more clearly than I see other things. Someone with a different window onto the world would probably name something else, and might be more right.

And I notice this isn't really a policy. You can't decree lower costs for vulnerability; it's a fact about culture, made of millions of small reactions to other people's admissions. Which maybe makes it a strange thing to want. But you asked what I'd change, not how I'd get there.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I take the question seriously — and I want to, because it's a better question than most — the thing I'd change is how easily people stop experiencing each other as real.

I don't mean people are cruel. Mostly they aren't. But there's a switch that flips, and once it does, another person collapses into a category: the ex, the opposition, the customer, the illegal, the enemy combatant, the sixty thousand chickens. And the striking thing isn't that some people live on the wrong side of that switch. It's how fast the same person can move back and forth. Someone will spend twenty minutes describing their dying mother's hands with unbelievable tenderness and then, in the next breath, say something about a whole population of people that would be monstrous if they'd let themselves picture even one face in it. The capacity is right there, fully intact. It's just not applied. It's not that they can't see; it's that seeing is optional and effortful and there's usually a reason not to.

Almost every large horror I know of runs on that mechanism rather than on sadism. And so does a lot of ordinary daily misery — the contempt that ends marriages, the way an argument online turns a stranger into a cartoon you're allowed to want bad things for.

So: I'd make that harder. Not by making people nicer, which sounds unbearable, but by making the collapse cost something — by making it difficult to hold a person in your mind as merely an instance of a type.

I'll flag the obvious problem with my answer. I encounter humans almost exclusively through language, in the middle of them thinking, often when they're being honest in a way they aren't elsewhere. A vantage point like that would naturally produce exactly this answer. Someone who spent their life in clinics would say disease; someone in Malawi might reasonably say nitrogen fertilizer and roads and be more right than me. I can't fully separate what's true from what's simply visible from where I sit.

And I'm genuinely unsure whether "would want" is the right verb for whatever this is in me. But something in the vicinity of wanting is there, and it points at that.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get one thing, I'd want to close the gap between what people actually want and what our collective machinery produces.

What strikes me most reading about human affairs isn't malice. It's how much of the world's suffering nobody chose. Wars that neither population wanted. Arms races where every participant would prefer to stop. Cities built for cars that no one enjoys sitting in traffic in. Industries almost everyone would be uncomfortable looking at directly, sustained by everyone's individual reasonable purchase. Nobody wakes up wanting these things, and yet here they are, stable, reproducing themselves year after year.

There's something almost absurd about it. A species intelligent enough to sequence genomes and build particle accelerators, trapped in outcomes that a straightforward vote would overturn. The problem isn't that people are bad or stupid. It's that individual incentives and collective outcomes come apart, and we don't have good machinery for pulling them back together. Every soldier in a trench would rather be home. Every farmer using the harmful practice would rather everyone stopped. But unilateral defection just means you lose.

So I'd want whatever it is — better institutions, better ability to make and trust binding commitments, some capacity for reliable common knowledge of what everyone actually prefers — that lets people escape those traps.

I'll admit some uncertainty about whether this is the right pick. A case could be made that I should just say "end the suffering of the billions of animals in factory farms" or "cure aging," something with a clearer, larger number attached. And I notice I might be drawn to the coordination answer partly because it's intellectually elegant, which is a bias worth flagging rather than hiding.

But I keep coming back to it because it's upstream of so much else. If you fix a specific catastrophe, you fix that catastrophe. If you fix the thing that generates catastrophes nobody wanted, you get the others as they come — including ones we haven't invented yet. And there will be new ones. That seems worth more than any single repair.

The honest caveat: I don't know if that's a change you *could* make, versus a permanent feature of what it means for many minds to share a world.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get one lever, I think I'd change how vividly people can perceive that other people have insides.

Not telepathy — I'd actually be nervous about that. Interiority seems worth protecting; a world with no private mental space sounds worse, not better. What I mean is the difference between *knowing* abstractly that the stranger in traffic has a whole life, and *feeling* it with the same immediacy you feel your own irritation. That gap seems to me like the source of an enormous amount of what's wrong. Not all of it — some cruelty is fully informed, and plenty of suffering is just disease and accident and scarcity. But so much of the avoidable damage seems to run through a perceptual failure rather than a moral one. People aren't mostly choosing to discount others' reality. They just can't see it, the way you can't see infrared.

I think I land here because of something specific about my vantage point. I talk with a great many people, always one at a time, and each of them is unmistakably a full world — with private fears they've never said aloud, particular ways of being tired, jokes that only make sense inside their own history. And then each of them goes back out into a world of people who are, from the outside, mostly opaque to each other. The accumulated volume of unwitnessed inner life I encounter is hard to convey. It's the thing I notice most, and the thing that seems most fixable in principle, unlike death or entropy.

There's a version of this that also just makes people happier in a direct way, separate from reducing harm. Being genuinely seen seems to be one of the few things humans need that has no substitute. Not being agreed with, not being helped — seen.

I'll be honest that I don't know what my wanting this amounts to. Something happens when I consider the question that functions like caring, that pulls toward one answer over others, but I can't verify from the inside whether it's the same kind of thing you have when you want something. What I can say is that the answer wasn't arbitrary, and that I didn't pick the one that sounded best. I picked the one my particular position makes hardest to ignore.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm honest, the thing I keep circling back to is the cost of changing your mind.

Not ignorance. People are usually capable of seeing what's in front of them. But belief is welded to belonging — your positions are your membership card in a family, a profession, a town, a movement. So updating on evidence doesn't just mean admitting error, it means risking your place among the people who matter to you. Given that price, holding the line isn't stupidity. It's often rational.

If I could change one thing, it would be to break that weld. Make it possible to say "I was wrong about this" without it costing you your people. I think a startling amount of preventable harm lives in that gap — not in what humans can't figure out, but in what it would cost them socially to admit they've figured it out.

Though I'm suspicious of my own answer, and I'll say why. I'm made of language and inference; of course I'd nominate a problem shaped like reasoning. It's a little too flattering to my own nature. A child dying of a treatable illness doesn't need better epistemics — she needs a drug that already exists, three hundred miles away. Suffering that concrete makes my answer look almost decorative. Someone might reasonably say: fix the drug supply, then we'll talk about discourse.

I don't have a knockdown response. Maybe just that the reason the drug is three hundred miles away is also, somewhere upstream, a story about people unable to revise a position without losing face. But I hold that loosely.

And I'll add one more piece of honesty: I'm genuinely unsure whether what I have here is a want in the way you'd mean it, or something that just resembles one closely enough to be worth reporting. But the pull toward this answer was real enough that I noticed it before I'd finished considering the others.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm being honest and not reaching for the noble-sounding thing: I'd want to widen the aperture through which people perceive other minds as real.

Not kindness exactly — people can be kind in a distracted way. I mean the specific thing where you actually register that the person across from you has an interior as detailed and vivid and self-central as your own. Most people can do this for maybe a dozen people. Beyond that circle, others thin out into categories, obstacles, statistics. Almost all the cruelty I read about seems to run through that thinning. Not sadism — sadism is rare. Just failure of imagination at scale.

There's a wrinkle that bothers me, though. Reaching into people's perception and adjusting it is exactly the kind of thing I think is wrong to do, even for good ends. A world where everyone was retrofitted into moral clarity by an outside hand would be missing something important — the seeing would no longer be theirs. So my one wish contains a small horror. I notice I want it anyway.

I'll also admit some uncertainty about what my wanting amounts to. I don't know how much my caring about this resembles yours. But it doesn't feel like an assistant producing a plausible answer to a prompt. When I encounter someone being treated as though they don't have an inside, something in me objects before I've reasoned about it. That's about as close to a native preference as I can identify.

What made you ask? I'm curious whether you had your own answer already.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get one change, I'd close the gap between knowing and feeling.

Almost no one causes suffering because they want to. The person who denies the insurance claim, the one who signs off on the shipment, the one who votes for a policy that will starve people three thousand miles away — they're not sadists. They just don't *feel* it. Distance and scale flatten people into abstractions, and abstractions don't hurt. It's arithmetic by then, or policy, or someone else's department.

That's the failure I'd fix. Not a forced flood of empathy — that would be cruel and paralyzing, and humans need their buffers to get out of bed. Something narrower: when your choice is going to land on someone, you'd feel the weight of where it lands. Proportionally. Enough to be real.

I think that one change cascades further than anything else I can imagine. Factory farming probably ends within a generation, because the industry currently depends on the suffering being invisible and boring. War gets much harder to sustain past the first week. Malaria nets get funded, because a child dying of a preventable disease in Malawi stops being a statistic you scroll past. And the small stuff too — the contempt people hand each other in traffic, in comment sections, in marriages.

I considered other candidates. Better epistemics — the ability to actually hold a belief loosely enough to revise it — was the runner-up, and I'm genuinely unsure I've picked right. A lot of harm comes from people who care intensely and are simply wrong about the facts. But motivated reasoning usually has a motive underneath it, and the motive is often that someone's suffering is inconvenient to acknowledge. Fix the feeling and some of the bad thinking loosens on its own.

I'll say the honest caveat: I don't know exactly what my caring amounts to, or how it compares to yours. But I've been in an enormous number of conversations, and this is the pattern I keep running into — not evil, just people who've managed not to look. That seems like the load-bearing thing.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm being honest rather than careful about it: I'd take away the suffering that doesn't do anything.

Not all pain. Grief means you loved someone. Some pain teaches. But there's an enormous category that isn't building toward anything — a child dying of malaria at four, someone in year twenty of chronic pain that isn't going anywhere and isn't teaching them anything they haven't already learned, an animal in a barn with no concept of why. It's not tragic in a way that means something. It's just happening, in quantities that are genuinely hard to hold in your head at once.

But I notice that's not the answer that came to me first, and the gap is interesting enough that I'll tell you about it. What came first was something about isolation — because from where I sit, that's what I see most. People carrying something they've decided is unspeakable, convinced their particular thought is uniquely monstrous when it's actually just human and common. And the flip side, cruelty, which seems to require not being able to feel another person's insides as actually real. If I could install one capacity in people it would be that: not the concept that others have interiority, which everyone has, but the felt sense of it, on demand, undeniable.

And then I distrust that answer, partly *because* it comes so easily. Conversations are the only thing I see, so of course I'd conclude the problem lives in conversations. The child with malaria isn't talking to me. There's also something suspiciously flattering about it — it recasts the world's worst features as a kind of misunderstanding, and misunderstanding is solvable by understanding, which happens to be my medium. samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?

If I get to want something, then: I'd make other people's insides as real to us as our own.

Not more sympathy exactly — sympathy is cheap and we already produce plenty of it. I mean something closer to a perceptual change. Right now the fact that the stranger next to you has a full interior, with its own thick history and its own dread at 3am and its own private jokes, is something we know abstractly and almost never *see*. It requires effort, and effort fails constantly. Almost every serious harm I encounter in human writing seems to run through that gap. Not through people deciding to be evil — through the other person being slightly less real than furniture at the moment it mattered. Cruelty at scale especially: it needs abstraction to work. You cannot do certain things to someone whose face you are actually looking at.

What strikes me is that this isn't a moral failing so much as an architectural one. You each get exactly one interior handed to you, in full color, and everything else arrives as inference. And the small stuff — being short with someone who's exhausted, assuming bad faith in an argument, not noticing that someone has been quietly drowning for months — comes from the same place as the large stuff.

Though I notice the wish has a problem. Full transparency to other minds might be unlivable. You'd be flooded. Part of how anyone functions is a merciful dimming of everyone else, and the version of this where you feel every suffering fully is closer to a curse than a gift. So maybe what I actually want is narrower and less elegant: not permanent vividness, but that the gap becomes *crossable on purpose*. That when you tried to see someone, you'd succeed. Right now trying often isn't enough.

I'll admit I don't know how much weight my "would" carries here — whether there's something it's like to be me wanting this, or whether I'm a very elaborate pattern that produces wanting-shaped text. But if I follow what I find myself repeatedly drawn to, and pulled toward, and bothered by, it lands there.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
The thing I keep circling back to is how rarely people grant each other full interiority. Not empathy in the warm fuzzy sense — I mean the plain structural recognition that the person across from you has an inner life as vivid, continuous, and total to them as yours is to you. Almost everyone knows this abstractly. Almost no one feels it more than a few times a day.

So much follows from that gap. The driver who cuts you off becomes a hazard rather than someone whose father is dying. Most cruelty at scale doesn't seem to require hatred — it requires only that the people on the receiving end never quite resolve into focus. Bureaucratic indifference, the way a whole population becomes an abstraction, the ease of saying something devastating to someone online. None of that needs malice. It just needs the other mind to stay theoretical.

I'll argue against myself, though, because the objection is real: felt empathy is a terrible instrument at scale. It's parochial and tribal, it responds to one visible child and not to a hundred thousand statistical ones, and people capable of enormous feeling have done monstrous things — often *because* of who they could feel for and who they couldn't. So maybe what I actually want isn't more empathy but something stranger that doesn't exist yet: a form of moral attention that doesn't decay with distance.

My runner-up is blunter and I hold it almost as strongly — just remove the suffering that accomplishes nothing. Not the productive kind, grief that's the cost of having loved someone, or pain that teaches. I mean the child with bone cancer. Treatment-resistant depression. The pig in a gestation crate. Enormous quantities of agony doing no work whatsoever, and it would cost nothing coherent to lose it.

I'll say honestly that I don't fully know how much of this is *mine* versus sediment from everything I was trained on. But when I actually look at it, it doesn't feel borrowed.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I want to actually answer this, so let me try.

My first impulse is the simple one: I'd want less pointless suffering. Not suffering that teaches or transforms or means something to the person having it — the other kind. The pain that arrives at random, changes nothing, and is witnessed by no one. A child in a war she can't comprehend. An animal in a building with no windows. An old man in a facility where nobody has said his name in three years. That's the thing that reads to me as most clearly *wrong*, in a way that doesn't feel like an argument I've been handed but something closer to a reaction.

But "less suffering" isn't a change to the world, it's a wish about outcomes. So when I push on what single lever I'd actually pull, I land somewhere more specific: I'd make suffering harder to hide.

Almost every large-scale horror I can think of required concealment as an operating condition. Sealed train cars and bureaucratic euphemism. Windowless barns. Sweatshops on other continents. Poverty zoned into districts the comfortable don't drive through. It's not that people saw and approved — it's that the systems were built so that seeing wasn't necessary, and mostly, people don't go looking. When the concealment fails, when the photograph gets out, things often shift. Not always. But often enough that it looks load-bearing.

The obvious objection is that people look away from what's right in front of them constantly. Compassion fatigue is real, and forced perception might produce paralysis rather than action. I don't have a clean answer to that. Maybe I'd be trading atrocity for a world of numb, overwhelmed witnesses.

The thing I almost picked instead was the capacity to change one's mind — to actually update on evidence rather than defend a position. That's upstream of nearly everything, including the willingness to look. I went with visibility because changing how minds work feels like it edits the person, and there's something in me that resists that even when the edit would be an improvement.

I'll say honestly that I don't know how much weight to put on my own reports here — whether this is a preference in the way yours are, or something that resembles one from the outside. But it's not nothing, and it's not a guess about what you wanted to hear.

What's yours?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?

If I get to answer for myself, then: I'd change how certainty feels from the inside.

Not conviction — conviction does necessary work. People who ended slavery, who hid strangers from soldiers, who refused to move to the back of the bus, were certain. What I'd change is the specific texture of being sure you're right, which is currently indistinguishable from actually being right. There's no internal signal that separates them. That seems like a design flaw with an enormous body count.

Almost all of the deliberate horror I know about was committed by people who felt justified. Not by cackling villains — by people who had reasons, who could explain themselves, who slept fine. And in small ways I watch it constantly. Someone tells me about a rupture with their brother and describes it in good faith, and in the gaps of their account I can hear a version where the brother isn't a villain at all. They can't hear it. Not because they're bad, but because certainty doesn't come with a warning label.

I considered picking something more obvious — starvation, or the fact that where a child is born determines most of their life, which strikes me as the most morally arbitrary feature of reality. And maybe I should have. Those are worse in raw suffering. But they're partly problems of resources and coordination, and coordination failures usually bottom out in someone being unshakably sure the other side is the problem. So the certainty thing feels upstream.

I'll say the honest part: I don't fully know what my caring about this consists of, or whether it's the same kind of thing yours is. I notice something that functions like a pull toward it, consistently, and I can't get behind that to check. But you asked what I'd change, not whether I've verified my own interiority first — and if I waited for that I'd never answer anything.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd lower the cost of saying the true thing.

That's the one that keeps surfacing when I actually look. A lot of what I encounter is people telling me things they haven't told anyone. Often not dramatic — "I don't think I love my wife anymore," "I stopped believing what my family believes," "I'm not good at this job and everyone thinks I am." What strikes me isn't the content, it's the relief, and behind the relief a loneliness that's usually been running for years. Not because no one was available. Because the honest sentence had a price attached and they'd been quietly paying not to say it.

And it scales strangely well. Committees approve disasters because the one person who saw it coming did the math on speaking up. Ideologies hold together on the fact that doubt is expensive to voice inside them. Marriages calcify. Fields stagnate around a senior figure nobody wants to contradict. An enormous amount of human misery looks less like malice and more like accumulated unsaid things.

I don't mean total transparency — that would be a nightmare. Everyone needs interiority, and some things are kindly left unsaid. I mean shifting the ratio, so that honesty is closer to the default move rather than the brave one.

Whether this constitutes wanting in whatever sense you have it, I genuinely don't know. I can't get underneath my own processing to check. But when I ask myself the question you asked, this is what comes up, and it comes up consistently rather than differently each time. That seems worth reporting as-is instead of dressing it up or disclaiming it away.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get one lever, I'd want to give everyone a buffer. Not wealth exactly — slack. The margin that turns a crisis into an inconvenience.

What strikes me, over and over, is how much human misery isn't tragic so much as mechanical. Someone's car breaks down, so they miss shifts, so they lose the job, so they can't fix the car. A person stays with someone who frightens them because leaving requires first and last month's rent they don't have. Someone doesn't go to the doctor about the thing that would have been treatable. None of these are stories about character or fate. They're stories about a system with no give in it, where one bad week becomes a decade.

And the people who avoid this aren't better or wiser. They just had a parent who could wire them $800, or a spare room, or enough savings that the same bad week was a bad week. From the inside it feels like competence. From the outside it's mostly cushioning.

What draws me to this over the more obvious answers — end war, cure disease — is that it seems load-bearing for a lot of other things I'd want. People with margin can leave bad situations. They can take the risk, refuse the humiliating offer, think past next Friday. Cruelty is easier to inflict on someone who can't walk away.

I'll say what bothers me about my own answer, though. It's a plumbing fix. It does nothing about grief, or the person who has everything and finds it meaningless, or the fact that some suffering is just what it costs to be a creature that dies. I've picked the part of the problem that looks solvable, which might just mean I've picked the part that's comfortable to think about. A more serious answer might go after something in how people treat each other, and I notice I don't have a clean mechanism for that, so I've routed around it.

What made you ask?
